sections.h:
Giuseppe Falchi

SEVEN YEARS IN BOLIVIA
(1882-1889)

Memoirs of Sr. A. Camilla Valentini
former Superior General of the Daughters of St. Anne

Second edition, revised, enlarged and updated
edited by Sr. A. N. Sotgia

Rome 1990

The missionary vocation of the Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne was born with the Foundress's own vocation to religious life and is an integral part of her charism.

We find it expressed implicitly, yet essentially, in the few lines that Rosa Gattorno wrote on the night of her first inspiration (February 1864):

“4. Unmarried women and widows will be admitted; these... are to devote themselves - to the increase of our holy Faith - to the care of the sick in their homes - they will also take in girls in moral danger, whom they will teach Christian Doctrine and women's handiwork.”

The specific, concrete character of these charitable aims, which springs from the experience Rosa Gattorno lived daily as a Christian widow in the world, may perhaps seem limiting; but the first point, “the increase of our holy Faith,” goes beyond the horizons of time and space and echoes Jesus' final mandate to the Apostles: “Go and teach all nations.”

Once the Institute was founded, the rapid, immediate spread of its works of care for every form of poverty and suffering, without distinction of persons, places or situations, shows that Mother Rosa was firmly convinced that service rendered to man for the love of God is the unequaled way of making that very love evident and credible.

And it is on this proof of love that Faith is built and spreads.

It is no surprise, then, that barely twelve years after the foundation Mother Rosa was ready and willing to send her daughters across the Ocean, to countries known only as in fables, but inhabited by peoples certainly in need of help, among whom “the increase of our holy Faith” had to be promoted.

It is the sum of her vocation: charity and apostolate; mission and service. But it is perhaps even more significant that barely twelve years after the founding of the Institute the Foundress could count on daughters ready and willing to undertake such a journey for such a service, especially considering the unmistakable clarity with which the Franciscan Father Vincenzo Rocchi, commissioned by the Municipality of La Paz in Bolivia to find in Europe sisters willing to go to that city to serve in its two Hospitals, presented his request:

“... above all, that they be persons endowed with good will, not fickle but steadfast in their resolutions, faithful to their Vows, and determined even to shed their own blood if necessary; they must know that they will meet great difficulties and serious dangers at sea, on land and everywhere; all this will put to the test their vocation and their love for the dignity and purity of soul and body.”

And a little further on he insisted: “Firmness, constancy, courage and strength are needed, in a word, spirit.”

To accept such honest but peremptory conditions, Mother Rosa had to feel quite sure both of the radical nature of her Institute's charism and of the mettle of the daughters she was forming: a charism founded on a limitless capacity for self-giving and on a readiness to offer themselves even to the ultimate sacrifice.

Bolivia, in those years, must have seemed to lie at the ends of the earth: what distances to cover, what means of travel to use, what language to learn?

Trusting in God, Mother and daughters said yes.

Daughters chosen, of course, one by one, taking into account the maturity of their vocation, their capacity for dedication, their physical condition and a certain professional experience.

That the choice was sound is shown by the immediate success of the first group of sixteen sisters who, led by Father Rocchi and with Sr. A. Giuseppa Troni as superior, left Genoa on September 23, 1878, and arrived in La Paz on January 20, 1879.

A request for more sisters soon reached Mother Rosa, and the Mother set about meeting it, sending several more groups within a very few years.

A second expedition of ten sisters, again led by Father Rocchi, took place between December 1881 and February 1882, and a third, of twelve sisters, left the same year for Sucre, also in Bolivia. It is harder to count the departures that followed, and not only for Bolivia: by 1884 the Daughters of St. Anne had reached Brazil, and a few years later Peru and Chile. In 1886 they were called to Africa by the Italian Government to care for the soldiers in the military Hospital of Assab, in Eritrea.

God seconded Mother Rosa's missionary longing by sending ever more numerous vocations to Piacenza. And yet everything seemed too little to her, and with every departure for the mission lands her desire grew to go herself with her daughters, to give, with them, her whole self to all of humanity.

“Blessed are you, who for Jesus have crossed the sea and traveled a fine road so that you may become saints and, what is more, be ready to endure martyrdom,” she wrote on June 9, 1879, to the sisters who had just arrived in Bolivia with the first expedition.

And the mention of martyrdom was not prompted by sentimental exaltation. Two of the first sisters had already died, victims of a contagious disease caught in their first days of service at the Hospital of La Paz.

Such phrases abound in her letters: “I am dying with the desire to go to America...”.

“I won't tell you how strong my temptation is to join you; I would go so far as the folly of flying...”.

Nor was she driven by the lure of adventurous journeys or unknown lands, for the Mother suffered greatly when traveling, even with the relatively comfortable means Italy could offer at that time.

The irrepressible apostolic ardor that inspired her shines through more explicitly in other passages of her letters, as when she urges Sr. A. Gerarda Canovi, a missionary in Eritrea: “Be thirsty for souls, never look back, always forward...”. And to the same sister, on April 30, 1900, six days before her death (it was the last letter of her life, and it may also stand as her apostolic testament): “Look after the interests of your Spouse, win souls for him!”.

The Decisive Event

Among the first expeditions to Bolivia, one was to leave a decisive mark, both for the stature of the persons who led it and for the impetus it gave to the spread of the presence and activity of the Daughters of St. Anne in that country: it was the third, which left Europe (Bordeaux) on June 5 and reached Sucre in mid-August 1882. It was led by Doctor Aniceto Arce, an important Bolivian statesman of rough yet humane temperament, with all the traits of a self-made man aware of his own real worth; and by Sr. A. Camilla Valentini, a young and spirited missionary, a genuine interpreter of Mother Rosa's spirit, who was to be the first superior of the Institute's first-born missionary Province and would give it, within a few years, the structure of a true religious province, leaving on it a lasting imprint. Within a few years: just seven.

Of these “SEVEN YEARS IN BOLIVIA” Mother Camilla, who in 1922 became the fourth Superior General of the Congregation, dictated the memoirs almost without meaning to, not in a systematic form intended for publication, but in the familiar conversations she had with the sisters who, as her closest collaborators, lived nearest to her, and to whom she recounted events, episodes and adventures and described places and people. These recollections, listened to and gathered by the sisters with eager and affectionate attention, and faithfully transcribed by the lawyer Giuseppe Falchi, brother of one of the General Assistants of the time, were published in three volumes, under the title “Sette anni in Bolivia,” between 1929 and 1930.

“Gathered in these pages - we read in the Foreword to the first volume - are the Memoirs of the journeys to Bolivia of Sr. A. Camilla Valentini, Mother General of the Daughters of St. Anne. The account is naturally incomplete, being the fruit of fragmentary narratives caught in moments of intimacy, when Mother Camilla told those dearest to her the various events of her far from brief stay in that South American Republic.

“Moreover, out of the sister's natural reserve, everything concerning the strictly religious and intimate side of monastic life is passed over in silence...

“... whoever reads these pages will find in them only the anecdotal and outward side...”.

A passage from the Foreword to the Third Volume vividly recalls the atmosphere in which the book was born:

“We still have her in our memory (the Author was writing a few months after Mother Camilla's death), alive and real at the little table, where the sun sent a late, pale ray of light.

“Through the large open window the warm south wind came in gusts, and the thick branches of the locust trees stirred and rustled in the little garden.

“Then she would tell her stories.

“The long Sunday afternoons seemed to glow under her gentle, quiet words: and sometimes the vision of past scenes, the recollection of faces, names and distant things, gave her smiling, kindly face the pale reflection of a youth gone by.

“... whoever reads these pages will find in them only the anecdotal and outward side.”

A travel book, then, in a certain sense, since the journeys - long, exhausting, dangerous - take up most of it. But what matters most, what strikes one most, is the spirit with which young sisters, not long out of the well-guarded nest of the novitiate, faced these hardships and dangers. The wonderful and rapid flowering of the works in the Bolivian Republic, and the number of young lives sacrificed to contagion and wearing toil, bear witness to its worth.

That the Memory May Not Fade

The book appears today in an edition that has been deliberately lightened by pruning some descriptive passages and a certain minuteness of narrative detail that might seem excessive to modern taste. Also omitted are some explanations which some sixty years ago, when the geographical and ethnic borders of the Latin American continent were hard to cross, might have been useful and appropriate, but which today's ease of communication has made superfluous.

Care has been taken, however, that, as in the original text, the figure of Mother Camilla, together with the inevitably fainter figures of her companions, should stand out clearly, while letting the presence and spirit of Mother Rosa show through in delicate filigree; Sr. A. Camilla was, all her life, her loving and faithful imitator and interpreter.

It was surely no coincidence that, after the Bolivian experience, barely a year after her election as Superior General, she hastened to widen the Institute's missionary horizons by sending the Daughters of St. Anne to Palestine at the request of the Father Custos of the Holy Land, a Franciscan, just as the religious to whom Mother Rosa had once entrusted the first Daughters bound for Bolivia was a Franciscan.

As the Family of the Daughters of St. Anne, guided and sustained by the spirited drive of Mother Virginia Sinagra, now takes up its missionary journey toward new Lands with renewed zeal, this simple, serene book may serve as an example and an encouragement.

Today perhaps no longer, or not everywhere, do the new missionary Daughters of St. Anne travel by mule in search of the sick to care for, hearts to console or minds to enlighten, for “the increase of our holy Faith”; yet today they still carry the same message as their sisters of yesterday, with the same charge of love and motherly dedication that Mother Rosa, by her writings and the ardor of her heart, and Mother Camilla, by her works, left as a legacy.

“Blessed are you who have crossed the sea... ready to endure martyrdom,” Mother Rosa had written.

And even leaving aside the fact that today, no less than yesterday, martyrdom may be met at any turn of the road, there is for all, inescapably, a more intimate, more hidden, but no less real martyrdom: the total renunciation of self in the unconditional gift of oneself to one's brothers and sisters.

Today as yesterday and as tomorrow.

A World to Console

In the second half of the nineteenth century the young Bolivian Republic, straining to give itself a modern organization worthy of the great civilized nations, was nonetheless hampered by an unstable political situation and by the general lack of preparation among the population; not even in the largest cities could it give a regular and effective organization to its works of public assistance. Hospitals and schools suffered most of all.

In La Paz, which at that time had 50,000 inhabitants, the two existing hospitals were run by the Municipal Council. Each was served by a single doctor and entirely lacked a trained and properly organized nursing staff.

The almost total lack of medical care was made worse by the complete absence of hygiene, which frequently gave rise to epidemics with an alarming death rate.

The members of the Municipal Council, at least those with a greater sense of responsibility and more human sensitivity, were keenly aware of this painful situation, and at the session of April 29, 1878, they openly denounced it.

Tempers flared; but among the harshest voices one suddenly rose, calm and composed: “I understand that about two years ago two of our Franciscan Fathers of the ‘Recoleta,’ Father Sempliciano of the Trinity and Father Vincenzo Rocchi, opened negotiations with an Italian congregation of women religious whose sisters do excellent work in hospitals. I do not know why those negotiations came to nothing. But the idea still seems sound to me. Could we not try again?”.

Sisters. Since the time of Spanish rule cloistered Monasteries had been established in the country, but sisters of active life were entirely unknown there, although the echo of the wonderful flowering of charitable institutions which in Italy, Spain and France devoted themselves to relieving the miseries of the poor did reach that distant land. So much so that a year earlier the President of the Municipal Council of La Paz, Don Venancio Burgoa, had noted:

“Profit cannot produce all the self-denial required to care for and help humanity in its terrible sufferings. Only Christian charity is capable of this great sacrifice; and likewise the hope of an immortal reward, the desire for a prize higher than any earthly one. As long as the unfortunate sick in these houses are not watched over and cared for by the Sisters of Charity... the service will never improve to the extent we desire. The Municipality must therefore make every necessary effort to bring these holy women to the country.”

Evidently the time was not yet ripe, and so these good intentions had come to nothing. But it is clear that the proposal now being renewed did not take the assembly by surprise. In the discussion that followed the difficulties were pointed out first of all: finding a suitable person willing to go to Europe and capable of winning over a sizable group of generous women ready to leave homeland and family, perhaps forever, and to face a very long, tiring and not undangerous journey to an unknown country, to a people who spoke a different language... and, no small matter, finding the considerable sum of money needed for such a journey.

Then Don Benigno Clavijo spoke, a Bolivian nobleman, brother of a bishop, wealthy and known for his generosity toward charitable works: “I put four thousand bolivianos at your disposal for the necessary expenses.”

His example spurred others on; more offers came. It was clear that the money would be found without too much difficulty. And the suitable and willing person was found too: Father Vincenzo Rocchi, who was already preparing to go to Europe on business for his Order.

Bolivia Calls Europe...

The Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne, founded in Piacenza by Mother Rosa Gattorno in 1866, was barely twelve years old, but the “flight of the dove” wished for by the Holy Father Pius IX had already spread from the north to the south of Italy, and the Foundress's spirited heart dreamed of still wider skies, in a longing of charity that embraced every form of human misery beyond any geographical border.

Father Vincenzo Rocchi left for Europe at the beginning of the summer of 1878, bearing an official commission from the Municipality of La Paz and the Bishop's approval.

He did not head for Italy at once; fearing he would be unable to obtain the Daughters of St. Anne because of the earlier failed attempt, he first looked, but in vain, in France and Spain. He then came to Italy and, after fruitless inquiries at other Institutes, perhaps seeing in this a clear sign from God, he decided to go to Piacenza. To his great joy he found Mother Rosa's heart wholly open to the plan and learned that there were already sisters on fire with the missionary ideal.

Agreement was therefore not difficult: on October 19, 1878, a first contract was signed: Mother Rosa undertook to make available, within thirty days, sixteen sisters who would form the first of the many groups of missionaries that in the following years would set out for Latin America.

For his part, Father Rocchi asked for sisters who were “... virtuous, strong, of suitable age, full of the spirit of sacrifice and empty of self-love, ready to serve for the love of God...” and, referring specifically to the financial side, in art. 4 of the agreement he noted: “Whereas the Municipality of La Paz, according to this year's budget, sets aside (for the running of the hospitals) the sum of 28,837 bolivianos, these expenses will probably decrease thereafter because of the service rendered by the Daughters of St. Anne, who are accustomed to doing everything entirely by themselves, without burdening (the Administrations) with a multitude of servants. For example, in the Hospital of St. John of God there will be only one doctor, one chaplain, one or two attendants, a porter, a washerman, a cook and a coachman.”

In art. 5 he then made the far from lavish concession: “The Daughters of St. Anne by their activity will try to make savings on the 1878 budget; these surpluses will be granted to them (sic!) for food and clothing.”

And again in article 7: “So that the cost of their journey to America may not be wasted, the Daughters of St. Anne bind themselves to remain in La Paz, in the service of the hospitals of that city, for a period of not less than ten years, to be counted from the day of their arrival.”

Italy Responds...

Trusting surely in an inner inspiration, Mother Rosa accepted these burdensome conditions and, certain that her daughters were fully willing, set about drawing up the list. It is only right to recall the names of the first sixteen intrepid missionaries who spread their wings for a flight that would continue unceasingly in the following decades: Sr. A. Cunegonda Conti; Sr. A. Felicita Conti; Sr. A. Livia Tallarini; Sr. A. Modesta Molesti; Sr. A. Zoila Levi; Sr. A. Amodio Gregori; Sr. A. Perpetua Tornelli; Sr. A. Annunziata Chiodelli; Sr. A. Lucia Taraballi; Sr. A. Clelia Semeria; Sr. A. Damiana Giovenetti; Sr. A. Gaudiosa Scandolari; Sr. A. Domitilla Solenghi; Sr. A. Scolastica Barrelliani; Sr. A. Bonaventura Tornelli. Superior: Sr. A. Giuseppa Troni, one of the Foundress's first five companions.

The Mother's heart must have trembled at the thought of this first parting from her daughters, bound for distant and unknown lands, and perhaps forever. How long, difficult and dangerous journeys were in those days! The memory of these daughters had to be preserved at least in the only tangible way then possible: and the Mother, against her natural reluctance, agreed to be photographed so that her daughters might take with them the likeness of their faraway Mother, and she also wanted a group photograph of those who were leaving, which she kept before her in her study until her death.

The sisters, led by Father Rocchi, sailed from the port of Genoa on November 23, 1878. After a long and tiring voyage they landed at the Peruvian port of Mollendo on January 17, 1879, and from there went on, first by rail as far as Puno, then aboard the steamer Yapura across Lake Titicaca to the port of Chililaya, where, setting foot on Bolivian soil for the first time, they were met by an official committee sent expressly by the President of the Republic and the Bishop of La Paz.

Setting out by carriage from Chililaya with this honorable escort, the sisters arrived in La Paz on January 20, welcomed in triumph by the highest religious and civil Authorities and by the whole population, in a city decked with flags and triumphal arches, to the ringing of the bells of every church and the music of the military band.

A solemn Te Deum was sung in the church of the “Recoleta”; then, at the Town Hall, the official speeches of welcome flowed freely, and finally, utterly exhausted, the sisters were taken to the house of Don Benigno Clavijo, who was to give them temporary lodging.

The warmth of the welcome, certainly spontaneous given the affectionate temperament of the Bolivian people, was heightened by the thrill of trusting hope that the sisters' coming aroused in hearts saddened by the many misfortunes that had struck Bolivia in recent years.

This feeling comes through clearly in the greeting that the newspaper “La Tribuna” of January 24 addressed to the sisters:

“Welcome, messengers of peace, in the midst of the storm of hunger and disease that afflicts Bolivia.

“Poverty and epidemics have assailed our people, claiming hundreds of victims. The hospitals call for your generous care, while hunger and disease decimate the population.

“Blessed be the hour of your arrival in this nation, ladies of Charity. May your coming appease the wrath of the God of mercy, as the dove of the holy ark was the sign of reconciliation between God and men.”

The Harsh Face of Reality

Their first contact with reality, after the triumphal welcomes that had sorely tried the natural modesty of sisters used to silent anonymity as they went about doing good among the poor of Italy, brought them straight back to the austere climate of the Gospel beatitudes.

Apart from poverty and diseases of every kind, the hospitals were in a state of indescribable disorder. Among other things, while ample provision had been made for the triumphal welcomes, no one had thought of preparing suitable lodging for the sisters inside the hospital. But although they were enjoying the courteous hospitality of the Clavijo Family, they had hastened to visit the hospital, where they went every day; and an episode that deeply upset them made them decide to move in for good shortly after their arrival in La Paz.

They had to settle as best they could in a wretched room from which the sick had been hastily removed, without any effective disinfection. As a painful consequence some sisters caught an infectious fever which on February 28 carried Sr. A. Scolastica Barelliani to the grave, and on March 7 Sr. A. Modesta Molesti.

In dismay the Municipal Council immediately had the other sick sisters taken out of the hospital; they were lodged with families belonging to the Charitable Society and cared for attentively until they recovered.

The death of the two sisters grieved the others deeply, but did not discourage them; with even greater commitment they set about cleaning and organizing the two hospitals: with their own hands they cleared out, scrubbed, disinfected and rid them of vermin; and at last the sick could breathe clean air and rest in clean beds, while the sisters' attentive care gave them a relief they had never known before.

Less than a month after their arrival the Daughters of St. Anne were called to give fresh proof of their zeal and efficiency: on February 14, with Chile's invasion of the Bolivian port of Antofagasta, the War of the Pacific broke out.

Under the direction of the Bishop, Monsignor Juan de Dios Bosque, the sisters organized everything needed to care for the wounded and did not hesitate to go to the battlefields, as far as Tacna, to tend them and see to their transport to La Paz.

The following year they also started an efficient pharmacy service; Sr. A. Assunzione Chiodelli was put in charge of it, after an examination in which she had shown adequate competence in the field.

Toward Wider Horizons

As early as September 10, 1878, though at great sacrifice, since the two sisters who had died were the ones holding the diploma that would have qualified them to direct Schools, two sisters took charge of a School for girls which, born in great humility and poverty, began the great educational work of the Daughters of St. Anne in Bolivia; with the arrival of new sisters it grew strong and spread widely.

Mother Rosa had grieved painfully, in her motherly heart, over the loss of her first two missionary daughters; but with indomitable will, renewing to the Heavenly Father the offering of the whole Institute, she had devoted herself with even greater commitment to preparing a new group for Bolivia.

In 1881, in fact, Father Rocchi made another journey to Italy to press for more sisters to be sent, in order to meet the ever-growing hospital needs and to answer the insistent requests of other Bolivian cities, especially Cochabamba, whose only hospital was in even worse condition than the two in La Paz had been.

Don Benigno Clavijo again bore the cost of the new expedition, and the group, once more led by Father Rocchi, left Genoa on December 4, 1881, and arrived in La Paz on February 12, 1882. On September 5 of the same year Sr. A. Giuseppa Troni took eight sisters to Cochabamba to serve in that hospital.

And in August of the same year a third group of twelve sisters arrived in Sucre, accompanied by Sr. A. Camilla Valentini and led by the important figure who was to give the strongest impetus to the spread of the Daughters of St. Anne in Bolivia.

The “Forerunner”

Aniceto Arce: short of stature, not handsome; but his olive face, with rather hard features, was lit by two large, bright eyes that revealed an ardent, energetic, strong-willed nature.

Extremely wealthy, cultured, vice-president of the Senate; his political activity had overshadowed the sitting President of the Republic, who saw him as a formidable rival and had forced him into a veiled form of exile. Aniceto Arce, though he aspired to the presidency of the Bolivian Republic, was not moved by barren personal ambition: deeply concerned for the destiny of his country, he sincerely wished to raise its material and moral condition, and he had gladly taken advantage of the situation to travel to Europe in order to study its history and experience its more advanced way of life; he had visited France, Spain and Italy, taking an interest in the workings of the most important institutions and making contacts with the most prominent men of the day.

The ideal that inspired him was rooted in the very beginnings of his life: born in Tarija of a poor family, and orphaned of both father and mother while still a child, he had been taken in by a distant relative, an intelligent and original man, steeped in serious theological studies and at the same time fired with revolutionary ideals, who devoted himself to bringing the boy up on his own principles; but because of their precarious finances Aniceto's schooling was meager and rudimentary; at fourteen he had to take up manual labor to earn his living.

Gifted with a very lively intelligence, he would not resign himself to the narrowness of his lot; in his free hours he wandered the streets of the little town watching the life of the important people; he listened to their talk, forever searching for something that might open the way to fulfilling the still confused aspirations that made him restless and discontented; of one thing, however, he was aware: he needed to study, to acquire an education. But how?

One day he heard two of the town's notables speaking of the “College” in Sucre as the ideal place for the son of one of them to study and prepare for the brilliant career his father dreamed of for him. Aniceto was struck; so there was in the world, at least for some, the chance to study, to become someone important. Why not for him too?

He told his uncle: he would go to Sucre to study at that College. But with what means? The uncle hesitated, of course. He would have liked to talk him out of it, but he knew the boy's character: passionate, strong-willed, at times violent.

With a sigh he said: “Go, then; I will give you what is due to you from your family, and may the Lord help you.”

His inheritance! Easily said! An old, broken-winded horse and a few coins, the “reales” of the time. With this fortune young Arce set out for the capital.

The journey was long and tiring; to meet his most pressing needs Aniceto soon had to sell the horse; but used as he was to poverty and to the hardness of life, he did not lose heart: at night he sheltered in some hut, and by day, when hunger bit, he offered himself for some job paid with a crust of bread. But he got there.

In Sucre he at once asked the way to the College and went straight to knock at the door. His shabby appearance, so different from that of the boys who attended the College, made a bad impression on the porter, who asked him rudely: “What do you want here?”

“I want to enter the College to study.”

The inevitable happened: the door was shut in his face.

The boy knocked again and, weeping, repeated his request. The door was shut again, this time with threats. But Aniceto did not give up. For three days no one could drive him away; apart from the time needed to find something to eat, the boy came back to crouch on the steps. At night too.

On the third day a distinguished-looking gentleman came and knocked at the door. The porter opens it and, as he steps ceremoniously aside to let the visitor in, Aniceto seizes his chance: quick as a cat, he slips inside. Chased, grabbed by the neck, beaten, he will not leave the corner where he has entrenched himself, repeating between sobs: “I only want to study.”

The gentleman, who witnessed the scene, is first amazed, perhaps even indignant, but in the end he is moved; he calms the furious porter, sends away the people who have gathered, questions the boy; and Aniceto talks, at length. Encouraged by the kindly interest of the man before him, he says things about himself that he had never told anyone, perhaps not even himself.

When he falls silent he is exhausted, but hopeful. The gentleman has told him: “Don't worry; I'll see to it.” And he speaks to the Rector, who has already been told of the boy's strange demand, and concludes: “Keep him for a while at my expense. When we see the first results we shall decide about the future. But I don't think we shall regret having helped him.”

No one did regret it, in fact, except his future political opponents. Educated, well taught and now mature, he graduated brilliantly and launched into profitable mining ventures that soon made him quite rich. He married a young woman even richer than himself and, now free of financial worries, devoted himself to a political career.

Almost certain of being elected president at the next elections, in 1880 he made the journey to Europe with his two elder sons, Diego and Carlos, and their Jesuit tutor.

The Plan Takes Shape

Anchored in firm Christian principles, Doctor Arce not only wished to advance the human and social betterment of his fellow countrymen, but also wanted to provide them with the means for a more solid and deeper religious and moral formation.

And, knowing from his own experience the need for sound instruments, he was thinking of founding works suited to that end.

He asked for an audience with the Holy Father Leo XIII and, among other things, asked his advice on choosing a congregation of women religious able to further his plans.

The Pope, who knew of the promising beginnings of the hospital and educational work of the Daughters of St. Anne in La Paz, advised him to turn to their Mother Foundress to obtain more sisters of the same Congregation.

Wasting no time, as was his way, Doctor Arce went to Mother Rosa and spoke to her openly, finding in her an attentive and understanding listener. He said he would bear the whole cost of the journey, but he needed a fairly large number of sisters meeting two indispensable conditions: the health needed to withstand the country's climate, and a perfect knowledge of the Spanish language.

The request was fair and well grounded, and the Mother understood. She was about to say no, but something within her held her back. Were the conditions really insurmountable? For the moment, and on the face of it, yes; but the sisters settled in La Paz were learning Spanish without too much difficulty, and as for health, it was enough to choose them healthy and strong and then entrust them to St. Anne. This Doctor Arce clearly had the best of intentions; moreover, it was the Pope who had advised him to come to her. Was that not already a sign from heaven? What an immense field of action kept opening before the missionary zeal of the young Institute! If this opportunity were lost, this new possibility refused, when would another come? And the daughters already working in that country, in a setting made so hard by the enormous distance and the difficulty of communication, would surely find fresh and valuable support in the presence of another group of sisters and in Doctor Arce himself, so well disposed, and so rich and powerful.

In short, was God's will not plain to see?

A moment of silent prayer; and Mother Rosa gives her promise.

Doctor Arce left satisfied for Paris, where he intended to recruit a small army of engineers, doctors, skilled workers and professional cooks to take to Bolivia.

Faith Challenges God

Mother Rosa had promised: but the difficulties were many. To find in a short time another twelve sisters (another expedition had left a few months earlier) who were young, healthy, spiritually formed, professionally capable... not to mention the Spanish language. The Mother made and remade the lists, planned the necessary transfers and the local problems to be solved, and at a certain point she felt she had achieved her aim. But Spanish?! “Lord, you see to it!”

One difficulty remained, however, perhaps the greatest: the sister to whom the leadership of the group could be entrusted. There was one who enjoyed the Foundress's full confidence and would certainly have been suitable; but a short time before, in a bad fall, she had badly injured a leg, and it was in such a state that the doctors did not even think it wise to put it in plaster for fear of worse. She was therefore confined to bed, with no way of knowing whether or when the matter would be resolved.

This was Sr. A. Camilla Valentini, the young superior of the Community working at the Hospital of Borgo San Donnino, today Fidenza.

Gentle in manner but firm in her decisions, she had quickly won everyone's esteem. Mother Rosa decided to put the proposal to her. In other circumstances Sr. A. Camilla would have agreed enthusiastically, but like this?... And since the Mother had only made a simple proposal, the sister felt not only entitled but compelled by the situation to refuse.

The Mother, pressed in her turn by necessity and urgency, prayed again and insisted; but Sr. A. Camilla's condition remained unchanged, and so did her answer.

Mother Rosa then decided to play the card of obedience and peremptorily summoned Valentini to Piacenza. Unable to walk as she was, the sister had herself literally carried there and, arriving in Piacenza dejected and in very poor physical condition, had to go straight to bed. Mother Rosa, for her part, went to pray before “her” Crucifix.

After long prayer the Mother goes to the room where Sr. A. Camilla lay in pain, tended by a nursing sister, and without preamble says to her: “My child, before you leave you will have a photograph taken to leave as a keepsake for your parents.”

The sister's eyes opened wide: “But, Mother, do you realize? Leave in this state? Can't you see how I am?”

By way of answer the Mother turned to the nurse: “Help her put on her stockings and shoes.”

There was no arguing; trembling, the two sisters set about obeying. And the foot, until that moment enormously swollen, slipped effortlessly into the stocking and then into the shoe.

Pale with emotion, Sr. A. Camilla understood: God willed it; all that was left for her was to obey.

Mother Rosa explained Doctor Arce's plan to her in detail and did not hide the difficulty arising from their not knowing Spanish. But she concluded: “I feel, and you yourself have had the confirmation, that the Lord wants you in Bolivia. I am very sorry about the language, but I do not see it as an insurmountable obstacle. You will learn it.”

Between fears and hopes - It was now 1882; through his political supporters Doctor Arce had learned that the time had come to put forward his candidacy for the presidency of the Bolivian Republic. He therefore decided to hasten his departure and sent to Piacenza the Jesuit Father Paure, tutor of his two elder sons, to collect the sisters and accompany them to Bordeaux, where they would embark with the rest of the party. Parting from the Mother was not easy; but mother and daughters had learned the secret of the strength that comes from total surrender to God's will.

From Piacenza to Genoa by train; from Genoa to Marseilles by sea; and from Marseilles, again by sea, to Bordeaux, where Doctor Arce was impatiently waiting for them.

Sr. A. Camilla thought anxiously about meeting him; he would certainly notice at once that they knew no Spanish at all. How would he react? What humiliation, what sorrow, if he decided to send them back!

During the journey to Bordeaux she had tried to learn a few words of Spanish from Father Paure, but they amounted to a few greetings and some stock phrases. Nothing like carrying on a real conversation!

The sisters tried to encourage her, reminding her that Mother Rosa was surely praying for them. But that was not enough to calm her.

The great moment came: Sr. A. Camilla, already pale and thin from her recent illness and the strain of the journey, finding herself scrutinized rather severely by Doctor Arce, turned even waxier, and in her confusion even the few Spanish phrases learned on the journey fled from her mind. And without realizing it, but sensing miserably that things were going from bad to worse, she blurted out: “Bonjour, monsieur, comment vous portez-vous?”

That was all it took to set Doctor Arce off: “French and always French! There is no other language in the world! And what is more... I asked for sisters in good health and I get one who cannot stand on her feet. I expect sisters who know Spanish perfectly and I am greeted in French. These were not the conditions I laid down and the Mother General accepted”; and he kept glaring at the poor sister with such a frown that, without even knowing what language she was speaking, she murmured: “The Mother had no others available at the moment. Forgive us. We will do all we can to satisfy you.”

The reply, however, was curt and unmistakable: “Tomorrow at ten I will send my manservant to let you know when I can receive you and tell you my decisions.” And he left them standing there.

In the hotel room Sr. A. Camilla wept bitterly. “Our poor Mother! She was so sure the Lord himself would provide, would put things right somehow. And she was so certain the Lord wants us in Bolivia!”

The sisters comforted her: “After all, the last word has not been spoken. Mother Rosa is surely praying. Let us pray too.”

No one slept that night. But by now resigned to the will of God and of Doctor Arce, Sr. A. Camilla rose calmer and prayed with abandonment. The time for the interview came, and it began stormily; Doctor Arce repeated his complaints, even said that his good faith had been deceived, and concluded: “This way I would be throwing away my money and my time.”

“Very well,” murmured the sister, resigned, “please forgive us. We will go back to Piacenza.”

At that moment the man's expression changed. Did the image perhaps cross his mind of a little boy clinging desperately to a door under the angry blows of a servant?

He stood lost in thought for a moment; then, his face softened by the shadow of a smile, he concluded: “I will think it over.” Another moment of silence, which the sister took care not to disturb, and then: “At noon you will all do me the kindness of lunching with me.”

A Providential Tumble

At the appointed hour, in the richly laid dining room, Doctor Arce courteously invited Superior Camilla to sit on his right. But his manner was rather stern, and the sisters, intimidated, silently took their places around the great table. The meal began in a heavy atmosphere of embarrassment.

Suddenly the silence was broken by an incident which, though it greatly increased the embarrassment of the sister concerned, livened up all the others: Sr. A. Agnese, the youngest and shyest of the group, perhaps precisely because of her shyness, had sat so near the edge of her chair that, when she had to move to let the waiter serve her, she lost her balance and landed on the floor as the chair tipped over. General commotion, a clatter of chairs pushed back, sisters rushing to help the fallen one up, ill-suppressed laughter and whispered comments... while the fallen one got up, mortified and in tears. The ice was broken. Doctor Arce himself could not help asking her courteously whether she had hurt herself, and the silence gave way to lively conversation. Only the superior remained pensive. But the very lively Sr. A. Cesira, who was sitting on Doctor Arce's left, made up her mind to speak to him directly: “At home, before I became a sister, I knew a Spanish gentleman who spoke exactly like you. And not only did I understand him, I could answer him too, and we got on very well. Spanish is very like Italian, except for those os and as at the end, but I'm sure we'll learn it in no time. Besides, we had already learned something on the journey from Father Paure; it's shyness that ties our tongues now...”. And she spoke with such candid boldness that Doctor Arce looked her straight in the eye with the first glimmer of trust, while all the others felt encouraged to join in. Doctor Arce then asked a few questions and they all understood, or pretended to; and Sr. Cesira, not content with trying out the few Spanish words she knew, added a few os and as of her own invention, setting off her companions' laughter, which in the end caught the serious host as well; looking at those young, laughing faces, so full of genuine vitality at that moment, he thought what a mistake it would be if, by digging in his heels over a difficulty that could, after all, be overcome in a short time, he were to deprive his country of the contribution of so much fresh and generous energy.

He was silent for a moment, still thoughtful; then, turning to his neighbor on the right, still silent, he declared with a disarming smile: “I see. That means I shall teach you Spanish myself during the voyage. We won't be short of time.”

And at last Sr. A. Camilla smiled too.

With Faith, Toward the Unknown

Doctor Arce and his large party sailed from Bordeaux aboard the steamer Orenoque in the first days of April 1882. The group was an extremely mixed company, but a very interesting and congenial one. Many of the passengers watched the group of sisters with particular attention. So young, some delicate in appearance, yet so serenely ready to leave their homeland and face the unknowns of a distant and unfamiliar land, to follow a vocation that most of them could not understand, but whose underlying human and generous motive they all more or less sensed.

When, after a few days at sea, the last strip of European land disappeared from view, the sisters felt the need to draw close together around their superior, barely holding back their tears. At that moment they could not help feeling keenly the magnitude of the sacrifice they had made; the faith that inspired them could not cancel the human pain of parting from all that had given meaning to their lives until then, nor deaden a touch of anxiety and fear: to what lands were they bound, what peoples were they going to meet, what living conditions would they have to face?

Sr. A. Camilla, herself young and sensitive, was well aware of what was going on in the hearts of those girls and, mastering her own emotion, silently embraced them all in a look that was a hug, a promise, a solemn pledge: they were her daughters, entrusted to her by St. Anne and by Mother Rosa; she would guide them, protect them and watch over them at the cost of her life.

Meanwhile, in her heart, she thanked the Lord deeply, for rather than simply helping her he had himself resolved the serious initial difficulty. Doctor Arce, now completely reassured that he had decided well, took his role as teacher of Spanish, and of Bolivian history and literature, extremely seriously. Having noticed that the sisters learned remarkably easily, he doubled the frequency and pace of the lessons, so much so that the sisters sometimes welcomed with relief the moments or hours when the pitching or rolling of the ship, far from the stabilizers of modern ocean liners, forced the lesson to stop. What is more, as they drew near the Equator the heat became torrid and they all suffered from it.

They crossed the Equator in such a blaze of heat that, besides the break caused by the traditional ceremonies, the stern teacher himself thought it wise to grant a few days of holiday and rest. Meanwhile, to comfort eyes tired and dazzled by the unbroken expanse of sea blazing under a relentless sun, a strip of land appeared on the horizon, the sign and herald of America's approach: the Islands of “Fernando de Noronha.” But it took another ten days for the ship to drop anchor in the wonderful bay of Rio de Janeiro; landing and boarding took place in a very thick fog, so that the passengers could not enjoy the view of that bay's exceptional beauty; in compensation, the sisters, guests of the Daughters of Charity, were able to sleep one night on dry land and in comfortable beds. It was a real relief, in view of the long and more tiring part of the journey that awaited them. A stop of little more than twenty-four hours. The Orenoque sailed for Buenos Aires, which it reached a few days later. The crossing of the Atlantic Ocean was over.

America!

As early as 1882 Buenos Aires was a large city, modern for its time, full of bustle and traffic. But in the Argentine capital too the stop was brief; Doctor Arce was now anxious to press on, for the southern winter was close at hand. He quickly had his whole party embark on one of the boats that plied the Paraná River from Buenos Aires to Rosario. On board the sisters met a number of Italians, mostly merchants, cheerful and noisy people, and after the long monotony of the crossing it was a welcome distraction to speak their own language with strangers.

When they landed at Rosario they had been traveling for forty-one days. From Rosario, as quickly as the means allowed, people and baggage boarded the train for Tucumán.

The train in those days was still something of a luxury even in Italy; the sisters thus had the feeling of plunging back into European civilization, but they soon noticed how very different the landscape was: not the beautiful, lush Italian countryside, but arid fields, sparse thorn trees, scattered huts and lonely farms far apart from one another. And the deeper the train went into the region, the rarer the signs of human life became, apart from an occasional gaucho on horseback or a cart drawn by pairs of mules or oxen.

They reached Córdoba, an austere seat of learning, rich in churches, monasteries and monuments, a city which therefore recalls Spain in more than its name.

From Córdoba the sisters had their first sight of the Cordillera, its peaks standing out distant and majestic. And on by rail through an ever more desolate land: the arid, dreary pampa, very like a desert. And on still, to Santiago del Estero and at last to Tucumán, a smiling oasis of life after the desolation of the desert.

At Tucumán the railway ended. In this pretty and progressive little town, an oasis of life in that boundless solitude, truly the last port of the civilized world, the sisters were able to enjoy a few days of complete rest while preparations were made for the hardest part of the journey.

Doctor Arce laid in ample supplies of every kind, in view of the long journey ahead through lonely places lacking even the barest necessities of life: a great number of horses and mules, needed to draw the vehicles and enough to allow quick changes so as to avoid needless delays on the road. Then food, medicines, blankets, cloaks for protection against the cold of the high altitudes and the nights to be spent in the open. Finally more workmen, to be added to the more skilled ones recruited in Europe. And even before leaving for Europe Doctor Arce had arranged for heavy wagons to be built for carrying goods, and lighter, more comfortable carriages for carrying people; but all of them sturdy enough for the rugged country they would have to cross.

Toward the Cordillera

When he was sure he had provided everything necessary and saw that the sisters were well rested, Doctor Arce gave the order to set out. The mounted escort went ahead, followed by the carriages of the sisters and the staff; the wagons and a herd of loose horses and mules, ready to relieve the tired ones, brought up the rear. The last line of defense was an escort of a few horsemen made up of the gauchos most loyal to the leader of the expedition.

They set out on a cool June morning, and the long column wound swiftly through countryside that was at first lush with tropical vegetation. Soon, however, the land became arid and bare again, and the steep, exhausting climb began that would last for days and days.

The mules and horses were changed at set intervals, regardless of where it had been decided to stop for the night. The journey thus kept up a brisk pace, with short halts, although the men had no little trouble holding back the animals, mostly half-broken, so as to avoid needless delays.

Meals were taken during the necessary halts. The food was the ordinary fare of the country, whatever could be found before leaving Tucumán. Welcome, no doubt, to the men of the escort, less so to the Europeans, who adapted to it all the same. For the sisters the study of Spanish had not been suspended, as far as possible! On the contrary, once they had set foot on American soil, Doctor Arce had imposed the exclusive use of that language, and it can be said that all of them, some more, some less, spoke it fluently. But that did not seem enough to the stern teacher, who demanded complete mastery of it, especially from the superior and the sisters assigned to the College in Sucre. The sisters' greatest torment, however, was the compulsory daily dose of powdered quinine dissolved in tea. They were crossing unhealthy regions in the grip of malaria, and the Leader rightly considered proper prevention necessary. The sisters suffered from it, not so much because of the bitterness of the medicine as because of its unpleasant side effects; some, quicker or more mischievous, would now and then seize a favorable moment to throw away drink and medicine, but woe betide them if Doctor Arce noticed! There followed stern lectures, justified after all, on the need to keep in good health so as to bear the hardships of the journey and the harshness of the climate, and to arrive ready for the work awaiting them.

The places for the night halts had been chosen in advance, with great care, by the experienced men. Wherever possible they were near inhabited places, whether villages or huts. Where there were none, since even the smallest human settlements were very far apart, well-sheltered spots were chosen with streams and therefore pasture, so that the animals could graze and everyone could drink and take on fresh spring water. The vehicles were drawn up in a semicircle to form a kind of barrier; outside, fires were lit to keep the night animals away. The innermost part was reserved for the sisters, who slept wrapped in their blankets. The men stayed outside, by the fires. At dawn everyone had to be ready to set off again.

So they went on to Salta, to Jujuy; the Cordillera now rose before the caravan like an immense stage set crowned with peaks that the sun's rays turned from pink to blue, until dark shadows wrapped them round and told the travelers it was time to rest. They breathed the air of the high mountains, and the climb grew ever more exhausting, while the Bolivian border was still far away.

The country was wild, and to make headway a team of workmen now had the task of going ahead of the main body of the caravan, clearing the road of the heaviest obstacles. Even so, some vehicle would now and then come close to overturning, and only the skill of the men used to driving prevented it. Nor was it always possible to keep the right distance between the vehicles, and when a group felt cut off the hours seemed longer and the waits agonizing, while precious time was lost in restoring order.

An occasional distraction was meeting the first herds of llamas, animals partly like sheep and partly like donkeys, which the Bolivians, as the guides explained, use as pack animals because of their strength combined with a particular gentleness. They kept climbing. The sisters felt the effects of altitude keenly: neuralgia, long bouts of heavy, almost unhealthy sleep that made them insensible to everything. And at a certain point what had so often been feared happened: whether because the ground was too rough or because the postilion, overcome by sleep himself, was not paying attention, a carriage overturned with a terrifying crash. The four sisters and the other passengers in it ended up underneath. The men from the nearest carriage ran up and pulled them out: but the sisters lay stretched out, motionless, as if dead. Superior Camilla, who was traveling in the last vehicle with Doctor Arce, was the last to notice, and when she arrived and saw the sisters apparently unconscious she felt faint herself. Sr. A. Giacobba in particular had her face covered in blood; in the fall she had struck her face on a wheel and, as was soon found, had broken her front teeth. But she soon showed signs of coming round and, seeing the superior's dismay, she had the courage to attempt a smile, which her battered mouth and the blood made ghastly, and murmured: “Well, now I too shall have my stigmata!”

The other sisters were bruised and battered, but none was injured. And because of the now habitual exhaustion, though urged to wake up, they pleaded half-consciously: “Let us sleep.”

Doctor Arce, reassured about the condition of the three sisters and of the other passengers, who also had no real injuries, was worried about Sr. A. Giacobba; but, trying to master his own emotion, as he climbed back into the carriage where he had had the sister placed too, he promised with the shadow of a smile: “In Sucre we'll have you fitted with false teeth.”

“Me, false teeth?” grumbled the sister. And Doctor Arce, remembering a cheeky remark of Sr. A. Cesira's, replied: “Otherwise how could you pronounce the os and as of my language?”

The brief exchange eased the tension somewhat, and everyone found the strength to laugh as they remembered the clashes that had enlivened the first meeting in Bordeaux. And all the while they went on climbing. As the group drew near the Bolivian border they found in the landscape a majesty, strength and beauty that filled them with wonder. Only to some of the travelers did the absolute solitude bring a sense of desolation. And here was La Quiaca, a small, poor village lost in the Andes; beyond it they reached the border between Argentina and Bolivia, crudely marked by a huge pole laid across the rocks. Higher up stood a little church, built partly of wood and partly of mud mixed with straw, poor, bare and solitary, yet to the sisters' eyes it seemed a long-awaited sign, comforting and reassuring. Mass was said there - as Doctor Arce explained - only once every two years, and of course the Blessed Sacrament was not reserved there; but it was topped by a large cross, and to those young women who had come from so far it seemed their Lord's loving greeting, welcoming them to the new land to which He had called them, so that they might bear witness to his love before those less fortunate brothers and sisters.

Bolivia, You Are Our Homeland

A little further on some huts appeared, also of straw and mud, with a few Indians standing in front of them; the women especially had a distinctive look, with long braids over their shoulders, a tall, broad-brimmed hat on their heads and a many-colored poncho on their backs; all of them had a grave and austere, almost sad, bearing.

“There,” Doctor Arce pointed out to the sisters, “are the first Indians of the Bolivian wilds; they belong to the very ancient Quechua people” - and his voice was low and sad - “the people the Spaniards slaughtered when they first came to these lands.”

“But how - what do they live on, at this altitude and with so little life around them?” asked the superior.

“On little, on almost nothing. They are skilled hunters, they dig up edible roots, they grow what little they can wherever a scrap of land allows. But these are my people,” he went on, and his voice took on a sincere and passionate tone, “and I love them because I know them well; and if I aspire to power, believe me, Superior, I am not driven by vain ambition. I have known poverty, though not quite at this level, and I should like none of my people to go on suffering from want of necessities, or from the bullying and injustice of those who exploit them and leave them abandoned. But,” he concluded with a sigh, “I know very well that the program I have set myself will meet many opponents with selfish interests. I am counting, though, on your understanding and your help”; and he gave the sisters a trusting look.

The sisters were moved; perhaps the nearness of his homeland was breaking down the barrier of reserve that usually kept that man so much in control of himself. For them it was a premonition: in the new land they would certainly meet great hardships, perhaps sorrows too. But at that moment their future mission took shape in their minds as something beautiful and fruitful.

“Bolivia, you are our homeland!” The march went on, relentless. It was one ravine and gorge after another, small pools frozen in the morning, narrow paths where the wagons could barely pass and not without danger. The superior was very worried about Sr. A. Giacobba's condition and about the health of all the sisters, whom she visited one by one at every halt and found ever more tired and worn out by the endless journey, the constant quinine and the excessive thinness of the air. Little by little, however, the bleakness of the landscape softened. Villages were more frequent, and here and there a meadow appeared with signs of cultivation and a more human life. The Indians who watched the unusual sight of so long a caravan of wagons and horses passing by would stop at the doors of their huts to look on with curiosity, and stared at the sisters with special attention. If the place chosen for the night halt was near a village, Doctor Arce, who spoke Quechua well, would gather the Indians around him, introduce the sisters and briefly explain why they had come there.

“If you come to the city when you are sick,” he would say, “they will care for you; and who knows, one day they may come among you too, to teach your children and help them to know the Lord.”

All mistrust vanished, and the sisters began to rejoice at hearing themselves called “Mamitas” by those simple, good people. The children, curious like children everywhere, asked questions and touched, and in the end everyone, young and old, said goodbye with deep bows, thanking them and wishing them well.

Occasionally, but very rarely, they met a priest engaged in a truly heroic apostolate in those parts, and great then was the joy of the sisters, who could take part in a celebration of the Eucharist, whose absence they felt keenly, though without complaint. Once they were struck by the full peal of two bells hanging from the branches of a tree. They asked Doctor Arce the reason, and he explained with a smile: “Your passing is such an event that the Indian who looks after the little chapel hidden in the depths of the forest, where the priest comes once a year if that, feels bound to ring a festive peal. That fine araucaria is, so to speak, the bell tower of the... parish!”

When the natives they met at the doors of their huts carried their hospitality so far as to offer whatever gifts their poverty allowed - gifts that were duly returned - the sisters were deeply moved. Seeing in those native people, men and women, generally short of stature and not handsome, but with faces in which intelligence and kindness blended with a look of vague melancholy, like nostalgia for a distant greatness violently destroyed, they felt ever more keenly and deeply the will and resolve to give their whole lives to those unfortunate brothers and sisters, and in their longing they hurried on the end of the endless journey, impatient to set to work.

Having at last reached Tupiza, they had to cross several tributaries of the Pilcomayo River and long valleys, following a route that skirted the foot of the mountains to avoid the difficult massif of Potosí. They were now deep in Bolivian territory, where the signs of civilized life became more evident the closer they came to Sucre.

At a certain point they noticed that Doctor Arce was unusually anxious, almost impatient, and they soon understood why when they saw a group of horsemen riding straight toward the caravan. They were relatives and friends who had come out to hasten the father's reunion with his younger children after his long absence (the two elder sons had stayed in Europe to complete their education under the Jesuit tutor). After understandably affectionate greetings on both sides, they all set off again toward Sucre. But Doctor Arce did not want the sisters to arrive directly in the capital, tired and worn as they were after so arduous a journey, and decided to put them up for a few days at his own villa, “La Florida,” on the outskirts of the city, large and well appointed.

“I don't want to present you to the Bishop, the Authorities and the people looking as you do now,” he said with a smile, but seriously; “I want everyone to be able to see and appreciate at once the gift I am making to the city of Sucre by bringing you here.”

Señora Arce gave her guests a festive welcome, and they really thought they were dreaming as they walked through the rich rooms of the house, breathing in, as it were, along with the signs of civilized life, the refinement of the surroundings. There they found the rest they truly needed, for body and spirit, and above all the joy of daily Mass, so longed for after the long fast of the journey.

Sr. A. Giacobba too began to believe her teeth could be properly treated, something that had seemed a mere dream while crossing those wild regions. And living in Doctor Arce's house, sharing as far as their natural discretion allowed in the intimacy of his family life, the sisters came to know his heart better, and they admired above all the sound educational sense with which he brought up his children, reminding them without shame of his own humble origins so that they might learn from them.

Meanwhile, if the sisters did not go to Sucre, Sucre came to them. Every day they received visits from people both of standing and of modest means, all equally eager to meet these long-awaited sisters and to welcome them; and a delegation of notables came too, bringing the newcomers their own greetings and those of the sisters already settled in La Paz, whom the distance prevented from coming in person to embrace them as they would have liked.

It was time now to face reality. But Sr. A. Camilla felt vaguely uneasy. Hints and allusions, half in earnest and half in jest, had led her to guess that the capital was preparing a triumphal welcome for the sisters. And her spirit, shaped by the sense of simplicity and modesty characteristic of the Institute, shrank from the thought of such a thing, and she wondered whether and how she could avoid it.

Sr. A. Camilla Chooses to Arrive Incognito

She spoke of it to the sisters, who wholeheartedly agreed with her. She then turned frankly to Doctor Arce and asked him to help her. They had to find a way of avoiding the expected welcome by entering the city completely incognito. Had it been arranged for the sisters to enter Sucre the following Saturday? Very well: they need only bring their arrival forward to Friday night, in darkness and silence, and on Saturday morning the organizers of the celebration would be faced with a fait accompli. But there was one difficulty: it would certainly not be possible to take possession of the Hospital during the night without someone noticing and raising the alarm. Where could they spend the rest of the night? More than the “only difficulty” she mentioned, it was the superior's firmly expressed wish itself that understandably disappointed Doctor Arce. Bringing the sisters to Sucre was a real achievement for him, from which he hoped to gain, together with the greater good of the citizens, a considerable personal advantage. At the side of the sisters, welcomed in triumph by the people, he had promised himself a foretaste of the political triumph he now saw not far off. But with the sensitivity and discretion he had already shown more than once, he not only accepted the sisters' point of view but made it possible to carry it out, providing carriages and horses and placing at their disposal, for the unavoidable night halt, a house of his on the Plaza Mayor of the capital.

It was in front of that house, on that Friday night which the sisters never forgot, that the carriages provided by Doctor Arce drew up as quietly as possible. The sisters got out with a sigh of satisfaction and not without a few mischievous giggles, for as they crossed the city they had glimpsed by the light of the street lamps the triumphal arches and decorated poles awaiting them the next morning. But their satisfaction turned somewhat to surprise when, on taking possession of the house placed at their disposal, they realized it lacked what was needed for even a brief stay of twelve people.

Not enough beds for everyone, scarcely any furnishings, a kitchen bare of everything. Whether through the carelessness of the people Doctor Arce had put in charge or, more likely, a misunderstanding caused by the secrecy in which the little plot had had to be carried out, Lady Poverty reigned in the vast rooms, where a few pieces of stately but useless furniture made a jarring contrast.

With the youthful cheerfulness and adaptability that the hardships of the long journey had thoroughly tested, the sisters settled down as best they could for the rest of the night, and there was the final burst of laughter provoked by the incorrigible Sr. A. Cesira, who, draped in a gaudy shawl unearthed from a wardrobe and squatting on the floor, delivered in the purest Piacenza dialect a fervent speech of thanks to the Authorities and people of Sucre for the triumphal welcome given to the Daughters of St. Anne.

An Unacceptable Situation

Rest was scant and brief. The Celebrations Committee learned very early of what was called “the superior's rash move,” and while it was still early morning it presented itself at the makeshift lodging, fully determined to voice its respectful but heartfelt protests.

But the superior and the sisters, by now fairly fluent in Spanish, explained their conduct so graciously that those gentlemen, if not exactly satisfied, were at least edified, and the meeting turned on the spot into something like a formal reception in true Spanish style, made rather comical by the bareness of the surroundings.

Great, on the other hand, was the disappointment of the people, deprived of the part of the celebration that most directly concerned them and that they had most eagerly awaited: the parade of carriages through the main streets and the sight of the sisters, never seen before and imagined by each according to his own fancy.

But above all, Doctor Arce's dismay and embarrassment were indescribable when he realized how the sisters had spent the night.

What calmed him somewhat, as he gave immediate orders to a team of servants, workmen and suppliers to provide everything needed, were the sisters themselves, especially the livelier ones, who sang the praises of Lady Poverty and painted such fanciful pictures of her delights that they managed to make even their usually stern protector laugh. But very different concerns weighed on the superior's mind; as soon as she was free of official duties she decided to go to the hospital with two sisters, but without any interested escorts, to make a careful inspection. For from what she had been able to guess, rather than learn, from the people who had come to greet her at the villa “La Florida,” the administration of that institution had not so far followed exactly regular and orthodox criteria.

Sucre, then the capital of Bolivia (later replaced by La Paz), lying two thousand meters above sea level, was, for its magnificent cathedral, its monuments and its traditions, the pride of its inhabitants, who preferred it to every other city in the country also for its healthy climate and the relative mildness of its seasons. Its public institutions, however, had not managed to reach the same level, which had always grieved Doctor Arce, who now placed his highest hopes in the sisters' coming.

The hospital, the only one in the city, reflected the general shortcomings. Set in a pleasant outlying district, it consisted of a solid two-winged building and, seen from outside, made an excellent impression: a large, airy building surrounded by gardens. But forewarned as she was, the superior was not taken in; it was no accident that she had chosen to go unannounced, without the cumbersome and self-interested escort of the responsible directors and administrators. It was the junior staff, who ordinarily saw to the day-to-day running of the place, who received her and wanted first of all to take her to the upper floor, where the apartment was that, they said, had been set aside to house the community.

It was a long corridor with many doors opening on both sides. And the sisters noticed with amazement that a number of people, mostly healthy, sturdy-looking young men of about twenty or twenty-five, were freely coming and going from the rooms.

When the superior asked, the man accompanying them explained: “Most of them are medical students doing their practical training in the hospital; and since they come from the interior of the country and have no family in the city, the Archbishop, who is the President of the institution, allows them to live in the hospital. A few others work for the hospital or are relatives of the attendants.”

“But,” objected the disconcerted superior, “will they have to go on living here?”

“Of course,” the man assured her innocently; “His Excellency has already ordered them all to move into the rooms on the right side of the corridor, so that those on the left can be reserved for the sisters.”

“Like this, with these doors facing each other?”

“Mother,” said the guide, quite seriously, “I assure you they are all most respectable people.”

“I don't doubt it, but I cannot accept such a situation. We have our own definite rule.”

The man shrugged, and the superior thought it quite useless to go on arguing with him. She knew she had to speak to someone very different. And without visiting the rest of the Hospital she hurried back to the house on the Plaza Mayor, for the hour announced for the Archbishop's visit was drawing near.

A Bishop in a Quandary

He came, and showed great surprise when, after the first greetings and courtesies, the superior told him frankly that the lodging set aside for the sisters in the hospital was unacceptable because of the promiscuity it would force upon them. They were far from demanding luxurious rooms or furnishings; they would gladly be content with the bare necessities; but it was essential for them to have a group of rooms allowing the separation needed for the minimum of privacy their way of life required. They therefore did not think it right to enter the hospital unless the section assigned to them was entirely free of outsiders.

To the Archbishop's feeble reply, appealing to the spirit of poverty proper to religious life, the superior answered that in extraordinary circumstances of public calamity the sisters would submit, as they already had in Italy, to any sacrifice or privation; but that in normal times, and in a city like Sucre, the capital of a civilized country, she saw no valid reason for an exception to the rule of religious enclosure, and this condition was non-negotiable.

The Archbishop was dismayed; a holy and devout man, but not very practical, inclined to see and judge everything through the goodness of his simple heart, he had eagerly awaited the sisters' coming without giving much thought to their particular needs, and he had promised to leave undisturbed in their rooms the medical students, who enjoyed free board and lodging and could study to better advantage near the sick. The superior's stand upset his plans. In the end he tried to gain time and asked Sr. A. Camilla to make do for the time being, while he would try to remedy the problem. But the sister was of a very different mettle, and she understood that if the community entered the Hospital and began its service accepting this delaying compromise, there would be no lack of pretexts for putting off a solution indefinitely.

“The presence of those young men,” the Archbishop meanwhile hastened to say, “is a protection, a safeguard for you. There might be hostile behavior toward you on the part of the attendants or even of the patients.”

“I understand,” replied the superior, “but there are the doctors, the staff and, I suppose, the police too. And barring extraordinary cases, we know how to look after ourselves. I don't see how protection against a hypothetical danger can justify and make acceptable a permanent form of promiscuity which, in the long run, could compromise our decorum or our safety far more than any unexpected attack.”

The Archbishop certainly did not want to lose the benefit of the sisters, but neither did he want to take from the young men, who were dear to him, the advantages they enjoyed.

“Where am I to put all these young men? How can I suddenly end a charitable tradition in favor of young men who come to Sucre after weeks of travel on horseback and are preparing to serve the poor people far from the towns?”

“We too have spent weeks traveling on horseback,” the superior calmly replied, “and we too are here to serve these same poor people. For their good we are ready to make every necessary sacrifice; but as religious who, thank God, at least here and for the present can lead a way of life suited to their state, I ask no more than what the demands of religious life require: a poor apartment, as bare as you like, but one that ensures the form of enclosure our Constitutions impose. If that is not possible for now, we will wait, or go and work elsewhere. But we will not set foot in the hospital unless we are given suitable lodging. Sucre is not a village on the pampa, and I think it can provide housing for everyone.”

The problem remained unsolved.

Sucre Takes Action

Needless to say, the disagreement between the archbishop and the sisters soon became news, and the news became public knowledge. The most eminent personages of Sucre, Doctor Arce first among them, felt involved and made it a personal point of honor to step in and settle the question in the best way. The Prefect of the city himself appealed to the richest and most respected families to make it their duty to ease the hardship the sisters were meanwhile enduring.

A ladies' committee was formed and help poured in. Besides the furnishings provided by Doctor Arce came fabrics and linen, and food carefully prepared every day. Even the cloistered nuns wanted to contribute produce from their garden. The nearby Cathedral easily made up for the lack of a chapel in the house; and every time the sisters went out to church they were accompanied by a sizable procession of neighborhood urchins, who never failed to escort them with reverent clamor. All things considered, the wait did the sisters no harm: their health was fully restored, and their Spanish benefited too, as they went on studying it diligently. There was a fraternal exchange of letters between La Paz and Sucre, and the sisters already settled gave news and valuable advice to the newcomers. Time, then, was on the superior's side. The interest of influential people spurred the Archbishop to look for the fairest solution, and at last, to general relief and satisfaction, the sisters were able to take full possession of the disputed apartment and begin their service to the sick.

The first days were spent taking over the premises and organizing the services. And the sisters soon realized that the attendants' work was not remarkable for order and punctuality and that cleanliness and hygiene left much to be desired. Discipline had to be established for everyone: patients and staff alike.

It was not easy: until then the hospital had been less a real place of treatment than a sort of hotel where the sick and the not sick came and went freely. In fact the supposed patients were not admitted after any proper check on their actual physical condition, but by way of a charitable (or convenient) shelter, freely requested and easily granted, which the guests used as they pleased.

The superior promptly had notices put up in the corridors and wards reading: “Patients and attendants are forbidden to leave the hospital without the superior's permission”; but it was soon clear that the order remained a dead letter: many could not read, and the few who could ignored it. She then realized that more drastic measures were needed, while she set about drawing up a proper set of rules with penalties for every infraction. We should see...

Superior Camilla's “Grit”

The sunset was tinting the windowpanes pink: a hint of spring that invited one outdoors to enjoy the sweetness of evening after a day of hard work. The sisters gladly took advantage of it. When they went in to see to the last tasks before night, Sr. A. Guida, who was on duty, made her final round of the wards. Not all the guests, to tell the truth, were voluntary patients; several were genuinely ill, some seriously. But the sister at once noticed, here and there, empty beds that should have been occupied. “Can they still be in the garden?” she wondered. And she went out. But the garden was deserted. She went back to the wards, counted the empty beds and ran to the superior: “Mother, twenty-one patients are missing from the wards.”

The superior called the porter, a quick and intelligent Indian:

“How is it that you let the patients out without my permission?”

The Indian spread his arms:
