“I assure you no one went out through the door. But as for the rest...” - and he pointed to the long, very low wall that served as a fence around the garden - “they don't need the door.”

“The time has come to act,” remarked the superior as she dismissed the porter.

With Sr. A. Guida she decided to walk in the garden and wait for the runaways to return; the air was soft and fragrant and the wait was long. At last - it was now the small hours - someone is seen climbing over the little wall, not without difficulties more subjective than objective, moving forward silently and vanishing furtively under the trees. A minute later, more shadows. Among the tall cacti and pepper trees it would be easy to pass unnoticed, but the sisters take up position at a point in the corridor through which everyone must pass to reach the wards. And soon they come face to face with the first two returning, who, staggering dangerously as they try to hold each other up like brothers, trip over each other's feet. Through the fumes of wine and the fog of a guilty conscience the drunkards think for a moment that they are facing two white ghosts and let out a cry; but the superior's voice brings them back to reality. They throw themselves on their knees and beg: “Mamita, forgive us, we won't do it again.”

Meanwhile the others arrive. The same scene. Among the drunkards is one of the attendants, by now more dead than alive. The superior looks at that motley crowd of men, mostly elderly, turned into children again, and holding back a laugh, but in a stern voice, orders: “To bed, for now!”

Fondly imagining that it is all over, the drunkards hurry into their beds. But little time has passed, and not all of them are yet asleep, when the wards fill with soldiers: measured footsteps ring out, curt orders echo.

Zero hour had struck: as soon as the escape was discovered, the superior had hastened to send a message to the nearby police station, with whose chief she had already agreed on what to do when the moment came. And now the culprits were called by name, shaken, hauled to their feet and held up by the burly soldiers, while the superior parleyed with the chief: “Now you will kindly take all these drunkards away and lock them up in jail.”

The officer is aghast: “Mother, this is too much: there is no article of law to that effect; I would be abusing my authority. A stiff reprimand, a threat, agreed, but I cannot take them to jail.”

“Please set aside legal quibbles and scruples; if we really want to reform these men we must teach them a stern lesson. Otherwise tomorrow they will repeat the prank they are now used to, and that goes against their own good, and I could not allow it. Would it not be worse for them if I were forced to send them all away, perhaps condemning some of them to die of want?”

“Mother, some of them belong to respectable families. They are what you call, I believe, the black sheep of the family, which is only too glad to be rid of them by letting them live here. But a scandal attached to their name is something they would not stand for. Think of the consequences; how can I take them to jail without any offense to charge them with?”

“Find one, then. Disturbing the peace at night, disorderly conduct, insubordination; besides, I take responsibility for it; I know whom to turn to. We are women, foreigners, exposed to a possible mutiny by drunken men. Is it not natural and understandable that I should ask the forces of order to step in to ensure our safety?”

“Well, if you put it that way!...”

“That's the way it is, clearly! And again, as for any consequences, I take that upon myself.”

“Very well, I'll put them in the lockup for tonight.”

“Not just for tonight. For as long as it takes to bring them to their senses. Every one of us here works only for their good; we would give our lives for each of them. But how are we to free them from their bad habits without using a little firmness? Besides,” and she smiled shrewdly, “I would ask you to order your men not to harm a hair of anyone's head. Fright and shame should be enough.”

So it was that, still dazed with wine and sleep and half dressed, the runaways were lined up and taken first to the Police Station, where they were charged with insubordination against Authority and the Regulations, and then led off to jail. They stayed there one day.

Once the wine had worn off they understood that Superior Camilla was not to be trifled with, and almost all of them - except a few who were dismissed because their presence in the Hospital amounted to sheer abuse - not wanting to lose the benefit of a comfortable free hotel, accepted the conditions laid down by the Regulations, backed by a few precise and strict penalties. Among the townspeople there was some momentary surprise; but in time most understood and approved. And the archbishop soon had the hospital garden enclosed by a less symbolic wall.

Life settled into a normal rhythm and the work began to flourish.

Adventures and Misadventures

Time passed quickly. Elections were held in 1884, but Doctor Arce was not elected. The honor and burden of beginning the reconstruction of the nation, exhausted by the consequences of the unfortunate war against Chile, fell to Señor Gregorio Pacheco, likewise a man of remarkable moral integrity and a sincere friend of the sisters.

The work of the Daughters of St. Anne had also developed rapidly. Following the directives of the Holy See, the Foundress had given an organic structure and unified direction to the Institute's various and by now numerous houses, grouping them into canonical Provinces. The Houses in Bolivia too now formed a Province, under the guidance of Superior Camilla, who had extended the sisters' presence to the hospitals of Cochabamba and Oruro, and in Sucre had opened a girls' College and founded a Novitiate, to which many young women were already coming. And to meet the requests arriving from every part of Bolivia, Mother Rosa had prepared a new group of twenty-four sisters: on their arrival Provincial Camilla decided to open a College and a hospital in Potosí, and the same in Tarija. She divided the newcomers into four groups of six sisters each, placed a superior at the head of each, and decided to accompany each group to its destination.

Today, with at most three or four hours' flying, one can reach the Bolivian towns farthest apart. Then it took a long time and well-equipped caravans led by experienced people. The first contingent consisted of the Provincial and the twelve sisters bound for Potosí, led by an adequate number of escorts. The whole journey was to be made on horseback, followed by mules carrying the provisions. The horses and mules were for the most part provided for the sisters by Doctor Arce, who remained the most devoted friend and the most valuable protector of the Daughters of St. Anne.

The twelve sisters, young and daring, cheerfully bade Sucre farewell and set out joking merrily about their poor horsemanship. The caravan was led by an arriero who showed the way; the sisters followed, and the escorts brought up the rear, leading the mules laden with arms, mattresses and provisions. The journey, quiet at first, was enlivened at a certain point by the adventures of Sr. A. Stefania and her mount. This sister, very lively by temperament but not an equally skilled horsewoman, had been given a mule as lively as herself. After several fruitless attempts to come to an understanding with her mount, Sr. A. Stefania demanded a change. It was the provincial, now an experienced rider, who gave her her own docile, gentle little mare, taking the contrary mule for herself. Sr. A. Stefania, true to her nature, showed her joy by lavishing hugs and kind words on the mare, and in the end, perhaps to seal the new partnership with a touch of devotion, she had the ill-starred idea of tying a scapular of Our Lady around its ears. If only she hadn't! Docile and gentle until then, the little mare made it clear she did not like that annoying addition to her harness at all, and began to kick and rear. The sister's attempts to soothe her were useless: a more vigorous buck sent her head over heels.

Much commotion, groans from the victim, comments and laughter from the others once they realized their sister had broken nothing. When she had been hoisted back into the saddle she was advised to rein in both her lively impulses and her devotional displays. And the journey resumed, calm and monotonous, winding for hours and hours along the paths cut into the mountainsides above Sucre. The journey became more tiring when they had to tackle the mighty, bare and deserted massif of the Potosí mountains, at four thousand meters. And deep was the sigh of relief with which the sisters greeted the sight of the first houses of the highest city in Bolivia, the goal of their journey.

Farewell to “Incognito,” Provincial Camilla!

When the sisters arrived, Potosí was no longer the rich, populous city of Spanish times, crowded with miners, adventurers and merchants. With the mines exhausted, that intense but artificial life had died out, and ruined churches and houses bore witness to its decline. Very lively, however, was the interest the townspeople showed in the sisters' arrival. A celebrations committee headed by a relative of Doctor Arce had prepared a solemn reception in the purest tradition of Spanish ceremonial.

A group of gentlemen was waiting for them at the entrance to the city: a brief exchange of courtesies, then a single procession formed to the spacious house prepared to receive the sisters with every comfort possible in that time and place. The procession stopped in the large courtyard in front of the house, and the gentlemen, according to ceremonial, hastened to offer the sisters their hands, on which each was to rest her foot and then spring lightly and, if possible... gracefully to the ground. In the confusion a particularly stout and important-looking gentleman stepped forward with a sweeping flourish of his hat, asking which was the superior appointed to the hospital of Potosí. Sr. A. Stefania was pointed out to him, still sitting stiff and upright in the saddle, and the gentleman rushed toward her to perform the rite. But whether from the cavalier's excessive emotion, hampered among other things by his own bulk, or from the sister's clumsiness, or both, the two of them lost their balance and tumbled to the ground. And that was the inglorious way in which Sr. A. Stefania, newly appointed superior of the hospital of Potosí, touched the soil of the city and in some fashion took possession of her new office and dignity.

The incident was smoothed over, chiefly by playing down its comedy. The group was shown into a richly furnished room where they found refreshment before making their solemn entrance into the Hospital, where they were awaited by the Authorities and the directors, doctors, nurses, students and a large crowd of guests, all bursting with more or less interested curiosity. And the inevitable round of speeches began. Every important person, and there were many, felt obliged to offer his greetings, to give thanks, to wish every possible good to the newcomers, to the institution and to the whole city, while someone asked his neighbor, in a low but not so low voice, whether the sisters would be able to reply, as custom required. The murmur, perhaps skeptical or mischievous, reached the ears of the new superior, who, fully recovered from her recent mishap, considered it her bounden duty to return the praise and good wishes. So, as soon as there was a pause, ignoring the provincial's tugs at her sleeve, she launched with astonishing nerve into a greeting and speech of thanks stuffed with ustedes and nosotras, buenos and bravos, mucho mucho, and plenty of final os and as, against an unmistakable background of Italian-Piacenza idiom.

The gentlemen listened in polite silence, but those rascals of students went wild and, with shouts of “bravo, bene, bis,” obtained a wicked encore, cut short only by the provincial's firm intervention. Once the courtesies and compliments were over, however, they got down to business; intense hospital work soon began, and Sr. A. Stefania had the chance to show her gifts as a practical and efficient organizer and a skillful and compassionate nurse, and to win applause less noisy but more substantial and better deserved than the first. At the same time, with fewer speeches but equal commitment, the girls' College was opened.

Having made sure the work in the two houses was properly under way, the provincial sent to Sucre for the group of sisters assigned to Tarija; and when they had arrived and rested a few days, they set off with the Provincial for their new destination.

Again long days on horseback through deserted places and impassable trails; but as they left the desolate lands of Potosí behind, descending from four thousand to two thousand meters, the sisters saw the signs of human and plant life belonging to a milder climate.

And here was Tarija, a charming little town gently spread out toward the river. The houses, mostly surrounded by vegetable gardens and flower gardens, looked cheerful, and the people were cordial; told of the sisters' arrival, they poured out of their houses and went to meet them, led by the Authorities and the pupils of the College of the Friars Minor. The welcoming ceremony was less solemn than in Potosí, but very spontaneous: shouts of welcome, showers of flowers, pealing bells; the crush made it hard even to dismount.

When, with difficulty because of the pressing crowd, they reached the house set aside as their residence, the string of speeches began: only a colorful reply from Sr. A. Stefania was missing, but there was so much excitement that no one missed it. And at last evening came: the sisters dreamed of nothing but a long, restoring sleep after the fatigue of the long journey and the emotion of their arrival.

Not a bit of it! Outside the crowd went on cheering and showed no sign of leaving. In fact... “Look, here comes the band,” murmured the poor exhausted sisters, “too much of a good thing! We really didn't need it. But listen, listen! Italian music: here's Donizetti, Bellini, Verdi...”.

The band strikes up:

“O Signor che dal tetto natìo ci chiamasti con santa promessa...”.

That was the last straw! What a pang of homesickness, at the thought of their homeland so far away, of home, of their mothers, of all the dear things and people left behind... The mournful, pleading music fills the rooms where the young sisters, in tears, repeat: “Yes, we are here for you, Lord, who called us; for you, in this unknown land, among this people of whom we know nothing, toward an unknown future. But you are here with us as in Italy, Lord... We trust in you!”

As the triumphal march from Aida bursts forth, merciful sleep descends on eyelids wet with tears.

The Unexpected

In Tarija, which together with La Paz (though in the opposite direction) was the house farthest from the center, the Provincial had decided to stay two months. She wanted to make sure the sisters had a sufficient command of the language and gained experience in their respective duties, while she worked to establish cordial relations and useful understandings with the Authorities and the people. She too, moreover, badly needed rest after the long, tiring journeys and before facing the one back to Sucre. But then came the unexpected: a letter from the Mother General ordering her to go at once to La Paz to replace Superior Giuseppa Troni, who had been recalled to Italy for good.

After a first instinctive reaction of surprised regret, the provincial managed to smile: “At once to La Paz! Easier said than done!” In Italy they had no idea of the distances and of the conditions of travel. From Tarija to La Paz meant crossing a good part of Bolivia, through country more mountainous and rugged than Switzerland. Going as fast as possible, no less than a month's journey. “No matter: we shall obey.”

Making use of the help generously offered by the Prefect of Tarija, Don Domingo Paz, and taking advantage of the company of some local gentlemen bound for Sucre, she set out for that city and arrived without incident. The journey from Sucre to La Paz, on the other hand, held many unknowns. First of all, lack of funds prevented her from fitting out a proper caravan, while the political situation was anything but calm and the President himself advised against the journey. But besides obeying the Mother, the provincial had of necessity to take two sisters from Sucre to La Paz: “Whatever it costs, I will go.”

The necessary help was found, from President Pacheco, Doctor Arce and the Archbishop, and a small expedition could be organized. As escort and traveling companion the archbishop assigned to it a priest he trusted, and the President, not to be outdone, entrusted the sisters to his personal majordomo. The group was completed by two escorts and a servant in charge of the mules carrying the baggage and the provisions donated by the well-to-do families of Sucre.

Men

Since the equipment gave her sufficient security, the provincial decided to take advantage of the journey to visit Cochabamba and then head for Oruro before reaching La Paz. At first no incident disturbed the peaceful ride; the monotony of the journey was relieved by the sisters' prayers and by the endless arguments between the majordomo and the priest. The former talkative and boastful, the latter rather taciturn but biting in his retorts whenever - and it happened often - he felt needled by his companion. And never in agreement on any point whatever. Decidedly opposite temperaments, which nonetheless had two things in common: a fondness for aguardiente and a remarkable dose of prudence which, when put to the test - and in due course it was - could be mistaken for plain fear. Evidently neither the archbishop nor the president knew their men well, for in truth they could not be considered shrewd guides or effective protectors; but for want of better, they served to enliven the company.

Discussions on the most trivial subjects often degenerated into quarrels, especially when a more generous drink had loosened their tongues. And the sisters were amused to note the obstinacy worthy of a better cause and the eloquence with which each defended and upheld his own point of view. The discord, however, subsided automatically at the sight of a little flag hoisted on the branches of two shrubs bent into an arch, the sign of a place selling liquor. Then the two were quick to slip away without a word, reappearing a little later trotting hard to catch up with the group, their cheeks rosier and their eyes brighter than before.

It was a great comfort to the sisters to be able sometimes to spend the night near a village, however poor, which let them break the fatigue of the march and rest a little more comfortably, even if inside a hut of mud and straw. And they also found the chance for a little apostolate among those good Indians, simple and unlettered but with hearts instinctively open to the word of God, and always generously hospitable. When people and animals had rested sufficiently, the caravan would form up again and set off, usually escorted for a few kilometers by the parish priest, if there was one, or by the village headman; and everyone was always generous with useful advice and warnings about the road to the next stage.

... and Beasts...

They came within sight of Cochabamba, the city lying in the valley of the Mizque River. They stayed there three days and left after a little rest, some discussion of small local problems, advice and mutual farewells. After Cochabamba the caravan began to climb toward the now very near mountains, along rough trails. The air was cold even in the sun. The men urged on the horses and now and then fired a shot to keep wild animals away and ward off dangers of every kind. Once over the summit, they began to descend toward Oruro. But suddenly the horses grew restless and began to kick and neigh as if sensing danger. The arriero spurred his horse to a gallop and scouted the road, standing up in the saddle to see as far as possible. Suddenly he wheeled his horse round and, spurring it on, sent it down a side trail, signaling to the others to follow and shouting: “The bulls, the bulls!”

The others dashed after him, whipping the sisters' horses too; the sisters, not yet grasping the real extent of the danger, let themselves be carried along, trusting in Providence and the proven skill of the guides. Meanwhile the arrieros, looking back, could already see a dense gray mass charging headlong toward the group.

“We must reach the river,” they shouted, “before the herd reaches us.” And they kept up the breathless gallop while the sinister bellowing of the enraged beasts could already be heard.

At last the shining ribbon of the river appeared below. “On, on!” urged the men; and the sisters, who now fully understood what danger threatened them, held on tight in the saddle and spurred on their horses. It was a miracle that, galloping like that over broken ground, none of them fell. They reached the river: “Quick, in!” and the horses plunged instinctively into the water just as the bulls, horns menacingly lowered, were about to catch them. Reaching the opposite bank, men and women dismounted and looked at one another. Pale, panting, but safe! On the other bank the baffled bulls sniffed the water, still bellowing; but they had lost some of their ferocity and gradually calmed down, scattering along the bank or going back into the trees, while the sun sank behind the mountains and the cold grew intense, making the poor survivors in their soaked clothes shiver. They went on toward Oruro only as far as was needed to find a suitable place for the night; fires were lit, they changed their clothes, setting the wet ones by the fire, and they had what supper they could.

After the sisters had prayed with inexpressible gratitude to God, everyone lay down to sleep.

The horses were left loose to find their own food; the men lay in a group, wrapped in their wide cloaks, their heads resting on their saddles for pillows. The sisters huddled closer together than usual, with blankets, cushions and saddles, their faces covered against the night frost. And everyone slept.

The provincial too had been asleep for some time, but she felt as if immersed in a kind of half-sleep in which she relived the recent adventure. There were the bulls still chasing her, ever closer, dark and monstrous, and the horses plunging into the water; but the herd did not stop: the bulls too were swimming, slow and menacing, coming closer; coming right toward her; she could even feel their hot breath on her face...

But... this feeling of warmth was real! The provincial opens her eyes: in the uncertain light of dawn a gray mass looms over her, two reddish, bloodshot eyes stare at her; a horrible stench passes over her face and she hears a sinister bellow; a shaggy head topped by two great horns is swaying above hers; it is not a dream, it is real! She rouses herself with difficulty and, overcoming the terror that freezes her, manages with a desperate effort to cry out: “Sisters, men, the bull!”

While the bull goes on sniffing, the provincial hears the arriero's loud shout: “Don't move, keep absolutely still!” She understands that she must keep as flat to the ground as possible so that the bull's sharp horns can find no hold on her body. She gathers her strength and waits, calling in her heart on St. Anne and holding her breath, also to master the nausea caused by the beast's horrible stench.

A few eternal minutes: shots ring out, there is a gallop of horses and bellows of pain; still motionless, the provincial opens her eyes: the bull is no longer over her. The men had cleverly fired so as not to kill it outright, lest its bulk collapse on top of her, but had finished it off further away; the huge, still mass lies not far off. She is safe, once again! The few other bulls that had crossed the river were scattered by the shots; not one is to be seen any more, only their distant gallop can be heard.

The men who had chased them on horseback return victorious and at the same time ashamed: they admit they had been careless, for the night before, exhausted, they had trusted in the false security of the river and neglected to set watches for the night. Meanwhile the provincial gave heartfelt thanks to Providence, which had guarded her better than the men, and told of that kind of dream which had turned out to be true, recognizing in it the hand of Providence. The sisters wept with emotion, and the men, deeply impressed, from that moment on surrounded the provincial with even greater respect and reverence. They gathered up cloaks and blankets, rounded up the horses, which had scattered when the bulls appeared, and after a light breakfast set off again through lonely mountains and valleys.

After crossing the Hailla pass, at four thousand meters, they made a steep descent and reached Oruro, the city ruled by sun and wind.

A Petty Dictator

When the sisters arrived, Oruro was somewhat like Potosí: in the middle of an arid territory more like desert than countryside. Lower, and less ringed by mountains, it nonetheless gave the same sense of bleakness. In Oruro the sisters stopped only as long as needed for a little rest and some shopping, and hurried on again through the monotony of the endless puna.

Along the roadside, set like sentries, tall pillars could be seen now and then. President Pacheco's man, who during the adventure with the bulls had shown singular discretion in word and deed, having now got his breath back, explained: “Those pillars marked the way for the Spaniards going from Lima to the silver mines of Potosí.”

“Is it true,” asked a sister, “that the mountain of Potosí is one whole cone of solid silver?”

“That is the legend,” put in the priest, also recovered and ready for fresh debate; “there was silver there once, and plenty of it. But now the mines are much poorer.”

“Not true,” the majordomo could not help contradicting; “the silver is still there all through the mountain. They don't find it because they don't know how to look for it.”

The squabble went on as the road continued monotonously; no sign of life, human or animal, except an occasional bird of some unknown species. But after the village of Sicasica the country changed, patches of green became frequent and the ground more uneven. In the distance the Illimani rose majestically, and opposite it the Sajama, equally white with snow. The majordomo again had to break the silence with his explanations: “Inside that mountain there is a very long staircase dug by the Incas, leading to the tomb of the Kings.”

“Another tall tale,” was the priest's retort.

“You don't believe it because you haven't seen it.”

“And have you?” the other asked sarcastically.

Unable to claim it in good conscience, the majordomo for once held his tongue.

The landscape grew livelier. Groups of vicuñas appeared and disappeared; small herds of llamas or donkeys, driven by pairs of cholos, dotted the land. The road grew steeper, the air thinner. At last real countryside appeared.

Leaving an ancient village on their right, the caravan went on. And so for a few more days, stopping briefly for frugal meals and sleeping in the open in the mild climate, until, having crossed the last barrier of mountains, they reached La Paz.

La Paz, today the seat of government, was then a pretty, cheerful little city spread over the slopes of the hills that crown the very high basin formed by the Cordillera Real. The Illimani towered imposingly above it.

The hospitals where the Daughters of St. Anne worked were then on the outskirts of the town. Great was their mutual joy at meeting, but after the night's rest the provincial had to inform Superior Giuseppa and the community of the Mother's order.

“My God,” said the superior, “I am ready to obey, but to avoid trouble we must inform Señor Zapata, president of all the city's hospitals, in good time.”

“We shall inform him,” said the provincial calmly.

But the meeting with the president, summoned urgently, was anything but calm. Conscious of the importance of his office, he did not hesitate to order the provincial to go back to Sucre without Superior Giuseppa, since in La Paz he was in command and recognized no other authority, either in Sucre or in Rome. The provincial, however, found a way to bring the name of the President of the Republic into the discussion, and that, together with the sister's long and patient arguments, finally brought Señor Zapata round to a milder view.

Deep down, the president's opposition, however unrestrained, did not displease the provincial. After all, it showed the esteem in which he held Superior Giuseppa and his fear of the harm the hospital might suffer from losing so valuable a director. In the end, invoking the looming shadow of the high officials residing in the Capital, and pressing the point a little, Sr. A. Camilla managed to get the superior away without further incident, and could then allow herself a two-month stay in La Paz, to Señor Zapata's entire satisfaction.

Unreliable Guides and Unwanted Protectors

With spring well advanced, the provincial decided to return to Sucre. The journey promised to be hard because the rains were imminent, but it was now urgent to leave. Among other things, Sr. A. Camilla had to take two sisters from La Paz to Oruro and pass through Cochabamba again to collect fourteen young postulants who were to begin their novitiate year in Sucre. Besides, the experience of the dangers faced and hardships overcome on her previous journeys had well tempered her, and she felt perfectly at home in those regions where the daily struggle against nature's pitfalls was the normal stuff of life. So she decided to set out.

There was no need to hire new escorts besides the man who led the pack mules. The priest and the majordomo who had come with her so far knew the road well and, now eager to resume their usual lives, declared themselves more than ready for the return journey. And it was rather comical to hear them lavishing assurances: “As long as we are here, Mother, you need fear nothing.”

The provincial, who had already tested their valor, kept silent and smiled to herself, trusting rather in Providence, of which she had had more convincing proofs.

They set out. And there was the familiar scenery: there was the village of Sicasica and soon after Oruro. A day's halt; brief affectionate farewells, a few recommendations, and off again.

They took the road to Cochabamba again; the puna reappeared, they recrossed the river that had saved them and climbed again the wearisome Tapacarí mountain. No sign of bulls. And it must be admitted that the two stalwarts were extremely vigilant: if they were lucky enough not to have to prove their valor, it was not their fault.

But... the last word had not been said: the caravan was already setting out on the last stretch of road to Cochabamba when it ran into a squad of mounted soldiers advancing at a furious gallop. When they reached our group, the man who seemed to be in command halted the little caravan with a hoarse “Halt!”; to avoid being ridden down it had pressed against the hillside.

A sort of interrogation began: the priest and the majordomo, who to make matters worse were rather befuddled by the fumes of a recent drink, were unable to stand up to the arrogance of the soldiers, who claimed the right to take the sisters into their charge - for their protection, since women alone could not do without their escort - in exchange, of course, for liberal drinks.

The provincial, who tried to protest and was quivering with indignation, could not make herself heard. The names of President Pacheco and Doctor Arce would certainly have carried weight, but the two men were unable to use them. Indeed they did worse: they let themselves be surrounded by the squad, almost like hostages, and all together trotted off toward a little flag not far away, the sign of a liquor shop. The sisters, disgusted, rode slowly on without deigning to look at them.

A short way further on, another furious gallop: a lone man this time, carrying on his saddle a sort of bundle he seemed to want to hide. Unluckily for him, one of the soldiers sitting at the tavern door caught sight of him and raised the alarm: “There's the deserter! That's the man we're looking for!”

The whole squad, forgetting to pay for their drinks, set off in pursuit, dragging the two half-dazed hostages after them; the deserter, for his part, had dropped the bundle as he fled. The sisters stopped, bewildered; shots were already echoing in the distance.

What were they to do? With both their escorts vanished, they were unsure whether to stop and wait for the man leading the pack mules or to go on without escort, trusting in Providence.

While they were discussing what to do they heard a wail, like a child crying, coming from the spot where the fugitive had dropped the supposed bundle.

“Could it be a child?” cried one of the sisters, and rushed toward the place the crying came from. It was indeed a child of about two who, freed from the cloak he had been wrapped in, was thrashing about in distress. A quick examination showed he had suffered only a few small grazes in the fall; he was tended, fed and comforted.

“Poor man!” said the sisters, thinking of the fugitive; “even if he is guilty of some crime, he must be in anguish, not only for his own life but for his child's.” The little one's babbling had in fact made the sisters understand that the fleeing man was his father.

Meanwhile the shouting and shooting had stopped, and the mule driver had not come. The sisters were alone in the vast, silent desert. But Providence did not fail them: after about half an hour's wait a horseman came toward the group who had every appearance of a rich merchant, judging by his thoroughbred horse and the luxury of the harness and weapons hanging from his saddle. He recognized the sisters as belonging to the same order as those serving in the hospital of Cochabamba, and at once put himself at their disposal for whatever they might need.

The provincial, reassured by the horseman's honest look and manner of speaking, told him of their situation.

The gentleman's face darkened: “So those two cowards have abandoned you? I'll see to it! Which way did the soldiers go?” They showed him, and he galloped off.

Some hours passed; meanwhile the mules with the provisions had arrived, and the sisters were able to eat and to care better for the child, who, having lost all fear, was now smiling and trusting. And at last, as evening turned to dusk, three horsemen appeared. The two in front seemed to be urged on by the whip of the one riding behind, who now laid it on the horses to make them hurry, and now - and it did not seem a mistake - on the backs of the hapless riders, who took it in silence.

“The deserter hasn't been found yet,” the gentleman told the sisters, “but don't be afraid; the soldiers have gone another way.” And without deigning to look at the two men, he went on: “I'll take the child with me. Rest assured I shall look after him.” And without giving the sisters time to say “thank you,” with a sweep of his hat and a bow worthy of a Grandee of Spain, he lifted the child onto his saddle, spurred his horse and rode away.

The End of the Adventure

The delay caused by these strange events meant that night found the little caravan still far from its goal. Fortunately one of the sisters who had come from La Paz and was bound for Cochabamba had a sister living not far from where events had held them up. She told the provincial: “My sister has a fairly large country house; she can easily put us up for the night.”

Everyone gladly accepted the offer, and so, for the rest of the night at least, the party could enjoy the comforts of a civilized, well-appointed home and rest from the fatigue and emotions of the day.

Late in the morning they set off again for Cochabamba. The two culprits kept silent, and the provincial repaid them with equal silence. At a certain point they were overtaken by a group of Indians carrying a wounded or sick man on a stretcher made of woven branches. Three mounted soldiers escorted them. The sisters realized it was the deserter; caught and shot by the soldiers, he was being taken to Cochabamba to stand trial. The sisters would have liked to do something for him, for he looked very weak - at least to find out the nature of his wounds and his general condition, and to give advice on how to carry him - but the soldiers would not allow it. The wounded man too showed a wish to speak to the sisters, perhaps to ask about the child, but he had not even the strength to raise himself. The two groups went on in the same direction, but each on its own.

Later the provincial, who stayed several weeks in Cochabamba, was able to see the deserter again, a patient in the hospital guarded day and night by a soldier. She heard a very sad story of poverty and misfortune rather than of guilt, and was able to reassure him about the fate of his child, who was being cared for and brought up as a son by the rich merchant. When the trial began the sisters were called to testify and did what they could to help the poor man, who was nonetheless condemned to death.

Sucre at Last

Summer was now close, and one rainstorm followed another. One morning that promised a mild, clear day, the provincial set out again for the capital with the group of fourteen postulants who were to begin their novitiate year in Sucre. The brilliant pair of the priest and the majordomo were there too, though after their inglorious adventure on the Cochabamba road they had become much less talkative and boastful. In fact, as they drew near Sucre, each was afraid, one of the President, the other of the Archbishop, whose trust had been so miserably betrayed.

“Will the provincial keep quiet?” each wondered inwardly, and they made themselves useful by tirelessly performing every kind of service.

The days were often punctuated by violent downpours that sometimes caught the travelers by surprise and from which poncho and sombrero were not enough to shelter them.

It was after a particularly rainy day, which had sorely tried the endurance of sisters and girls alike, that the idea arose of making a small detour to Doctor Arce's large estate, where they could stop for a little rest and check over all their gear, which the bad weather had damaged.

The owners were not at home, but the steward welcomed them with every attention, and the rest was truly welcome to all. They left after two days, hoping to reach Sucre by evening. But at midday the sky suddenly darkened, and the rumble of thunder announced another storm.

“Hold tight in the saddle and quicken the trot,” shouted the majordomo; “a nasty storm is coming, and now we absolutely must reach Sucre before nightfall.” But the girls' lack of skill made it impossible to put the horses to a gallop; and in the darkness, which had fallen early and was split by lightning, the road became dangerous. After a few slips the horses fell into a walk by instinct. The women, bewildered, automatically followed the men, who went ahead shouting to show the way... The priest, on that occasion, was entirely himself again. Knowing the road well, quick and efficient, he went back and forth on foot, splashing through water up to his calves, and with curt, precise orders gave everyone confidence.

It was an ordeal lasting several hours, but they pressed on until, in the exhausted silence of men and beasts, the distant lights of the city were glimpsed through the threads of rain.

“A little more and we're there!” shouted the priest. “Courage!”

They took heart again and, dripping and soaked to the bone, reached their goal.

A Difficult Obedience

In the summer of 1885 the College in Sucre, where the provincial had resumed her office as superior, was running splendidly, as were the other works in the city.

As far as the distance and the relative punctuality of the postal service allowed, Mother Rosa was kept informed of everything and had full confidence in the provincial's work. But the speed with which her daughters' work was spreading in a land so far away and so different from Italy made her anxious. She therefore felt the need to hear from the lips of the person most directly responsible a description of the situation in all its aspects. And having also decided to bring some sisters home while she was preparing others for a coming expedition, she summoned Provincial Camilla to Piacenza.

Though ready to obey, she clearly saw the difficulties that her absence, inevitably a long one, might cause the Bolivian communities. So she set out to deal, as far as possible, with every humanly foreseeable difficulty before she left. Nor did she hide from herself the difficulties she would certainly meet from outside as well: from the Arce family above all. She decided to visit them at once; then she would go to the archbishop, who as a priest - so Sr. A. Camilla thought - would understand and, if anything, make things easier.

Welcomed with the warmest cordiality by Doctor Arce and his wife, she listened in courteous silence to the expected protests of the lady, who pointed out the dangers that might arise from her long absence, especially for the more recently established communities. Doctor Arce, on the other hand, said nothing.

“The Mother orders me to go,” the provincial said at last, “and all I can do is obey. I do not hide the difficulties from myself, but I am taking the necessary steps to deal with them as far as possible. The communities are headed by wise and prudent superiors, and as for what I cannot foresee, I entrust myself and everything to the Lord.”

Then Doctor Arce spoke: “I too think that the provincial's absence is untimely in itself. But if she has received an order, she must go.”

As always, his mettle as an honest gentleman showed through, strict with himself and with others where duty was concerned. The Provincial felt comforted.

“The Mother has written to me too,” Doctor Arce went on, “explaining the reason for the summons. And I have already replied, assuring her that I would put no obstacle in the way; on the contrary, the provincial could count on me for anything she might need.”

Everything had been said. All three fell silent, visibly moved, and after a brief discussion of some minor details the provincial took her leave, satisfied.

She went straight to the Archbishop, regarding this visit more as an act of dutiful deference than as an obstacle to be overcome. Instead, to her surprise, it proved the opposite.

Once the initial disagreement had been overcome, relations between the Archbishop and the provincial had become most cordial, and their mutual understanding had greatly helped the founding and strengthening of the works. The Archbishop was now a true father to the sisters, especially to the provincial, who was greatly surprised to hear him say flatly: “You cannot go to Italy. It's absurd.”

“Your Excellency,” she stammered, “it is an order from the Mother General.”

“The Mother has written to me too, and I think it is an invitation rather than a real command. And although she has assured me you will return, I think it unwise to leave communities and works just now, and for who knows how long.”

Sr. A. Camilla tried to insist, but was told: “Write. Set out the whole situation in writing, but don't move for the time being.”

The sister understood that at that moment it was best to say nothing and withdraw; the prelate's firm opposition had caught her off guard; what if he was right? Pray. Pray, and have others pray, to know God's will. But... was Mother Rosa not its most legitimate interpreter for her daughters?!

For some days she lived in anguished perplexity. In the end she went back to the Archbishop resolved to follow his advice, whatever it might be. And to her great surprise she found him completely changed. When she told him she was ready to follow his directions, he seemed to make an effort to turn away from some greater thought that absorbed him inwardly.

At last he spoke slowly and in a low voice: “I repeat that I do not like to see you go, for who knows how long. You are needed here. Your energetic presence gives the sisters peace of mind and keeps out any untimely interference by outsiders. The Authorities esteem and respect you... But if you regard the Mother's summons as a precise expression of her will, go. After all, only God knows which may be worth more, your going or your staying.”

He was silent again, as if lost in thought, then went on: “I foresee that during your absence various things will happen” - and he named them - “perhaps none of this would happen if you were here, but, I repeat, God alone knows the future.”

“Your Excellency, I hope it won't happen.”

As if he had not heard, the Bishop went on: “Go to Italy. God will help you. Remember me when you are in Rome.”

“Your Excellency, I don't know whether I shall go to Rome. The Mother is calling me to Piacenza.”

“You will go, my child, I am sure of it. You will go with the Foundress. And by then I shall no longer be on this earth.”

“Father, what are you saying!”

“I should so much have liked to have you beside me at the end. But perhaps that was only selfishness. God's will be done.”

Tears were now running down the face of the sister, who could not speak.

“In Rome a Franciscan father will bring you the news of my death. Pray for me then, pray a great deal.”

The tall, gaunt figure seemed to sway, but he raised his hand in blessing. The provincial knelt, gazing at that face from which a glow of light seemed to shine. And she withdrew in silence, her heart in turmoil. On the way she tried in vain to give the Prelate's words a less dramatic meaning.

“Perhaps he is not well and thinks he will die soon. But I hope he is mistaken.” Yet the disquiet remained as she busied herself with preparations for her departure.

The Good Seed Sprouts

Meanwhile, within the walls of the College, a little conspiracy was being hatched under the eyes of the sisters, who saw and... did not see.

The boarders came from the best families of Sucre and the surrounding area, but the school was also open to day pupils, among whom were many girls from families of very modest, if not actually poor, means. In the absence of any organized assistance from the Municipality, several of them could not obtain the books, exercise books and all the school supplies they needed. The sisters remedied the inequality this created among the pupils as best they could, so that no one should lose the benefit of attending school, but sometimes they could not spare the less well-off some small but unpleasant humiliation.

One fine day a tiny committee of boarders, led by young Miss Inés Arce, aged thirteen, came to invite the provincial to a farewell evening they had organized. The guest could do nothing but accept.

The evening began and went on with music, songs, dances, dialogues... But at a certain point, at the climax of the party, the little president of the committee came forward and, with a short speech suited to the occasion, handed the astonished and moved provincial a purse full of gold coins, asking her to buy in Italy all the school supplies needed, bearing in mind as recipients their poor classmates who could not afford them.

For Sr. A. Camilla it was a moment of real joy and great encouragement: if the education given by her sisters bore such fruit, she could leave with an easier mind; the works were in good hands.

A Hotel of an Unusual Kind

Soon the little caravan was ready: the provincial, two sisters going home, and an Oratorian Father1, a native of Bolivia, who was going to Italy for the first time. Led by two utterly faithful arrieros, it set off through the mountains of the Cordillera.

It is easy to imagine the sisters' feelings as they traveled again along roads they knew. How many happy and sad events, how many dangers safely overcome must they have recalled! But with what different feelings: they had come full of anxiety about the unknown, and now they carried in their hearts a longing for a deeply loved country.

Mountains, rivers, villages; here was Tupiza, the last little town before the border. It was the rainy season again, and the weather was unkind; great gusts of wind made riding hard and dangerous. The loneliness of the country took on a threatening look, and their nights were often disturbed by thunder and lightning.

One evening when the weather was particularly bad, Father Taborga, the Oratorian, remarked: “Tonight it will be impossible to sleep in the open. If we don't find shelter in time, I would advise staying awake and riding on slowly; we'll rest tomorrow, whenever and wherever we can.”

But before night fell, in the middle of a green little valley, a small square building appeared, closed on all sides except for a small window two-thirds of the way up the wall.

“Here's something for us,” said the Father; “if it's big enough it will house us all.” And he urged his horse in that direction. But when they reached the foot of that strange building the provincial asked: “And the door?”

“There it is,” said the Father, laughing, and pointed to the window. And seeing the sisters' mistrustful expression he added: “You can see we have no other choice.”

But the sisters still hesitated. “Don't be afraid,” insisted the Father, who knew the ways of that land; “it is certainly a very ancient Inca dwelling, perhaps belonging to a well-to-do family, since the poor Indians lived in huts; that opening is both window and door, placed high up for defense.” The arrieros nodded.

“As you see,” the Father went on, “the opening faces east, so that the inhabitants, as soon as they woke, could address their prayer to the Sun god.”

The wind blew ever more furiously, but the sisters' skepticism did not give way. And to add to the difficulties one of the arrieros spoke up: “I won't set foot in there in any case, because the spirits of the dead live in those little houses.”

The other said nothing, and only after a few ironic remarks from the Father did he make up his mind to stand up in the saddle and look in through the window to see whether there were animals, brushwood or other obstacles inside. Meanwhile night was closing in.

With his head and shoulders through the window, the man struck a match and inspected the inside of the house, if house it could be called; it was really a cell, empty and fairly clean, but so small that only the three sisters could get in, which did not seem to displease the arriero.

They made up their minds. The maneuver to take temporary possession of the ancient Inca dwelling was long and difficult, but with much pushing and slipping the three sisters got inside and received blankets and food from the men.

By candlelight they examined the whole place carefully: no apparent danger, but little room; they could only crouch as best they could; but the walls gave good shelter from the rain and wind.

The men settled down outside, sheltered from the wind by the house, and made a sort of trench around themselves with the saddles and baggage. And they slept a short sleep heavy with fatigue, wrapped in their wide cloaks. At dawn, after helping the sisters with their laborious exit from the refuge, they set off again. By evening they reached the Argentine border at La Quiaca.

Does Mother Rosa Intervene?

They now had to come down from the crest of the arid mountains that crown the Jujuy region with menacing ridges, while the roads were slippery with rain and mountain followed mountain, giving the distressing feeling that they would never end. The arrieros seemed a little uneasy: they were about to enter a dark forest where it was not unusual to meet hyenas and panthers.

“Let's try not to be caught by nightfall,” said the man acting as guide after they had gone a long way. But as darkness began to fall they found they were still deep inside it. The men grew more and more worried; to keep wild animals away they fired a shot now and then. Suddenly, as the darkness thickened, they thought they saw a reddish glow among the trees.

“It's a fire!” cried the man in front in alarm. “The forest is burning!” And he was about to flee and make the others flee when Father Taborga, looking more calmly, shouted: “Stop! The fire isn't spreading. There are people there.”

Among the flames, in fact, human figures could be seen moving, their outlines growing gradually clearer. “They're children,” one of the sisters said a moment later.

“It must be some Indian village,” said the guide with relief; “then we're saved.”

Through the tree trunks, which now seemed less dense, they could see some little boys busy feeding the flames with dry branches. When the party came closer the boys came forward with broad smiles and bows and signaled to them to follow up a small hill on which stood a hut. Out of it came an Indian couple, who greeted the sisters without a trace of surprise, as if they had been expecting them, with a deep bow and respectful words.

“I had my sons light the fire to show you the way,” said the man with a satisfied smile.

“But how,” asked the provincial in amazement, “did you know we would pass this way?”

“This morning a lady dressed like you, but with a very, very sad face, came and said to me: ‘Perhaps tonight my daughters will get lost in the forest. You are a faithful servant of Jesus Christ; try to come to their help.’”

“A lady dressed like me? Where did you see her?”

“As I told you, this morning, in the forest.”

And the man spoke with such simple truthfulness that the sisters fell silent, like people faced with an intervention that nature cannot explain.

“St. Anne? Or... Mother Rosa? Could the Lord, among so many gifts, have granted her that of bilocation?”

“You see, mamita,” the Indian went on, “I thought: if they have to cross the forest, it's a good idea to light a big fire. They're bound to see that even from far away, and so they'll come to us.”

The man's simplicity was matched by the silent emotion of the members of the caravan. Even the guides had moist eyes. Only for the Indian was it all quite normal, and he went on smiling contentedly while his wife busied herself preparing food.

After eating they lay down to rest, but the sisters could neither sleep nor stop talking among themselves:

“A lady dressed like us! Provincial, what are we to think?”

“Let us think how great and good the Lord is, sisters. He alone can. He alone knows. Let us say together: thank you, Lord, for saving us once again!”

A last soft murmur of prayers and at last sleep. Stillness and warmth. The fire kept the wild beasts away, and even the forest seemed to fall silent.

In the morning, a quick bustle of men and animals. To the sisters, who thanked him with emotion, the Indian said: “When you come back this way, come to us again. We'll be waiting for you.”

“We don't know; but if it happens, we will certainly come again to greet you and thank you.”

And they said goodbye with deep emotion.

Never Had Europe Seemed So Far Away!

A brief stop at Jujuy. Then on, along the roads already traveled by the expedition led by Doctor Arce. From Salta to Tucumán still on horseback; by train from Tucumán to Córdoba; by train from Córdoba to Rosario; by river boat from Rosario to Buenos Aires. And there was the Atlantic Ocean; on the far shore, Europe; but no one, not even the Captain, knew how far away the European shore would prove to be this time!

Among the many steamers rocking in the waters of the port of Buenos Aires, the Adria stood out chiefly for her age. But she was the only Italian ship ready to sail, and Father Taborga was in a hurry to reach Italy. Old, but decently polished, was the Adria. Young Captain Rapallino set store by appearances, and the old steamer, freshly painted and with gleaming brass, managed to give herself airs. The passengers took their cabins, and a few days later the ship sailed.

Two days later Montevideo came into view, low on the coast beneath the Cerro.

A day's stop: passengers getting off, others coming aboard; a noisy crowd made up mostly of merchants, Italians among them, all absorbed in financial discussions. Families who can count themselves lucky because they are going home. Curious tourists. The ship sails again.

For some days all goes normally: calm sea, light wind and clear sky. But suddenly the ship gives an unexpected lurch, slows, and shortly afterward stops.

The captain, who was chatting on deck with Father Taborga, rushes to the hatch but comes straight back to reassure the alarmed passengers: “No need to worry; it's a minor fault in the propeller, which will soon be repaired.”

Indeed, after a careful examination and a makeshift repair the ship sets off again, but she seems to labor somewhat, and the uneasy passengers keep bombarding the crew with questions.

The captain decides to cut the already reduced speed to a minimum and sail along the coast to Santos, where the fault will be properly repaired before facing the open ocean.

The mountains of the Brazilian state of São Paulo come into sight; but as the ship prepares to enter the long channel leading into the port of Santos, the sailor on watch reports strange signals coming from the signal station. The captain raises his binoculars and deciphers: “Entry to port forbidden. Remain in quarantine.”

“Quarantine! Why?” mutters the astonished captain; and he orders a message sent ashore that there is no one sick on board. But the ban persists, inexorable: “Remain in quarantine!”

“Rather than sit in quarantine I'll face the Atlantic!” protests the indignant captain; he orders the crew to try to improve the propeller repair and, with a not exactly respectful farewell to the port authorities of Santos, heads for Rio de Janeiro.

Meanwhile the sea grows heavy and the ship makes her way through the waves with greater difficulty. Suddenly another unexpected stop, a clear sign of a further breakdown; greater panic among the passengers, ill-concealed dismay on the captain's part. With great effort the propeller is put right again, and for greater safety the sails are unfurled. But because the sail area is small the speed increases only a little, while people realize the new problems created by the unexpected loss of time, not least that of food supplies.

With great regret the captain is obliged to announce that he has ordered food and drink to be rationed, at least until the situation is safer.

At last the distinctive peak of Corcovado comes into view, and the ship hurries as best she can toward the wonderful Bay of Niterói, while the captain anxiously scans for signals through his binoculars. And once within sight, there comes the dreaded order: “Not allowed in here either,” mutters the exasperated captain, “if only I knew why!”

The first mate orders the signal flags made ready for a reply, but the captain whispers to him: “Leave it. I'll pretend I haven't understood and force my way in.”

And the ship keeps moving forward while the signals against it become frantic.

But since the Italian ship evidently takes no notice, a little gray puff rises from the shore, followed by the boom of a cannon.

“They're firing from the forts,” an elderly gentleman explains to the sisters, who are anxiously following events; “just blanks for now, but if we kept going...”.

Scenes of panic break out on deck. From the ship, now stopped, an explanation is requested from shore. And at last it comes: “Cholera has broken out in Italy, and ships flying the Italian flag are considered suspect and must go into quarantine.”

It is decided to sail on, while fresh causes of anxiety spread among the Italian passengers: who is not thinking of their loved ones, exposed to the danger of infection?

All hope of repairing the propeller in any port vanishes for good, and the engineers set to work with the utmost care. Sea and sky too have become calm again. They will keep hugging the Brazilian coast until the moment comes when the open ocean can no longer be avoided.

A Dramatic Arrival

Apart from doubts about the propeller, the most serious problem remained food supplies; but the crew, who had always shown themselves skilled sailors, turned themselves into able fishermen and managed to provide everyone with at least one ample dish a day. And on they went bravely, under the relentless June sun, toward the Equator.

They crossed its invisible line safely, with due observance of the traditional ceremonies.

Within sight of the Cape Verde Islands, the good weather and the propeller, which was holding, decided the captain to sail straight on to Genoa; and once past the Strait of Gibraltar everyone felt safe at last.

In the friendly daily conversations between the captain and the little group of sisters, one noticed in him an ever livelier excitement and a new light in his eyes. He himself simply revealed the reason: “In Genoa my young wife and a little girl of five are waiting for me. Every homecoming is like a renewal of life for me, a joy that always tastes like the first.”

The sisters answered with a smile.

Slowly the old ship, wounded but victorious, appeared at the entrance to the port of Genoa, but once again the signal station ordered her to stay offshore. This time, however, the captain did not worry. Indeed, after a cursory medical inspection and thorough disinfection, only three days' wait were prescribed.

On the morning of the fourth day, as the quay drew ever nearer and the passengers expressed their grateful satisfaction to the captain and crew in a thousand ways, the young captain kept peering at a spot in the harbor that was clearly familiar to him, but he seemed puzzled and anxious. No one was waiting for him.

Soon a launch put out and made swiftly for the ship; three men came aboard, and the one with the most authoritative air drew the captain aside and spoke to him; he seemed thunderstruck: “My God, it can't be, it isn't possible!”

Possible, alas, and painfully certain: cholera had visited Italy and taken his wife from him.

In the Mother's Arms

During the days of waiting outside the port of Genoa the provincial had been able to telegraph the Mother of their arrival, and the two secretaries, Sr. A. Benedetta and Sr. A. Celsa, had come to meet the returning sisters. When all the formalities had been completed they went on to Piacenza, where the Mother was anxiously awaiting them.

It was July 26, the feast of St. Anne. The Institute's first missionary provincial and her companions were given a solemn and most affectionate welcome. Everyone wanted to see them, hear them, and have news of the faraway sisters and their adventures. The Cardinal Protector too, who was in Turin, wanted to see Sr. A. Camilla at once; she went to him on the 28th and in the eight days she stayed there told him of all her work.

But her joy was complete when, in Piacenza, she could resume her daily talks with Mother Rosa. Among other things she told her of the strange episode in the forest: the fire lit for them, the hospitable hut, the mysterious Lady...

The Mother listened and smiled: “Do you really think St. Anne is there for nothing?”

Prophecies Fulfilled

“Remember me when you are in Rome.”

“Your Excellency, I don't know whether I shall go to Rome.”

“You will go, my child, you will go with the Foundress.”

Sr. A. Camilla must have remembered her last conversation with the Archbishop of Sucre when she heard the good news from the Mother.

Since the Institute continued to spread with extraordinary rapidity, especially in the central and southern regions of Italy, Mother Rosa - urged to do so also by the Holy See - had decided to move the Generalate from Piacenza to Rome, whose geographical and political centrality would allow her to follow more easily the progress of the many Communities and to maintain more directly and immediately the contacts she was bound to keep with both ecclesiastical and civil Authorities.

The new headquarters was to be inaugurated in January 1886; the General Chapter, attended by the Superiors of the most important Communities, had been called for March 15 of the same year; and since she was in Italy, Mother Rosa wished Provincial Camilla to take part as well, as indeed she did.

The Chapter had barely ended when the provincial was told that a Franciscan Father from the nearby Friary of St. Anthony had come asking for her, a certain Father Lardani. Although she was sure she had never met this Father, his name stirred in Sr. A. Camilla a vague apprehension, like an indefinite but sad memory. She received him with her usual courtesy, and the conversation turned naturally to events and works in Bolivia. Suddenly the Father said: “By the way, what prompted me to come and see you this morning was a letter I have just received from a priest in Sucre, a friend of mine; among other things he tells me of the death of Monsignor Fuchi, the archbishop you knew so well.”

The provincial turned pale: within herself she heard again, clear and distinct, the Archbishop's words: “Pray for me, my child, for by then I shall no longer be here.”

The Prophecy Had Come True!

So he truly was a saint, that prelate who, despite some inevitable early disagreement, had been a real father to the Daughters of St. Anne!

When Father Lardani had gone, Sr. A. Camilla felt the need to withdraw and pray in the new, quiet chapel. She prayed for a long time, for the Archbishop but even more for herself and for her faraway sisters, thinking of the events the Prelate had foretold, some of which had already come to pass. She now felt an urgent need to go back.

She went at once to Mother Rosa.

“We Shall Reach La Paz!”

The Mother was very sorry to see this daughter go, for her presence would have been valuable in Italy too, but she understood.

“Very well, the group of sisters who are to go with you to Bolivia is ready now, and we can bring forward the departure. But I must tell you something: you know how much the building of the Generalate and the Church has cost. I was thinking of keeping you a little longer, in the hope that Providence would send me the money to pay off some debts and properly meet the expenses of your long journey. For I must confess that at the moment I have very little to give you, certainly not as much as is needed.”

“Mother, for my part I should like to put a concern of mine to you. As you have told me, I am to accompany fourteen sisters, and the experience of the journeys I have already made gives me much to think about. After months of traveling on horseback over mountains and through forests, the sisters arrive nearly all of them ill, and some then need a long time to recover. I was wondering whether it might not be better to try the route by sea; it is longer, but free of the dangers and hardships of journeys on horseback.”

“Agreed, you are the one with experience; study the route and we shall see.”

“I have already studied it, Mother; I was waiting for a chance to speak to you about it. Basically it is the route followed by the first sisters, led by Father Rocchi. We would cross the Atlantic again from Genoa to Montevideo. Then take one of the ships of the English Company that sail from Argentina to Chile through the Strait of Magellan; from Chile, Valparaíso, to Mollendo in Peru. And from Mollendo...”.

“So many changes!” remarked the Mother, a little taken aback.

“That's true, but so much less fatigue for the sisters. No worries about baggage, since the Company takes full responsibility for transport; no long rides and nights in the open.”

“Agreed, go on.”

“From Mollendo by train to Puno. Across Lake Titicaca by steamer to Guaqui; and from Guaqui to La Paz by stagecoach.”

“You really have thought of everything,” the Mother smiled, “except yourself. I haven't forgotten that you suffer badly from seasickness; what would such a long voyage do to you?”

“The last journey was very long too, even if the sea part was shorter, and I ended up getting used to it. Believe me, the other route is far more dangerous and tiring for all of us.”

“Very well,” said the Mother, and was lost in thought for a moment; “I assure you that this time you won't be seasick at all. There remains, though, the big problem of the money needed. Meanwhile we shall make the necessary inquiries.”

Three days later she called her again: “I have made the inquiries and done the sums; I find that with the help of Providence I can pay your whole journey as far as Mollendo. For the rest... there are only two hundred lire left. It's not much, I know; but the Lord and St. Anne will help you.”

The provincial smiled, a little disconcerted, a little amused.

“It really is very little, Mother, if we look at things humanly. But I trust in St. Anne and in you. We shall reach La Paz!”

A “Yes” Said Once and for All

In the port of Genoa the steamer “Matteo Bruzzo” was preparing to weigh anchor for Latin America. Not a very fast ship, but big and solid. Fifteen places were booked on her. Sr. A. Camilla hurried off to Turin to take leave of the Cardinal Protector and talk with him, and on the way back she stopped at Oleggio, her home town, to say a last goodbye to her mother. She found her gravely ill, and had to leave again with the sad certainty that she would not see her again on earth. But the ship was ready and the sisters were waiting for her in Piacenza. A last farewell to the Mother, a last moving blessing, and away. Exhausted and grieving, but ready for any sacrifice, she rejoined the sisters in Piacenza and set off with them for Genoa, where they sailed on the “Matteo Bruzzo”; she was a solid, fairly modern ship, but... of ill repute. During the cholera of 1884-85 she had had at least forty sick people on board, mostly poor emigrants, and had been turned away from every port in superstitious terror. From one port she had even been driven off with cannon fire, and after months at sea, during which she earned the nickname “specter of the seas,” she had brought back to Genoa a grieving, broken cargo of starving survivors.

The Shipping Company had worried about the consequences of this terrible adventure, which discouraged travelers, and after having the ship thoroughly disinfected and overhauled, had given command of her to an elderly, prudent and energetic captain who knew all the seas of the world: Captain Caffarata.

In Genoa the Daughters of St. Anne had found valuable support in the kind interest of the Marquis Adorno-Fieschi, who had personally accompanied them to the ship and warmly recommended them to the captain.

On board they found the usual crowd of ill-clad, undernourished emigrants braving the sea and unknown lands in search of a better lot for themselves and their families. And as on every voyage, comforting and helping those poor people would be an effective apprenticeship for the younger sisters in view of the mission awaiting them in Bolivia.

Once through the Strait of Gibraltar the ship faced the ocean under the best of auspices; clear skies and calm sea gave a general sense of security, but in one of the cabins assigned to the sisters hours of anguish were being lived: Sr. A. Aurelia, one of the youngest, had been struck by a violent fever, and the ship's doctor had diagnosed typhoid. For several days the sister hovered between life and death, but her strong young constitution, the doctor's care and her sisters' prayers got the better of the illness: slowly the patient began to recover.

After rounding the Canary Islands and sighting the Cape Verde Islands, the ship anchored in the roadstead of São Vicente to take on coal. Then she resumed her course under a torrid sun, heading for the Equator.

The “Specter of the Seas”

A few days after leaving São Vicente the provincial saw Captain Caffarata coming toward her, very pale and agitated.

“What is it, Captain?”

“Bad news: a passenger has been taken to the sick bay with unmistakable symptoms of cholera.”

“How is that possible, after so many days at sea?”

“Do you remember the poor, wretched family that begged me to take them on board at São Vicente? Precisely because they were so wretched I hadn't the heart to refuse: father, mother, four children. It's the father; and now I fear for the rest of the family and for contagion on board.”

“You will have isolated them all, I suppose.”

“Yes, but I have no illusions; they have had the chance to infect other passengers. Believe me, Provincial, I am deeply shaken.”

Two days later the poor sick man died. The sister who had nursed him to his last breath prayed and wept while, in the darkness of the night, two sailors carried his body on deck, wrapped in a sheet and laid on a plank, with a heavy stone tied to his feet. At a sign from the captain the plank was rested on the rail at the feet end and raised at the other. The body slid down the slope, traced a curve in the air beyond the rail and sank into the water with a dull splash. A small whirlpool, and the sea, the immense grave of countless dead, closed over him.

“And he won't be the only one,” sighed the sister.

Indeed, two days later one of the dead man's children died, and another passenger showed symptoms of the same disease. Then another, and yet another; it was no longer possible to hide the sad truth from the passengers, while the sick bay filled up. The “Matteo Bruzzo,” the “specter of the sea,” was living up to her sad reputation.

The panic among the passengers was indescribable; and since, as always, the comic mingles with the tragic, everyone felt ill, everyone demanded care and attention, and the confusion made it impossible to treat properly those who really needed it. The sisters spent themselves tirelessly; the provincial trembled for their safety, invoking St. Anne's protection. And not one of them fell ill.

In the end there were no more deaths, and the few convalescents could leave the sick bay, while the island of Fernando de Noronha appeared on the horizon. It was a moment of real relief for the passengers, who crowded the decks to enjoy the sign that land was near. But there were also those weeping for one or more loved ones who would not disembark with them: they lay buried at the bottom of the sea.

“Sister, Is This How You Trust in Providence?”

There was the headland of Cabo Frio; there the rounded summit of Corcovado. The ship entered the immense bay of Guanabara, but the beauty of the place did not make the captain and crew forget their grim adventure and its inevitable immediate consequences. The Matteo Bruzzo anchored offshore, well away from the port proper, and waited. When the Authorities came on board for the usual formalities the sad truth could not be hidden from them, and swift, precise orders followed: leave the roadstead the next day and quit the Brazilian coast. The local Authorities would see, with due precautions, to the passengers bound for Rio de Janeiro. No one else was to land, for any reason. The captain of the Matteo Bruzzo was to take the other passengers elsewhere, provided it was outside territorial waters, for the prescribed quarantine.

The blow was hard for the sisters, who were still almost at the start of their journey. Where could they spend the quarantine? And would they be able to board the English ship at Montevideo to go round South America and up the Pacific coast? In any case there was time to think it over until they came within sight of the Uruguayan coast. Until then the provincial preferred to keep her worries to herself.

The next morning the plan was carried out. When the passengers for Rio de Janeiro had been landed and taken to the quarantine station, the Matteo Bruzzo put out to sea again with her cargo, heading south.

From inquiries he had made, Captain Caffarata had learned that the Uruguayan government sent passengers bound for Montevideo who were subject to quarantine to the Flores Islands, six hours' sailing from the port. There they would stay for the prescribed time under the supervision of trusted doctors; with this news the captain tried to reassure the provincial, telling her they would not miss their connection with the Cotopaxi, because the English ship itself would call at the Flores Islands to pick them up at the right time. The quarantine would not last more than seven days.

Instead of being reassured, Sr. A. Camilla received the news with dismay: “Seven days!” she exclaimed, turning pale.

“What are seven days?” retorted the captain, and the sisters echoed him; young and lively, they saw the whole thing as a pleasant change from the monotony of the long voyage.

But the provincial's distress continued, and it was so obvious that the captain insisted on knowing the reason; when he heard it he was thoughtful for a moment, then burst out laughing: “So, Sister, is this how you trust in Providence?”

These words sounded like a reproach to the sister, who heard in them the echo of Mother Rosa's words: “The Lord and St. Anne will help you.”

“Forgive my unbelief, Lord. I trust in you and in St. Anne.”

On the Flores Islands

High, arid and dark, the Flores Islands rose against the background of the Uruguayan coast, and the travelers soon saw that the name hardly suited the place, whose meager vegetation offered nothing pretty or flowery to the eye. The steamer slowly approached one of the islands, on whose shore stood a long, low, all-white building.

“Because the water isn't deep enough the ship cannot dock at the pier,” the captain explained, “but I'll take you ashore myself in my own launch.”

Landing people and baggage went fairly quickly. As soon as they were ashore, the group led by the captain was directed to the building that served as a lazaretto, while the sailors set the baggage down on the ground.

As he was about to leave, Captain Caffarata turned to the provincial: “Mother, a few days ago I took the liberty of reminding you of the existence of Providence, in which I firmly believe, because among other things I have had countless proofs of it in my adventurous life. And since I am responsible for you, at this moment I feel personally entrusted with its part. Don't worry. I have spoken to the administrator of the lazaretto and commended to him both you and the other passengers in quarantine, so that you will be treated with every consideration. As for the expenses you will have in these days, I take them upon myself and will answer for them personally to the Management of the lazaretto.”

While the provincial and the sisters thanked him with tears in their eyes, Sr. A. Immacolata, who never lost her strong practical sense, was checking the baggage to make sure nothing was missing, and suddenly exclaimed: “There's a mistake here. This crate isn't ours.”

The captain asked with a smile: “You, whose presence on board the Matteo Bruzzo was providential in the hard and painful time we lived through together, won't you accept a present from my old, unlucky ship? You won't regret it, for you'll find things in it that will be very useful for the rest of your journey. And pray for me.”

Having said these last words almost gruffly, to master his emotion, he quickly cut short their thanks and went to find the Director of the Lazaretto. Shortly afterward he said a final goodbye and got back into the launch to return to his ship. From a distance he waved his cap once more and quickly climbed aboard. The sisters, standing on the shore, silently watched the ship weigh anchor, seeing in her, with understandable sorrow, the last piece of their homeland leaving them.
