The days spent in the Lazaretto, though they broke the monotony of the voyage in one way, were no less monotonous and sad for that. The only diversion, and not a cheerful one, in their long idle days was visiting the cemeteries: one for those who died of cholera, one for those who died of yellow fever. On the gravestones, a few Italian names. They prayed for them all.

The doctors and staff of the Lazaretto were full of consideration. But the atmosphere was heavy all the same, and everyone anxiously awaited the end of the enforced stay. The provincial took the opportunity to write at length to the Mother and tell her, along with their unhappy experiences, of the first visible intervention of Providence.

On the eighth day of quarantine, with English punctuality, the “Cotopaxi” appeared on the horizon. A fine, very solid ship, she anchored roughly where the Matteo Bruzzo had dropped anchor and lowered her boats to collect the passengers waiting on the shore. Captain and crew were all English. The sisters' hearts sank at hearing that unknown language. “If only they were Spanish! Now we really have left Italy,” sighed one sister. But Sr. A. Immacolata winked at her: “Leave it to me, I have a smattering of English. I appoint myself official interpreter.”

The Cotopaxi in the Storm

The voyage began on a calm sea, and the days settled into a regular, monotonous rhythm: prayers, a little handiwork, meals, Spanish lessons, long conversations full of homesickness but also of hopes and good resolutions. The provincial was constantly with her sisters and did her best to keep the conversation lively, while the fair-haired captain, tall and taciturn, his everlasting little pipe in his mouth, would pass by and greet them with measured British reserve. Only Sr. A. Immacolata's outgoing liveliness could draw a smile from him, and then he would stop for a moment to give some information about the route and the weather.

The ship approached the Strait of Magellan in unbroken fine weather, which suddenly changed in the afternoon. A strong wind rose while the sky clouded over. To Sr. A. Immacolata, who was questioning one of the crew with her eyes, the sailor said: “It's one of the usual sudden storms of these seas; nothing to worry about; in fact the good weather has lasted too long.”

The night passed with the ship rolling and pitching; two of the sisters were sick, as were some other passengers.

Dawn brought no change: the crew, however, sure of the ship's soundness and used to such storms, stayed calm and reassured the passengers.

But the ocean began to rage: little by little life on deck ceased, apart from the few sailors handling the ship; the captain stayed riveted to the bridge. Things grew worse when the rain began to pour down violently, and toward evening passengers had to be told not only to stay in their cabins during the night but to strap themselves to their bunks with the leather belts provided for such emergencies.

On the third day, from a few vague words let slip by a sailor, they understood that the ship was out of control. And the captain, faced with Sr. A. Immacolata's questioning but trusting look, set aside his natural reserve: “I've made this crossing fifteen times, Sister, but I've never had to face a storm like this.”

“But is there serious danger?”

The captain answered with a vague gesture.

In the days that followed the storm went on raging. Nearly all the sisters were seasick, and some could not hide their fear: “Are we really going to die here?”

The provincial, as Mother Rosa had promised, was free of seasickness this time. Strengthened by this “sign” as well, she encouraged the others: “Don't be afraid, sisters. Our Mother is surely praying for us, and besides, let us trust in the Lord, who is our good Father. How many times I have experienced his protection!”

But there came a moment when the sisters read a kind of bewilderment on the captain's face. As if moved by an inner impulse, Sr. A. Immacolata went straight to the provincial's cabin. “Mother, I have no illusions; things really are going badly. I want to put Our Lady to the test.” And she showed the medal of Our Lady of Pompeii that she held in her hand. With a violent effort she moved the iron bar that held the porthole glass, but immediately turned her face away in horror at the frightful chasms formed by the waters. She waited a moment; then, as a new abyss opened beside the ship, she let the medal fall, murmuring a prayer.

The storm did not stop, but the pounding of the waves seemed to grow less violent. In the hearts of the sisters gathered in prayer, trust grew stronger. Toward evening the sea was still very rough, but the captain was able to announce that the danger could be considered past. Everyone breathed a sigh of relief and the saloons filled with pale but smiling passengers. The captain, grown almost talkative, explained: “I've just taken our position; the violence of the storm drove the ship about forty kilometers off course, but with a calmer sea and the engines in good order we'll soon make up for lost time.”

The sisters had gathered joyfully around the provincial when very young Sr. A. Irene, who had suffered less from seasickness than the others and after several days of near fasting was feeling the pangs of hunger, cried out, striking her breast: “We have Captain Caffarata's crate! Sisters, what are we waiting for?” Some backed her up, and three of them disappeared and came back shortly afterward laden with bottles, salami and ship's biscuits. And they all ate their fill, with expressions of gratitude toward their generous benefactor.

The next morning the thin line of Cape Virgenes could be made out, still far off, and the reappearance of land was greeted with joyful relief by the passengers crowding the deck. When the ship had passed the first narrows of the channel separating Patagonia from Tierra del Fuego, the sea, now completely calm, stretched out as far as the eye could see, but the Cotopaxi kept her speed down to avoid the reefs and shallows typical of those waters, as far as Punta Arenas, where she anchored for a stop needed to give the crew proper rest and to make a general inspection of the ship and engines. She sailed again in full daylight for safety and continued through the Strait. The cold was bitter, but the passengers never tired of admiring the striking scenery. “It's like traveling in a dream world,” murmured the provincial, gazing at the green backs of the mountains rising sheer, their peaks gleaming with snow. More islands, inlets, gulfs and fjords, until, within sight of Cape Pilar, the captain announced: “We have left the Strait of Magellan and are entering the Pacific Ocean.” The passengers answered with applause.

A Strange Traveling Companion

Days and days of sailing along the Chilean coast, until the ship came within sight of the bay of Valparaíso. Because the Cotopaxi was late, the Ayacucho, the small ship that was to take on the passengers for Mollendo, was waiting impatiently. And the stop was brief.

Once the transfer was made, the Ayacucho sailed. This small ship, which carried the mail between the ports of northern Chile and Peru, had on board a crowd of merchants, miners and Indians who made a picturesque company. The general conversation revolved around the recent storm, in which several ships had sunk, and people were amazed to learn that the Cotopaxi, apart from the delay and discomfort, had suffered no more serious damage.

The sisters thought of the act of trust in Our Lady of Pompeii, and the provincial urged them all to make their faith in Providence ever more alive.

“The crucial moment is drawing near,” she thought meanwhile, “when I shall have to meet new expenses and I have only the two hundred lire Mother Rosa gave me. But Providence will help me, as it has so far.”

The captain of the Ayacucho was English too, but he was at home in Spanish, and he took a kind interest in the health of the sisters who had been most tried by the previous voyage. On the whole they felt more at ease than on the Cotopaxi.

Coquimbo, Huasco, Antofagasta... The ship made almost daily stops to deliver and collect mail and goods. The short stops, the slower pace of the voyage, some special attention to food for the weaker sisters: all helped them quickly regain their strength. And they all began to take an interest in the ever-changing scenes of life along the shores of these American countries. The provincial, meanwhile, went over in her mind the various sources of financial help she might find, the different doors she might knock on when the need arose.

The ship had reached Iquique. There a middle-aged gentleman of prosperous appearance came aboard: tall leather boots, good-quality clothes, a heavy gold chain across his waistcoat and a broad sombrero. He had the look of a man used to fighting and winning, yet not without traces of a certain humanity.

The group of sisters caught his attention at once. He clearly felt a lively curiosity about them, for every now and then he openly came close to the group as if to listen to their talk; but since they usually spoke Spanish, he could not make out their nationality. His persistence began to annoy the sisters, who when they went up on deck had to speak in whispers so as not to be overheard.

“Soon we'll be at Arica,” the Provincial said one day, having decided to reveal to the sisters their difficult financial situation, “and then from Arica to Mollendo; and then...”.

“Don't worry, Mother,” Sr. A. Giulia urged her, half joking, “if we find no other way, we'll go begging. Don't so many of our sisters do it in Italy? And didn't Mother Rosa herself do it many times to feed her orphans?”

“And besides,” another put in on a more spiritual note, “this time it's St. Anne's turn to help us. The storm was calmed by Our Lady of Pompeii; St. Anne will remedy our poverty.”

Without realizing it they had raised their voices, until they noticed that the gentleman with the heavy gold chain had come closer than discretion allowed, and they stopped, but not before Sr. A. Genesia had grumbled: “There's that busybody! How can we get rid of him?”

“Listen,” snapped Sr. A. Immacolata, “it's true we don't all come from the same region, but our dialects are close enough for us to understand one another. Let's speak dialect. This nosy rancher may understand Italian, but he certainly won't understand dialect.” And raising her voice a little she went on: “Provincial cara, ch'l'an perda el curagg le', per carità, el Signor l'provederà qualcosa, ch'la n'abbia paura” [Dear Provincial, don't lose heart, for pity's sake; the Lord will provide something, don't be afraid].

“Yes,” the provincial went on, playing along, “but se a Mollendo a treuve nen in counsul boliviari c'a m'aiuta, a sai propri a che sant vouteme” [but if I don't find a Bolivian consul in Mollendo to help me, I really don't know which saint to turn to].

But a Venetian sister interrupted her, more with her eyes than with her mouth: “Provincial, so mia se l'è peor el tacon ch'i buso!” [Provincial, I'm not sure the patch isn't worse than the hole!].

The gentleman, in fact, had not only come closer but had rushed upon the group and, pale and wide-eyed, was gasping: “But you really are Italian! How... Me sembra minga vera! [I can't believe it!] Son milanes, milanes autentico de Porta Nueva [I'm from Milan, a genuine Milanese from Porta Nuova]. You, Sister, are from Romagna - no, from Emilia, it's all the same, oh, it's still Italy, the Italy of the Po, you understand me... oh, what luck!” And he went on talking incoherently, gesticulating and attracting the curious attention of the other passengers, while the sisters, once their first surprise had passed, smiled; now they understood the stranger's indiscreet persistence.

Meanwhile the conversation became calmer and more to the point: “I'm a merchant,” he explained, “and I'm doing quite well, though in the early days I knew poverty. Till now I've met only a few Italians in these parts, mostly adventurers greedy for riches or hard-nosed merchants like me, used to the roughness of life. Never calm faces or courteous manners. And nuns... who had seen any since childhood? Dressed like you, though, I never saw any even as a boy. What sisters are you?”

“Daughters of St. Anne.”

“A fine name! I can hardly believe I can talk with Italians without having to argue about money or even quarrel. Where are you heading?”

“To Arequipa, for now,” the provincial answered briefly.

“Well, what do you know, I'm going to Arequipa too.”

He was silent a moment. “Perhaps before the end of the voyage I'll tell you my whole story. You sisters, who undertake such long, uncomfortable journeys, surely only to do good to people you don't know, inspire such confidence in me.” He was moved. But the provincial preferred to keep a prudent reserve.

Confidences

The next day the ship entered the port of Arica. Time enough for the usual operations, and she sailed again. As she put out to sea, the Milanese gentleman leaned on the rail beside the provincial. He stood a long while gazing silently at the expanse of water, and at last seemed to make up his mind to speak: “I'm in a hurry to get to Arequipa, and at the same time I'm afraid,” he said, as if talking to himself.

Then, suddenly: “I haven't told you my name yet. My name is... Have you ever heard of my family, in Milan?”

“No, actually, but you see, I'm from Turin.” “But my family name is, or was, quite well known even outside Lombardy. Ah... who knows whether my father is still alive!”

“Whether he's still alive?” the provincial exclaimed in surprise. “Aren't you in touch with your family?”

“No, unfortunately. I broke off all relations many years ago, causing my family great sorrow. My mother had died a few years before. I was young, lively, violent even. I wanted to live my own way, and my father was rather strict. One day... I broke open the safe in my father's study and took everything in it except my mother's jewels. I was nineteen. I wanted to have a good time. I ran away from home. Wanted by the police, I managed to escape them and stowed away on a ship for Argentina. I got to Buenos Aires. I had money. I tried the kind of life I had longed for, I lost myself in it, I found companions worse than me who followed me for what they could get, until the money ran out. Then they all left me. I certainly couldn't go home. In rags and starving, I was tempted to kill myself, but my strong character and, who knows, my mother... I decided to fight. I began to work hard, relying only on my own strength. I did every kind of job, from the humblest to the hardest. I lived on little and saved. With every small gain I felt a kind of furious desire to earn more, to pile it up... By thirty I was almost rich and making a name for myself. Perhaps I dreamed that one day, who knows, my name would reach as far as Milan, as far as my family.”

“It was a long way to Milan,” smiled the provincial.

“I know, the road was and is long; but I was aware of my guilt and felt the need to make amends, yet I never found the courage to get in touch.”

“What a pity! But it's never too late.”

“You see, now I'm afraid my father and sister are dead, and going back would be even more bitter. And if they are still alive... let them think me dead by now. I live in Chile now; I married a young Chilean woman who brought me a large dowry. We're rich, we love each other. But I'm not at peace. As I said, I still have something to do. That's why I'm going to Arequipa.”

He fell silent, and the provincial did not think it right to press for further confidences. There was a long silence while the man was evidently struggling with himself. At last he went on with an effort: “I think meeting you has been a real stroke of luck for me. I have a big favor to ask of you, but I'll speak to you about it another time. Now let's change the subject: I don't know myself - or perhaps I do - why from the first moment I saw you I felt strongly drawn to you, and, as you will have noticed, I was even indiscreet. I apologize, but I caught a few phrases... You have money troubles, isn't that so? Tell me everything.”

“Ah, yes, unfortunately!”

“Listen, I know this country well, and I know it isn't easy to get help from strangers. But I flatter myself that I'm no longer a stranger to you. And I have ample means. Trust me.”

“But it's Providence that sends you!” burst out the provincial.

“Leave Providence out of it,” said the man, his face darkening; “I've told you I'm a self-made man, and it's me you must rely on.”

The provincial preferred to drop the subject, but she thought: “Lord, let me be an instrument of your grace for him!” And she went on: “Owing to a combination of circumstances I am left without money for the rest of the journey to Bolivia. But a loan for the journey from Mollendo to Arequipa will be enough. In that city I have someone who can help me and also enable me to repay your loan.”

The man interrupted her with a sort of shout: “Loan! What an ugly word. I don't lend money to a nun. Anything you may need is at your disposal. But then... you talk as if, once in Mollendo, you could just take the train to Arequipa and off you go. This isn't Europe. In Peru the trains run when there are passengers; otherwise they stand still. So you have to book and wait. When the management has made sure of a certain number of passengers, it orders the train to leave. Once a week, twice at most; and if there aren't enough passengers, even less often.”

More and more clearly the provincial glimpsed the hand of Providence in that strange traveling companion. How else would she have managed?

“That's settled,” he went on, more and more excited; “as far as Arequipa you needn't worry about anything. If only I could free myself from my own worry so easily!”

“Well then,” the provincial felt moved to say, “let's hear this worry of yours. And if I can help you be rid of it, I shall be very glad.”

“I'll tell you after lunch.”

A Difficult Task

After lunch in the saloon the Milanese made a discreet sign to the provincial, who understood that he wished to speak to her privately again; and she followed him on deck.

The man took off his sombrero; his forehead was damp with sweat. He began to speak quickly, as if he wanted to be rid of a heavy burden at once: “I've told you about the follies of my youth, but I haven't yet told you everything about myself. Later on, alone and in need of affection like every human being, I had a lasting relationship with a woman, without bothering to start a family. In these parts it's very common. A little girl was born whom her mother didn't want and perhaps couldn't have kept. She left her in a foundling home in Arequipa. Here it isn't the custom, as I've learned it is in Italy, to leave a token of recognition on children entrusted to such institutions. So the little one was left completely abandoned. Later, having broken off that relationship for good, I married, but, perhaps as a punishment from fate, we have had no children. I've thought of adopting one, with my wife's agreement, but naturally I'd like to get back my own, whose existence my wife knows nothing about. It would all be simple, except... how am I to find, and above all recognize for certain, my own child? Will it be possible? I know well where she was placed, and I hope she's still there, but how can I recognize her? That's where I need your help, Provincial.”

“It's a truly difficult task! First of all, what about the real mother?”

“She died two years ago.” “How old is the girl now?”

“Eight years and three months.”

“She's already a big girl. She may already have been adopted by others. And then, really, how could she be recognized? If one could see a strong resemblance, say, to you or to her mother, it would be somewhat easier. But what can I do?”

“First of all you can help me find a way of seeing the girl. I know that in the Institution where she was placed, when someone comes who wants to adopt a child, they usually organize a little party, with songs and poems or the like, so that the person concerned can see all the children and express a preference. You will be kind enough to come with me; you will look carefully at all the girls who seem to be my daughter's age, and if you see one who looks at least a little like me... I don't know, you believe in God; ask your God to let you recognize her somehow. I only know I shall have no peace until I find her; may I at least make up for this wrong, among the many in my life. May my child have a family!”

The provincial was moved, but also worried: “What a responsibility you want to lay on me!”

The man's gruffness reawakened, perhaps also as a reaction to his emotion: “Well, do you believe in God or not? Take it up with him.”

“Pray, certainly,” thought the provincial; “we'll all pray. God has let me find the solution to my problem in this brother who went astray and is perhaps on his way back. He will give me the chance to help him solve his.” And she felt calmer.

From Mollendo to Arequipa

Mollendo. A strange port in those days, crudely equipped and certainly not suited to comfortable embarking and disembarking, even for passengers. Making its way through the high waves that crashed noisily against the dark rocks, the ship managed to anchor quite close to the shore, and the “unloading” of passengers began at once. “Unloading” is the right word, for a gigantic hand-operated crane, worked by a complicated system of winches, lowered onto the ship's deck a large basket in which four passengers, evidently familiar with this system, took their places first. And so on with all the others. Giggles, comments, a few half-suppressed squeals from the few women besides the sisters who were traveling on the Ayacucho.

This was the only way, the captain explained to the passengers who watched the unusual maneuver from the deck in amazement and dismay, to unload goods and people, because the violent surf prevented any boat from approaching the shore. “And after all,” he concluded with his usual phlegmatic shrug, “it's no worse a system than any other.”

The sisters too had to be hoisted in the baskets, and they reached land hiding behind a smile the palpitations caused by the swaying of this unusual lift.

As soon as the sisters were ready, the Milanese went into action; with his natural exuberance and the assurance of a man used to getting what he wants, he saw to the unloading and collection of the baggage, took them into town and found a suitable hotel.

He found a room for himself in another hotel and lost no time in booking seats on the train to Arequipa. As he had foreseen, the train was not ready but was being made up, and the booking of sixteen seats hastened its preparation; within three or four days it would set off.

The train was one of those real old-time “coffee pots” that puffed laboriously up the gradient. After some twenty-four hours' travel through desolate country they reached Arequipa. The Milanese gentleman saw once more to the unloading of the sisters' baggage, then said: “Since, as I understand, you have people here who can arrange your lodging, my task is over for the moment. But I'll certainly come and see you, and we'll meet again at the foundling home.” And with a wide flourish of his sombrero he went off.

The lodging Sr. A. Camilla had counted on for the necessary stop in Arequipa was none other than the foundling home that the Milanese so longed for. Two years earlier the Daughters of St. Anne had for some months given hospitality at the hospital in La Paz to the superior of the Arequipa foundling home and some of her sisters, and had received from her warm assurances that the hospitality would be returned in case of need.

So they knocked at the door of that Institution with some confidence. But the first meeting was not without embarrassment on both sides. Truth to tell, the sudden arrival of a group of no fewer than fifteen sisters would understandably throw anyone into confusion who had to take them in. With some difficulty the community managed to find room for seven; the other eight would have to look elsewhere. Led by Sr. A. Immacolata and directed by a little girl they met in the street, they knocked at the door of the College of the Sacred Hearts, and to their great relief were welcomed with the utmost cordiality. From the back of the grille, which remained in shadow - for it was an enclosed monastery - a serene voice rose: “Sisters, with the Lord's blessing, welcome to our poor house. We will gladly share our bread with you, and as for lodging, the pupils are on holiday and the College is almost empty. You may stay as long as you like.”

So the problem of lodging was solved for all of them.

The provincial, who had stayed at the foundling home with good reason, at once confided her financial situation to the superior and asked to borrow the sum needed for the rest of the journey, promising to repay it immediately through the respective Embassies as soon as she reached Bolivia. And she was assured she would have it.

She also told her about the Milanese gentleman and his distressing problem. The superior confirmed that there had been a custom in the past of holding little parties at which, on the occasion of a visit from some foreign personage, the joint management of the two institutions, for boys and for girls, allowed the two sections to come together for joint performances of songs, dances and recitations. The system, however, had not worked well, because it had happened that some benefactor, carried away by sudden enthusiasm, had asked to adopt a child and then, after a short time, had sent the child back, to the poor little one's great distress. And the custom had lapsed.

With due caution Sr. A. Camilla gave some more concrete details, so that the superior, struck by the unusual nature of the case, promised to approach the Management so that they would be willing to hand over the girl if the request came with all the proper guarantees. “Fortunately,” she said at last, “things fall out well. In a few days there will be a performance by the two Institutions, already scheduled in the ordinary way. With the Management's permission we will invite the gentleman you are so concerned about, and then we'll leave it to God.”

Meanwhile the Milanese had not failed to visit the sisters, and he was overjoyed to learn that the longed-for performance would be held the following Sunday and that he could attend as a guest. Needless to say, neither of them slept on Saturday night. “What if I'm wrong,” Sr. A. Camilla thought, “what if a freak of nature has produced a misleading resemblance? On the other hand, what can I do? I entrust it all to St. Anne.” The father's state of mind can easily be imagined.

The Ways of Providence

The hour of the party came. A party like every children's party in the world: a big hall decorated for the occasion, children's chatter, innocent displays of budding vanity on the part of the little girls, self-importance on the part of the little boys, and songs, poems and dances.

From where she sat, Provincial Camilla gave all her attention to the faces of the girls roughly the age of the child they were looking for. Suddenly she felt a kind of shock: “But that one... I'd say she's his living image. The color and shape of the eyes, the smile, the expression...”. But was that enough? Could she point her out to the father with real certainty? She waited, watching the child with the closest attention and praying in her heart. Meanwhile the party was in full swing. A little play was being performed that was, one might say, like the story of which the child was the unknowing protagonist, and, by a twist of Providence, she was the protagonist on stage too. The provincial saw her come forward alone on the stage: a little beggar girl who by chance meets the father she has never known. At the end of the scene, as the audience applauded with emotion, Sr. A. Camilla caught her breath. The child, as if drawn by an inner force, had gone up to the Milanese sitting in the front row and, looking at him with a smile, had hugged his knees. And the astonished guests could not understand why that middle-aged gentleman burst into tears as he clasped the little girl to his heart.

The provincial was weeping too. And a few hours later she was congratulating the father, who still could not master his emotion. When the registers were checked, the child's age and the date of her admission were found to match. There could be no doubt.

“I'll try to speed up the adoption formalities as much as possible,” said the Milanese, “and then I want to fulfill another duty: go back to Italy and look for what remains of my family. I hope at least my sister is alive” - and his voice trembled. “But,” he went on, “I haven't thanked you yet. Without your intervention perhaps the door of the Institution would not have opened to me in such favorable circumstances, and my little girl would have gone on living without a father, without a family. What would have become of her? How much I owe you, Sister!”

“I did nothing. I'm not sure I would have had the courage to point her out to you, even though I had noticed the extraordinary likeness. But considering how things turned out, why won't you acknowledge the intervention of a higher Power? Acknowledge it, come back to God, and then you will find in full the peace you have sought in vain for so many years and need so badly. Listen to me!” He was confused: “I don't know. I have so many things to think about, I must reflect. Pray for me, I ask you with all my heart. And know that at any time you can count on me as your most grateful and devoted friend. And pray for me!” he repeated, with a lump in his throat.

Two days later, as the sisters were about to leave, the Milanese came to say goodbye with the little girl dressed like a little queen. “I can't go back to Chile yet; they won't let me take the child with me until all the adoption formalities are completed. But the main thing is done. Thank you again, with all my heart.” The provincial never saw him again. But she often prayed for him.

Providence at Play Again

They were leaving. And they left with easy minds, for the sisters' health was excellent and the financial problem essentially solved. There remained the debt to the superior of the foundling home, but that could be dealt with calmly. As she went to the station to buy the tickets, the provincial saw an elegant gentleman coming toward her, who greeted her by name with a broad smile: “Hermana Camila, back at last! How are you?” The provincial at once recognized the Bolivian Foreign Minister, Señor Gutiérrez.

“Your Excellency, I'm very glad to see you.” “But do you know everyone has been worried about such a long absence? Not to mention Doctor Arce: he's furious. But I ask too: how come? Reasons of... the Order's internal politics?”

“Well, there were some internal reasons,” the provincial answered on impulse, “but not political ones; financial ones, rather.” “You don't say!” Almost regretting her impulsive remark, Sr. A. Camilla tried to smooth it over: “We had to undergo an unexpected quarantine at Montevideo which drained all our resources, and we suffered the consequences afterward.” “Mother, I know how much Bolivia owes you and your sisters. Count on me from this moment. You won't have to think about expenses as far as La Paz.”

“Thank you, but the superior of the foundling home here has already come to my aid. It's true I'll have to repay her, but when I reach Bolivia I'll find...”. “Don't even mention it.”

The courtesies were brief. The superior of the foundling home was not sorry to have her money back sooner than expected, and Sr. A. Camilla was even less sorry to be free of debt. Providence was true to form. The Minister personally bought the tickets for all the sisters as far as La Paz.

In Bolivia at Last!

Still traveling, then, from Arequipa to Puno, where they would take the boat across Lake Titicaca. The train climbed toward the Cordillera, and the air grew colder and thinner. They had to cross altitudes of over four thousand meters, and the sisters, apart from the provincial, who was used to such changes, showed clear signs of suffocation, appearing as bouts of unhealthy drowsiness that made their heads heavy to the point of fainting. But since this was a common and well-known phenomenon, the Railway Management normally kept remedies ready, empirical and rather Spartan in kind.

These were sturdy men, nurses of a sort but with long experience, who took it in turns to slap the faces, arms and limbs of the affected passengers to keep their circulation going for the whole of the climb. After Crucero Alto the train at last began to descend toward the high plateau and Puno, Peru's main port on Lake Titicaca and the usual route to Bolivia.

The boat Yavarí took all the travelers aboard and moved fairly swiftly over the calm waters of the lake. Sr. A. Camilla kept the sisters interested by telling them some of the legends handed down about this lake, which was the cradle of the worship of the Sun god and has only one Christian presence, the Shrine of Copacabana, which however cannot be seen from the boat because it lies hidden in the shadows of the peninsula of the same name.

The cold was intense, but the sisters lingered on deck to enjoy the incomparable beauty of the scenery. When the boat reached Bolivian soil at Guaqui, where they were to spend the night, it was already dark. The next day the shortest but most tiring stage of the whole journey awaited them: the trip from Guaqui to La Paz in a sort of prehistoric omnibus drawn by several pairs of mules, with jolts and bumps and a tremendous racket. But, as God willed, they arrived safe and sound in La Paz. The long, troubled journey was over.

Back to Normal

In La Paz the provincial had at once to devote herself to an important and delicate task: reorganizing all the communities, beginning with the most urgent and necessary measures, including those connected with the observations made by the Authorities during her long absence. The work was done partly at her desk and partly in visits to the houses, at least the nearer ones, while the newly arrived sisters took the rest they needed and gradually adapted to climates and surroundings so different and far from those they were born to. When she saw they were ready, Sr. A. Camilla judged that they could set out for their destinations; she divided them up and assigned them according to the needs of the works in Oruro, Cochabamba and Sucre.

The journey from Cochabamba to Sucre was disturbed by the serious illness of one sister, which forced the caravan to make an unscheduled stop at the hospitable hut of a good Indian. A rich gentleman who lived not far away, however, placed at the sisters' disposal the means to carry the sick sister more comfortably, and so the group was able to reach the capital only slightly late.

From Sucre the provincial had to wage a strenuous battle by letter with the usual Señor Zapata, who flatly opposed the departure of a sister whom Mother Rosa had personally assigned to Tarija. And although Sr. A. Camilla called on the weighty intervention of Doctor Arce, the petty dictator would not budge: to avoid further unpleasant incidents another sister had to be sent to Tarija instead.

A Bad Fall

When the autumn and winter of 1887 were over, the provincial organized a small caravan to go to Potosí on one of her regular periodic visits.

The rough, tiring life of long rides began again. The Cachimayo and the Pilcomayo, low at that season, were easily forded. They reached Potosí without incident.

After staying in that city as long as needed to take the measures that proved necessary, Sr. A. Camilla and two fellow sisters set off on the return journey.

One morning the mule carrying the provincial was nervous and restless. They were about halfway between Potosí and Sucre when the animal suddenly shied and with a violent swerve threw its rider onto the stony road, where she fell with a dull thud. She lay motionless on the path while an intense pain shot through her arm. The arrieros and the sisters leapt from their saddles and rushed to her side: her sleeve was torn open, and the limpness of the arm together with the violent pain left no doubt that it was broken.

They realized the provincial could not get back in the saddle. And Sucre was still too far away to think of carrying her there on a litter.

All around there was no sign of human life; only in the far distance a thin wisp of smoke could be seen rising into the sky. They decided to carry her in that direction, and the group, led by an arriero with a mule carrying what was essential for even a rough shelter, reached a hut inhabited by an elderly Indian couple, who willingly gave it up to the sisters for a small payment.

The provincial had a fever; she was laid on the poor bed prepared in haste, and they discussed what to do. One of the arrieros, taking the fastest of the mounts, galloped off to Sucre to bring one of the doctors from the hospital there with the necessary remedies. The rest of the caravan would wait, trying to relieve the injured sister with the meager means they had.

Three days passed, days of severe pain for Sr. A. Camilla and acute anxiety for the sisters. On the morning of the fourth day they heard with relief a rapid gallop: the arriero was coming back with no fewer than three doctors, who set to work at once.

The arm was broken in two places, and the ends had already begun to knit out of position. Correcting it called for difficult movements that were extremely painful for the patient. Then arm and shoulder were completely immobilized. Considering the patient's poor general condition - the fever persisted - two of the doctors decided to stay a few days while the third returned to Sucre. They improvised a tent nearby and divided their time between caring for the patient and long hunting trips in the surrounding country.

When the fever subsided and the provincial seemed to regain a little strength, the doctors left, entrusting her to the sisters' loving and attentive care and promising to send food and medicine from Sucre for as long as needed. And it was some twenty more days before the pain stopped and the arm could regain a certain freedom of movement.

At last they could set off. The taciturn Indian couple took leave of the sisters with warm affection, and they resumed their way to Sucre, riding rather slowly so as not to tire the convalescent.

An Eventful Night

Their first night on the road found them near a half-ruined building that was large enough for a makeshift night shelter; it had no door, and through the broken roof patches of sky could be seen. But it was better than nothing. Supper was cooked on fires lit outside, the place was cleaned as well as possible by candlelight, and the little mattresses were laid out. The arriero in charge lay down across the entrance, armed with a pistol and wrapped in llama skins.

The sisters prayed, put out the candle and, fully dressed, wrapped themselves in a blanket to wait for sleep. But sleep would not come to Sr. A. Guida. Seized by a strange uneasiness, she tossed in her blanket, listening to the thousand noises of the night: distant howls, nearer neighing, the hum of insects, rustling in the dark... But strange rustlings, quick, insistent, too close. The sister understood: the hut was infested with mice. Should she wake her companions? No, better let them rest, unless they woke of their own accord. But how revolting! She tried to cover herself as best she could, feeling the mice running over her body; suddenly she felt one on her cheek and, instinctively putting her hand to her face, found between her fingers a warm, quivering little body, which she flung away in horror. A scream rose from the other side of the room: Sr. A. Pasqualina, who was also awake and struggling with her disgust, had suddenly felt the violent impact of a live missile on her mouth, which she instinctively bit... and spat out in horror. The hut filled with cries. When the candle had at last been lit, the menacing figure of the arriero appeared in the doorway, half asleep and gripping his pistol, while dozens of mice raced madly for their holes and Sr. A. Pasqualina wept. There was certainly a comic side to it, but disgust overcame every other feeling.

It was useless now to try to get back to sleep, even with the candle lit. They waited impatiently for dawn, and as soon as the first glimmer lit the sky they set off again.

And Another, a Dramatic One

It was another day on horseback; throughout the afternoon the sky had been clouding over; but they reached the river as they had planned, with an hour still to go before sunset. They found it had risen, perhaps because of the rains that had begun to pour on the crests of the Cordillera. The water was swirling, carrying along tree trunks and debris.

“We must hurry and cross the river before dark,” said the leader of the caravan, “because rain is threatening and we'll find no shelter here. And I'm afraid the crossing won't be easy.”

Thunder was already rumbling.

“Is the crossing very dangerous?” asked Sr. A. Pasqualina.

“In itself it wouldn't be, but the swirling current is carrying some fairly big trunks; there's no ford, so we'll have to swim the animals across.”

First they sent down the mule laden with the baggage, to make sure what was needed for the rest of the journey got across safely, and the animal, used to it, went resolutely into the water while its driver, partly dressed, swam alongside holding it by the reins. The other two arrieros also plunged into the water, while their horses, used to such maneuvers, went down into the river on their own.

The men swam vigorously, but the current carried them a good way downstream from the point opposite where they had left the sisters waiting. Having tied the horses to a tree trunk, the leader said to his companion: “The current is strong, but for now there's no real danger. Let's go straight back to the other bank to help the sisters cross the river on their horses.”

The man with the mule stayed on guard; the other two dived in. Reaching the other bank, they asked: “Who's going first?”

“I'll go,” answered Sr. A. Pasqualina, “but blindfold me, because the current makes me dizzy.” And blindfolded, clinging to the horse's neck, the sister went down into the water, and the two men swam alongside holding the animal by the reins. In midstream a tree trunk swept by very close to the group, and it was a real miracle that it did not knock them over. The blindfolded sister did not notice, but the provincial and Sr. A. Guida, standing on the bank, saw it in dismay.

“Will we both manage to cross the river before it's completely dark?” murmured the sister. “You'll go now,” said the provincial, “I'll wait and go last.” The sister protested: “No, you must go now.”

“The captain is the last to leave the ship,” quoted Sr. A. Camilla. She said it with a smile, but Sr. A. Guida heard a peremptory order in her tone and did not argue.

So the maneuver was repeated, but with greater difficulty. And when they had reached the bank with great effort, the men realized that it would be impossible to try to recross the river without certain danger of death for themselves and for the provincial. The sun had completely disappeared and it was beginning to rain.

Sr. A. Camilla was left alone. She looked with relief at the group of sisters and men gathered on the other bank and took comfort in seeing them safe. But what would become of her? She saw the water swirling more than ever, the rain growing heavier and darkness closing in. She saw the men, after an agitated talk with the sisters, making signs to her, pointing alternately at the water and at the land behind the bank. She saw the sisters making gestures of despair. In the failing light the provincial understood: she must withdraw inland, because there was also a danger that the swollen river might overflow the bank and carry away whatever it found, things and... people. But would she find shelter? By the flashes of lightning she saw the sisters weeping. She waited for another flash to wave reassuringly, and taking her horse by the bridle she set off inland.

Now she really was alone. “But St. Anne is with me,” she told herself, “and the sisters are safe. All is well.” As far as the darkness allowed, she could see no sign of life. Further on she came upon a small hill that could protect her if the river rose, and under its far slope she found a deep hollow, almost a cave. “Here is my cell,” she murmured; “here I shall spend the night, alone with my God.” She felt a deep peace.

For hours on end the rain poured down and the thunder roared. Rosary in hand, wrapped in her poncho, Sr. A. Camilla prayed. Between flashes of lightning she could see the horse, which almost by instinct had come close to her, and feeling its warm breath on her face now and then she thought of the Cave of Bethlehem and felt that the distance separating her, a human creature, from that poor four-legged beast was almost wiped out; both creatures of the good God, lashed by the elements in the horror of the night, they entrusted themselves to Him. Together.

But the night seemed endless. Only toward dawn, when a faint light spread from the east, did the rain begin to ease. Sr. A. Camilla tried to move, but she felt almost paralyzed by the cold in her limbs and the weight of her clothes, which were soaked in spite of the shelter of the cave. While her teeth chattered with cold, the horse splashed through the puddles in search of food and clear water.

Sr. A. Camilla sat down on a tree trunk. Suddenly she saw, still some way off, an Indian coming toward her. He was looking in surprise at the horse, which, being saddled, could not be a stray. But he was even more astonished when he saw the sister. “Who are you?” “I'm a sister.”

“Impossible. Sisters stay in the convent at night, not alone in a forest.” The provincial took off her sombrero and showed her veil and crucifix. The old man was even more scandalized: “It's not proper, you know, to be here alone at this hour. Not proper at all.”

“Now I'm going to get a sermon too, you'll see,” thought the sister, suppressing a smile. And she began patiently explaining to the Indian how and why she was there alone at that hour. But as she spoke she saw something like a light kindling in the man's eyes; all at once he took off his hat and, bowing his head, showed a scar: “Mamita, now I know who you are. You treated this wound for me, don't you remember? You, in the hospital at Sucre.”

Sr. A. Camilla tried hard to place that face among the many, many Indians treated, cared for and comforted at the hospital in Sucre.

“Now I'm a free man,” the Indian went on, “but then I was a slave, under a cruel master who beat me and broke my head because I was too weak for the work he forced on me. Now I'm poor, but I'm free,” he repeated with a glint of pride in his eyes, “and I'm alive because you treated me.”

Now the provincial remembered - not that particular man, but the sad procession of Indians who kept arriving at the hospital in the most pitiful condition. Treated like beasts of burden by cruel masters and savagely beaten, they took refuge in the hospital with broken bones and festering sores. Many died of gangrene.

“Now, in my hut, I have a son sick with smallpox. You would cure him for sure,” the man went on with simple trust, “but my hut is far away, and you have to cross the river, as you told me, to join your companions.”

“I don't even know when I'll be able to cross it, but I certainly can't go away from here; in fact I must go nearer the bank now so that they can see me when they come looking for me.”

“I'll go and see, and you can be sure I won't leave you as long as you need me.” He went off and disappeared behind the slope of the hill.

The sky was clearing, and the rising sun warmed Sr. A. Camilla's clothes, raising a haze of steam around her. She tried to get up, but her limbs felt weighed down by an overwhelming heaviness. Her arm, healed but still weak, ached. She waited a while longer, until the Indian reappeared: “Mamita, there are lots of people on the other side of the river, and there are two sisters crying.”

Now it seemed easier to get up and follow the man.

Safe

The evening before, the sisters and the arrieros had managed to reach a country house not far away, where they had been warmly welcomed. When the owner heard of the distressing situation in which they had had to leave the provincial, he at once saw to it that help would be ready by the following dawn. So at first light they had reached the bank: the sisters, the arrieros, the owner of the house and two skilled swimmers called in to help.

As the men had feared, the river had risen still further in the night, and the provincial meanwhile remained out of sight, sheltered by the sort of refuge where she had spent the night. The sisters were terrified: had she been caught and swept away by the water in the dark?

The sight of the Indian and his reassuring signs dispelled their fear; and when they saw the provincial walking with difficulty toward the bank, leading her horse, they burst into shouts of joy.

At once a scantily dressed man threw himself into the water. He swam vigorously with his right arm and held his left arm high, carrying a sort of little pot in his hand. Their hosts had thought of everything, even of a first meal, which Sr. A. Camilla certainly needed after her disastrous night.

But alas, when the swimmer reached her and, with a gesture of homage that had something chivalrous about it, held out the little pot, the provincial could see at the bottom nothing but a whitish mush in which floated a piece of meat soaked in mud. The splashing of the waves combined with the swimmer's vigorous strokes had done the damage. The man offered to swim back across the river to fetch more food, but the provincial, finding the strength to smile, held him back: “Never mind; it would arrive in the same state. Let's see instead whether it's possible to cross.”

But the flood did not go down. The sisters on the other bank made gestures of despair, while the Indian said gravely: “Mamita, if your brothers can't get you across the river until the water goes down, I'll build you a hut here and find you something to eat.”

The hours went by. Only in the early afternoon did the fury of the current and the amount of debris it carried begin to lessen. Sr. A. Camilla, exhausted, had leaned against a tree trunk and dozed off, though the stabbing pains in her arm were getting worse. The Indian, calm and solemn, watched over her.

Woken at last by the voices of the arrieros, who had managed to cross the river and were now standing beside her, deeply worried by her exhausted look, Sr. A. Camilla got up and, with a supreme effort of will, overcoming the weakness of her limbs and the pain in her arm, mounted her horse again and plunged into the river, supported by two men swimming at her side. She literally fell into the arms of the sisters, who welcomed her weeping and happy, while from the other bank the Indian waved his hat in farewell.

They at once gave her something to eat and drink, and all together they made for the hospitable house. A long, restoring sleep allowed everyone, and especially the provincial, to recover their strength, but it took some time more to set to rights clothes and baggage soaked with water and caked with mud. Their hosts lavished the most thoughtful attentions on them.

When everything was ready for departure, the gentleman said: “I thought it best to send a servant of mine ahead to President Pacheco's estate, which is a day's journey from here. Set your pace so as to arrive before evening. You will certainly find excellent hospitality there.”

And the Pacheco family's welcome was indeed most cordial. Besides the master and mistress of the house, the famous majordomo, sadly remembered for his inglorious adventures on the road to Oruro, put himself out so much that he showed himself in a much better light.

The way the sisters left the Pacheco estate was interesting and amusing. They had to cross a bend of the river that ran for some distance through the President's land. In the absence of a bridge he had had a contraption built rather like the one linking the ships with the port at Mollendo. Here too a large hand winch set in motion a pulley that ran along a long beam, from which hung an enormous basket that could hold two people at a time. And amid swaying and creaking the basket was gently set down on the opposite bank with its load.

The animals, on the other hand, led by an arriero, swam across.

With much waving from both banks of the river, the caravan formed up again and set off.

When they reached Sucre the sun was setting.

Warning Signs

November 1887.

Arriving in Tarija on one of her periodic visits, the provincial saw how violently political tension had broken out, even in the parts of the country farthest from the capital, as the presidential elections drew near.

Despite the period of calm that had marked President Pacheco's four years in office, or perhaps precisely because of it, his was now being called “el gobierno inútil,” the useless government, and the names on everyone's lips were those of Arce or Camacho, the opposing leaders of the moment. And the rivalries, the conflicting interests, the ambitions centered on these two men erupted everywhere in frequent and often bloody incidents.

The provincial herself had unwillingly witnessed one of these incidents, in which a young arriero utterly loyal to Doctor Arce had been the victim.

More than anyone, the sisters working in the hospitals had the sad opportunity of seeing, and in a sense paying for personally, the consequences of the fighting, which grew fiercer as election day approached. And if, out of gratitude, well-founded esteem and long friendship, the sisters could not help privately preferring Doctor Arce, their Christian spirit and their foreign origin enabled them to view the situation with calm objectivity and to stand realistically above the parties, whose opposing reasons they could sense. And their suffering was just as deep whenever, regardless of the victim's politics, they had to struggle hard to snatch from death or save from irreparable mutilation young men in their prime who, engaged in more peaceful and reasonable pursuits, could have brought far greater benefits to their country and to society.

Even among the girls and young women in the Colleges, belonging to families politically committed to one side or the other gave rise to displays of animosity and sudden quarrels which the sisters could only quiet with difficulty.

In May 1888 the elections were finally held, and Doctor Arce won them by a large majority. But peace did not come; on the contrary, the reaction broke out with such violence that civil war loomed, for the losing party showed no sign of accepting the fait accompli.

The Uprising Breaks Out

On September 8, according to a custom rooted in the religious spirit of the Bolivian people, the new President was to be officially installed in the Cathedral of Sucre. The ceremony was set for ten in the morning, and even before that hour the church was packed. But the Archbishop's procession - whose part, according to ceremonial, was to wait for the President at the church door and offer him holy water - arrived somewhat late and met the presidential procession in the square in front of the church, so that, as it happened, the two processions merged and Archbishop and President walked side by side to the entrance.

This unforeseen detail upset the plan of a group of soldiers who supported Camacho; they had agreed to take advantage of the moment when the President crossed the square to attack him and kill or kidnap him as circumstances allowed. The soldier who was to give the signal for the attack by firing a pistol shot hesitated when he saw the Archbishop beside the President, and did not fire. And while the ringleaders, themselves at a loss, were deciding what to do, Doctor Arce was already inside the church and the solemn Mass had begun.

The sergeants who were to direct the first operations argued; their annoyance, disappointment and uncertainty gradually turned to rage, and the men did not care whether passersby overheard them, so that even those who knew nothing of the plot could learn of it.

Among others a boy happens to pass by, late for the ceremony. He hears Doctor Arce's name mentioned and, since he is the son of one of the new president's followers and knows his father is in the church with him, he stops to listen.

“We can't put it off because of this stupid hitch,” says one of the conspirators.

“Let's wait for him when he comes out; we'll shoot him then, as we would have before,” says another.

“And what if he comes out with the Archbishop again?”

“Unlikely, and if he does, now that we're ready, we'll shoot anyway. We know how to use a pistol, don't we? We'll be careful to hit only him.”

“I'll fire first; it's my turn.”

“And if you miss, I'll be ready.”

“And me too,” adds another, “if need be.”

As the plans multiply, their voices rise too, and the boy has understood everything. He decides to run into the church to warn his father, so that the President, warned in turn, can take precautions. But as he is about to go, a soldier spots him:

“What are you doing here? Were you listening?”

“Me? I was passing by. I don't know anything.”

“I know you. Your father is one of Arce's spies.”

“I don't know anything!” The boy tries to wrench himself free, but others catch hold of him. One of the most hot-headed, without thinking, shoots him. The boy falls without a groan.

“You madman, what have you done?” shout the soldiers. But the fatal step has been taken. The waiting battalion takes the sudden shot as the signal for the revolt to begin, and the soldiers raise the war cry “¡Por Camacho!”, firing their rifles into the air.

The leaders in the square, also taken by surprise, see how hard it will be to hold back troops already out of control, while on the other hand they see it is impossible to organize a coordinated action on the spot. And in a vain attempt to bring some order to the squads they rush about giving and countermanding contradictory orders, adding to the confusion.

Suddenly the main door of the Cathedral, which had been barred from inside at the first sign of disorder, is flung open, and four canons in their sacred vestments slowly come forward, holding high a pole to which a white cloth is tied.

Sergeant Arana, who in the confusion following the shot has found himself in command, realizes it is time to negotiate and, approaching the group, asks: “What do the reverend gentlemen want?”

“Rather,” comes the reply, “what do you soldiers intend to do in this sacred precinct?”

“We don't want to harm anyone; we don't even want to enter the Church without your permission. Give us Arce and we'll go.”

The spokesman of the delegation suppresses a smile: “You cannot expect us to hand over to you with our own hands the lawful President of the Bolivian Republic. We ask you to clear the square so that the Archbishop and the faithful can leave and reach their homes unharmed.”

“We'll grant an hour's truce, on condition that you give us Arce.”

“I have said it is not for us to give him to you, just as unfortunately it is not in our power to prevent you from taking him if you can. We simply demand due respect for the place and the persons.”

An agreement is reached. The soldiers stand aside, but post a picket of four men outside each of the church's three doors to make sure, as the faithful leave, that the President is not among them, while undertaking not to harm a hair of anyone else's head, even of the opposing party. When the church is empty, if the president has not appeared, they may enter, unarmed and accompanied by the same committee of canons, to look for him and, if found, take him into custody. The soldiers accept this agreement rather naively, for they ought to realize how much time they are giving the president to get safely away.

And indeed, when they begin searching, rummaging in corners, looking inside the confessionals, climbing the bell tower and checking the roofs, they find no trace of the President.

Sergeant Arana Repents

Tired, sweaty and furious, going home to eat, Sergeant Arana tried to console himself: “We haven't found him, but we will. Meanwhile the revolt is under way.”

His wife greets him in tears. “What's the matter?”

“What's the matter,” she answers in exasperation, “is that you're a reckless, ungrateful brute.”

“But what's it got to do with you, woman?”

“What's it got to do with me? How can I not care, when you want to have the President killed, after all the good he has done my family?”

The sergeant, tired, says nothing, preferring silence to a furious quarrel. But his wife does not keep quiet, and she explains what her husband perhaps did not know, or knew only in part: her family, once in comfortable and respectable circumstances, had suffered a financial collapse years before, with serious consequences for its good name too. Doctor Arce had saved it by a generous intervention, enabling it to keep its dignity and face the future with confidence again.

“You brute, you knew all this; I'd told you. And now? If you had a conscience you'd save Arce from his enemies instead of joining them.”

The man says nothing, but he thinks. A certain uneasiness has arisen in him. He stays silent and frowning for a good while.

Suddenly: “I'm going out. I'll be back soon.” “Where are you going now?” “Don't worry, I'll be back soon.” He has made up his mind. He is almost sure of the inviolable place where the President must have taken refuge, and he heads for the Seminary. If he can, he will get him out of there and take him to his own house, where surely no one will think of looking for him, until he can get him out of Sucre safely.

The true claims of order and justice were making their way in him; after all, the President had been elected properly, so his authority was legitimate. The revolution was a reprisal without legal foundation, and all things considered... Camacho was no better than Arce.

In knocking at the well-guarded door of the Seminary the sergeant was not mistaken; as soon as he heard the first shots and guessed their cause, the President, guided by a priest, had left by the back door of the sacristy, which the rebels had not had time to guard, and taken refuge in the nearby Seminary.

Now the sergeant knocks, but the door does not open. Only after much knocking does a window open high up and a head cautiously peer out.

The soldier pleads: “Open up, please. I mean well, believe me.”

Believe him? Difficult and dangerous. No one answers, and the window closes noiselessly.

More knocking at the door; the window opens again. Inside they had held a council.

“What if this soldier really does mean well?” Such sudden changes of side, by individuals or groups, were not uncommon, after all. Why not try? Of course they would not show him the President, nor even confirm that he was in the Seminary; but letting him in with due precautions, since he was certainly alone, would cost nothing. Much might be lost, on the other hand, by refusing to receive him.

The door opens just a crack and a voice comes through: “What do you want?”

“You'll understand I can't talk like this from the street, and it's dangerous for me to hang about waiting. Let me in. I swear I mean well and I'll prove it to you.”

Very cautiously the door opens.

Brought before the Rector, the sergeant wastes no time: “I've come to free the President.”

Recovering from his first surprise, the Rector smiles ironically: “I know you. You're one of the leaders of the revolt. And you of all people have come to free the President of the Republic?”

Ignoring the irony, the soldier insists: “I assure you I have no other intention.”

“I can't believe it.”

The man decides to speak. He explains his state of mind and the reasons for his decision. But the priest hesitates; this conversion seems too sudden to him.

But the sergeant insists so much that in the end he decides to take him to the little cell, which Arce was pacing with long strides like a caged beast.

A heated duel of harsh, cutting words spoken in anger begins. But in the end Arana manages to get a calm hearing and sets out the plan he has meanwhile worked out. The President looks at him, astonished and unsure; but perhaps he can be trusted. He quickly weighs up the situation: he cannot stay a voluntary prisoner in the Seminary forever; a few days' complete absence from the political scene would be enough for his position as lawfully elected President to be irreparably and ingloriously compromised. Better to take the chance.

“I accept, though I don't rule out that you mean to kill me as soon as we're outside.”

The soldier draws his pistol and hands it to him: “When we're outside, if you feel I'm going to betray you, you can kill me.”

They exchange an eloquent look.

The preparations before leaving were long and laborious. While talking with the Rector the sergeant had looked him over carefully and had noticed that he had the same height and build as the President. Dressed as a friar, without his mustache and sideburns, wearing spectacles like the Rector's and with the hood over his head, the President would hardly be recognized in the dusk. All the more so since the streets would be almost deserted; for fear of the uprising people would stay shut up at home; and the fact of being in the sergeant's company would be enough to dispel any suspicion. The greatest danger came from the soldiers. But if necessary he would say that a friar called to attend a dying man, having to cross the city, had asked for his escort for protection. He was sure they would believe him, and in any case the risk had to be taken.

They went out. For a while they walked unhindered. Only when they met a patrol did he say loudly: “Father, don't be afraid, you're safe with me”; and he gave the soldiers a knowing nod. The inexpert slap of the false friar's sandals alternated more confidently with the sound of the soldier's boots.

They reached Arana's house. The President was able to eat and rest a little without trouble. Then, in the middle of the night, still accompanied by the sergeant, he went to two of his trusted supporters and made arrangements to reach “Villa Florida” by back roads and under good escort. From there they would leave for Oruro that same night. The plan for his comeback was already clear in his mind. If Camacho wanted war, war it would be.

On the Edge of the Uprising

The sisters and all the pupils of the College were supposed to attend the solemn Mass for President Arce's installation. But a series of mishaps had delayed them so much that in the end only two, Sr. A. Damiana and Sr. A. Guendalina, managed to be in the Cathedral, entering at the very moment the President did.

When they heard the shots inside the Church, the sisters looked at each other anxiously.

Could the sisters and girls be out in the street now?

No, it's late; let's hope they stayed at home.

But how can we warn them not to venture out?

When the Cathedral door was opened to let the group of canons through, on a sudden impulse they slipped out too and ran across the square, trying not to be noticed. And no one paid any attention to them, since everyone's eyes and attention were fixed on the unusual delegation.

Still running, the sisters reached the College door and knocked loudly: “Quick, open up, the revolution has broken out!”

But the sound of the shots had reached inside the College walls too, and it had not been hard to guess the cause. The reactions, however, were strange and contrasting: the sisters looked serious and worried, the girls cheerful and merry: “A revolution at last! We'll have some fun!”

A sister recently arrived from Italy stared aghast at the little rascals: “Whatever are you saying?!”

“Why, of course,” said one of the older girls, “it's been such a long time since there was a revolution. When I was little they had them often, and Mamma and I used to watch from the window.”

“Well, after all,” said another placidly, “what's so strange about it? It means they don't like this president and want to make another one.”

“Mother,” called the astonished sister, “just listen to how these girls talk.”

The Provincial smiled: “You're new here, and you're right to be surprised. But you must know that in these young republics there is still a great deal of political instability, so uprisings follow one another quickly and are sometimes quite violent, but usually short and without lasting consequences. Often it's the army that, because of its position in the country, feels it has the right and, as they see it, almost the duty to intervene by force to depose one president and put in another, whom they may depose themselves soon afterward. Besides, it isn't long since revolutions followed one another in quick succession in Italy too. Here, in the last four years, there has been an unusual calm that many didn't like, so much so that good Señor Pacheco's government was called ‘el gobierno inútil.’ It was to be expected that peace wouldn't last long. I'm sorry for Doctor Arce, who really does have the best intentions and could be a good ruler if they let him. And above all I'm sorry because there will inevitably be dead and wounded and ruined families, and a legacy of hatred hard to lay to rest. God grant it ends soon. Among other things, we can't rule out that we too may be targeted, since everyone knows we are under Doctor Arce's protection. But we are in God's hands, and for now there is nothing for us to do but pray and wait.”

Pray and wait. Night fell on the city but brought neither peace nor silence. Shots rang out in the streets around the College too, and threatening voices were heard: “¡Muera Arce! ¡Abajo las monjas! ¡Abajo las gringas!” (Death to Arce! Down with the nuns! Down with the foreign women!). But no one dared to molest the College directly.

In the morning the community met to discuss what to do. Fortunately, a few days earlier, in view of the rainy season, ample supplies had been laid in, and the pantry was well stocked. Daily bread would be easy to obtain, because their baker's oven backed onto the wall surrounding the College garden, and every evening a basket could be let down from the top of the wall without opening the door or leaving the house. For leaving the house was out of the question while the worst of the disorders lasted. They could only hope that the Chaplain would be able to come every morning.

The parents of some of the boarders, mostly from families opposed to Arce, came to take their daughters away, but most stayed in the College, where they knew they were well looked after. And the girls were delighted to stay in the city, eager as they were to “see the revolution.” This kind of self-imposed siege lasted more than a month. The girls alternated hours of study with lively recreation, and even put on impromptu plays that gave some relief to the sisters too, who, naturally more worried, wondered when this painful situation would end. At last the provincial, who was receiving accurate news from the Chaplain, became concerned for the sisters at the Hospital, by now exhausted by the intensity of their work, and decided to join them with some of the College sisters to relieve those who were most tired or might have fallen ill.

They went out one evening when a strange torpor seemed to hang over the city; no civilians to be seen, the shops shut; but shouts and shots in the distance were a reminder of reality.

They hurried through streets and squares without incident.

At the hospital the sisters knew not a minute's respite. The wounded and dying of both sides were brought in without pause, while nearly all the male nurses and many of the doctors had disappeared, either to join the rebels or for fear of compromising themselves. The sisters had to do the work of a hundred to replace those who were missing, shouldering every burden. And despite their tireless devotion, many of the wounded reached the hospital only to die.

One can imagine the joy and relief with which the arrival of the provincial and her sisters was greeted.

In the Thick of Civil War

Not all the government troops had joined the uprising at first. Real civil war broke out when the rebels, feeling betrayed by the artillery regiment - which by prior agreement should have mutinied on the morning of the President's installation but had done nothing - attacked it in reprisal in its own barracks. From there the revolt spread to the detachments outside Sucre, considerably strengthening Doctor Arce's enemies, who, now convinced that he had managed to leave the capital, set about spreading the revolution throughout the country.

The movement spread in sudden waves that raised hopes of a swift victory; but gradually its impetus began to slacken, chiefly because General Camacho, who was in La Paz, hesitated, although his supporters, the real authors of the revolt, called on him and urged him to seize the favorable moment.

A soldier by choice, perhaps his sense of discipline and legality struggled with his desire for political revenge, and he could not make up his mind to take the initiative, giving the impression of being incapable of firm and final decisions. This had a bad effect on the rebels' morale, while Doctor Arce, having joined the government troops that had remained loyal to him at Potosí, was marching to retake Sucre.

To increase his forces, which in truth were not large, Arce called up the National Guard, ordered the enlistment of volunteers, and by opening lines of credit at the banks and scattering gold with a lavish hand he fueled his propaganda.

He thus managed to form a fairly large but poorly armed army, while his enemies had arms and ammunition in plenty, since they could draw on the depots of Sucre and the nearby detachments. What they lacked, however, was unity and coherence of command, whereas Arce, turning himself into a military leader, organized his forces firmly, and when he felt sufficiently prepared he sent messengers to the enemy camp demanding their surrender.

The surrender was refused, but the bold, artfully made gesture gave the impression that the President could count on far larger forces than he actually had.

So, avoiding a head-on clash, the rebels moved slowly into position on the hills of Karikari, where they had the advantage over Arce's troops, who were lower down and easily exposed to heavy fire from the enemy artillery.

In an open battle the presidential army would certainly have had the worst of it.

The first day passed without action; but Arce's mind was not idle; aware of the danger, he took the necessary measures. As soon as night fell he silently moved his troops right up under the hills on whose summits the enemy was camped: that way the shots would fall on the plain and on the trenches hastily and badly dug in the previous days, but would not reach the men.

Events proved the President's plans sound: in the middle of the night the rebels unleashed a hellish barrage, sure of catching the enemy asleep. The well-prepared government troops did not return fire, giving the impression that they had already been wiped out, and the others gave vent to their misplaced enthusiasm by firing on and on, using up ammunition they thought they no longer needed. But at dawn, as they were preparing to overrun the enemy camp and plunder it, they saw the entire government army bearing down on them, now better armed than they were.

Surprise, confusion, unstoppable panic. The leaders, themselves stunned, try in vain to stem the flight. Hotly pursued by the government troops, the battalions break up and scatter in disorderly trickles. The President's victory had the further merit of making bloodless a battle that could have been a real slaughter; there was only one dead and a few wounded.

On reaching Sucre, Arce had the capital and its surroundings strongly garrisoned. But the war did not end. The rebels, fearing further reprisals, decided to stake everything. They tried to regroup and attacked again. The victors' reaction was then inevitably ferocious: the harsh repression filled the hospital once more with the wounded and dying.

And a few days later another scourge, more impartial but no less violent, struck as if to put an end to the fratricidal scourge of war: typhus.

From Hospital to Prison

Despite the epidemic, once order had been restored in the capital and relative calm in the other provinces, the President wanted to celebrate his victory according to State tradition: the religious ceremony so tragically interrupted the first time was to be held, and a splendid procession was organized, in which, this time, the sisters and the College pupils took part. There was a solemn Mass, the singing of the Te Deum, thunderous applause. But peace was still far off, and the sisters' hearts in particular were closed to joy.

The hospital wards were still full of wounded men arriving from the distant rear, and they were the most serious cases. Badly treated or treated too late because of the distances, battered by the long, hard journey, most of them died, while the victims of typhus were also dying without cease.

And typhus struck the sisters too: first one, then two, three; victims of contagion and of exhausting work that had worn down their bodies.

Meanwhile the days went by, and the President decided to return, with a visit to the hospital, the formal call the provincial and a small group of sisters had paid him at the seat of government.

Doctors, nurses and sisters received him, all lined up. But one could sense in the air a feeling of unease and almost of suppressed fear. Besides the wards for typhus patients, the infirmary was still full of men convalescing from war wounds, most of them from the rebel ranks; the President went through the wards more like a general reviewing his troops than a compassionate visitor to the suffering; and they in turn looked at him with resentment barely tempered by an equally evident fear. Some saluted, others did not. Only one, either because he was truly repentant or because he was more frightened than the rest, tried to free himself from his crutches to throw himself at his feet, weeping and begging forgiveness. The President stopped for a moment as if taken aback; then, with a frown only slightly less stern, he said: “God has punished you enough already,” and walked on.

Sr. A. Damiana, who was anxiously following the scene, noticed that the President's face had softened somewhat, and she started. “Perhaps... who knows!”

The condition of the sisters with typhus grew worse: the first died, others fell ill, and given how little help was available there seemed no hope of saving any of them.

With the deaths from typhus the number of patients fell, but those who had survived their wounds went to fill the prisons. And the prison became a hospital, because the convalescents, crammed into unhealthy, overcrowded quarters, grew worse again. And the doctors did not come: those loyal to the President, so as not to compromise themselves; the others, because they had vanished from Sucre. Besides, it was known that the Court Martial would soon sit to try the rebel soldiers, and no one had any illusions about the prisoners' fate.
