So why prolong lives that human justice was about to cut short anyway?

From the hospital the sisters knew the sad condition of the prisoners they had already treated, and it grieved them deeply. In the end they decided to make an attempt on their behalf and spoke of it to the provincial. With her agreement they asked for an audience with the Prefect of the Province.

The Prefect hesitated: what could he do, if the doctors were deliberately keeping out of sight?

“If the doctors aren't there, allow us to go and care for them in the prison. These are men who were our patients, whom we know and who know us; it would simply be continuing the care already given in the hospital to people who are still sick.”

“The situation is delicate, you must understand; I can't decide on my own. I want to consult the President.”

Permission was granted at once.

A Bold Request

And a period of new and harsh sacrifices began. Typhus had decimated the sisters, and the survivors still had a great deal of work at the hospital. But they found the time and strength to go to the prison every day with baskets of bandages, cotton wool and medicines and to lavish on the prisoners the most loving care, although they felt themselves received with icy suspicion.

“Why do you come, mamita?” one would say. “Don't you know they'll kill us anyway?” Slowly the sisters watched those men grow brutalized under the crushing sense of death near and inescapable.

“It's Arce who sends you, isn't it?” another would say bitterly. “He has us treated because he wants the satisfaction of killing us himself!”

The sisters felt like weeping. “It is God, my Father and yours, who sends me, to remind you that you are his son, that you must hope and trust in him.”

“Hope for what? Will he save me from the bullets of Arce's thugs?”

“Pray, my sons! While there's life there's hope!”

But their hearts remained closed, poisoned by a despair that bred fresh hatred.

The sisters suffered no less when they came in contact with the prisoners' families, to whom they longed to give comfort and hope. But how?

Sr. A. Damiana could not rest. She prayed and thought. The situation really did seem hopeless, but the sister had not forgotten the slight change she had noticed on the President's face the day he visited the Hospital. No, she would not give up hope. But they had to act before it was too late.

“God's will be done,” she said to herself one day, “but the provincial must help me.”

Sr. A. Camilla too was very saddened, and she listened attentively.

“My dear sister, do you realize what you want to ask the President? Nothing less than to release the rebels?!”

“We know the President well; deep down he's a good man. He's a good Christian. He can't hate. And he mustn't forget that in his hour of danger he was saved by a man who had already declared himself his enemy. He must give back what he has received.”

The provincial finally agreed. “We'll go together, and may God help us!”

At the sisters' bold request the President flared up. But trying to suppress his indignation, he listed the arguments against granting it: the prestige of the State, respect for justice, the guarantee of national security... But the two sisters, once launched, had no intention of giving way either. To the socio-political arguments they opposed others of a human, religious and even sentimental kind: magnanimity is the finest quality in a statesman; for a Christian, forgiveness is a duty; and then, why plunge so many poor families into mourning, make so many poor innocent orphans...

With the debate conducted on two such different planes, agreement was truly difficult. And the exchange, more a tussle than a real discussion, was long and exhausting for both sides. Until, perhaps caught in a moment of weariness, the President came down from the level of principle to that of expediency and let slip: “But what would I look like?”

Was this the first crack? Sr. A. Damiana did not let it pass: “But we're not asking you to send them home free! We only ask that they not be condemned to death.”

And constitutional law came back into play: “It's the Court Martial that decides; not even the President can interfere with the judiciary.”

“But the Constitution gives you the power to pardon a man condemned to death!”

“Granted, but in an isolated and well-justified case. Not for a group, and against the security of the State.”

“Well, haven't several been executed already? Isn't that example enough for the security of the State?” objected the provincial.

“And besides...” put in Sr. A. Damiana, this time untimely, “can your deeply Christian conscience, without real misgiving, send to their deaths so many wretched men poisoned by hatred, perhaps incapable of repentance?”

The provincial nudged her with her elbow. Appealing to the salvation of souls was all very well; but harping on hatred in front of the very man who was its object!

The President appeared not to notice.

“To pardon them all,” he went on, “would be a blunder harmful to general discipline and therefore to the good of the nation.”

“Doing good for its own sake,” ventured the provincial, “has never harmed anyone.”

“And my personal prestige?”

“Apart from the merit you would gain before God, your personal prestige would gain too; you would show your spirit to be superior to that of your opponents.”

By now weariness was setting the pace of thrust and parry; in the end the President promised that he would try to use not his authority but his personal influence, unofficially, with the Court Martial, so that the death penalty would not be applied to the prisoners still awaiting trial.

A week later two sisters burst joyfully into the prison to give the good news: no death sentences; hard labor for all.

After a moment of incredulous surprise the prisoners' closed faces opened into a more human expression. The certainty that their lives were saved made the hard punishment awaiting them seem less hard.

And a few days later a long line of men, escorted by armed soldiers, was sent off toward deserted mountains, to heavy labor in the mines. Toward a wild, exhausting existence full of dangers, far from their families. But it was life all the same. And then... who knows!

A Slow and Contested Recovery

In the city life was slowly returning to its normal rhythm, but in the hospital lives were still ebbing away. One after another, five sisters had died, and many patients.

For the surviving sisters there was one consolation: the knowledge of good done unstintingly and without seeking official recognition. But that was not lacking either: public recognition by the Authorities and the applause of the townspeople were followed by the tangible gift of a country house near the city, placed at the sisters' disposal so that they could take turns to rest properly before overwork and the privations they had suffered claimed more victims among them.

The holiday, which restored their bodies somewhat, was followed by a course of Spiritual Exercises that gave back strength and serenity to spirits troubled by the sad experience of such cruel rivalries and every kind of misery.

In the country, however, there was still no peace: disappointed ambitions, damaged interests and wounded pride fed grudges that were hard to lay to rest.

As soon as he took office the President would have liked to launch the policy of moral renewal and civic progress he had always dreamed of; but the opposition gave him no respite and forced him into empty disputes over delaying proposals, when there were not fresh attempts at rebellion that had to be crushed with renewed harsh repression. And the hospitals were never empty, and the prisons stayed crowded.

Sr. A. Guendalina, now superior of the hospital, with Sr. A. Damiana and the other sisters, had to intervene again, not always successfully, to save men newly condemned to death. So much so that the President, half joking, came to say: “When I decide to visit the hospital, I must first make sure there are no condemned men to pardon.”

And he kept to that resolve.

The Long Reach of Hatred

Though President Arce's iron hand had put down the civil war, the guerrilla war of resentment, suspicion, prejudice and slander did not die out; it was now turned, in an underhand but no less effective way, against all the President's supporters, and it did not fail to reach the sisters - especially the provincial, who because of her office was the most exposed.

Perhaps, outside Sucre, even some sister unwisely gave credence to it; and the echo, distorted as always in the worst sense, reached Rome and painfully wounded Mother Rosa.

The Mother would have liked to hurry to America to see for herself the truth of the situation and of the insinuations, but apart from her always frail health, it was clear that she could hardly leave Italy for a long period without regrettable consequences.

With great sorrow she decided to summon Sr. A. Camilla to Rome, asking her to accompany personally a group of sisters whom she had arranged to bring home, in order to replace them with stronger and fresher forces.

The unexpected summons, at an extremely delicate moment in the life of the various Bolivian communities, astonished and alarmed the provincial. But once the first inevitable moment of surprise and worry had passed, the spirit prevailed: if the Mother thought she should go to Italy, she would obey.

This time, however, she did not think it wise to inform Doctor Arce. He might easily guess the reason for the recall and take drastic action. She asked the Archbishop's advice, and he encouraged her: “I think your going to Italy is a good thing; the misunderstandings probably caused by malicious reports can be cleared up more easily, so that afterward everyone can work in peace. And you will do well to leave without telling anyone; once out of the country you can inform those concerned. Meanwhile you could prepare the sisters better by organizing a course of Spiritual Exercises.”

Since the sisters to be sent home nearly all belonged to the communities in Sucre and were indeed those most tried by the events of the past year, Sr. A. Camilla could easily give reasonable grounds for the series of transfers. And while she arranged for replacements for the sisters who would be leaving, she released the latter and sent them to rest for a short while at the country house the Municipality had placed at their disposal.

It could not be helped that a course of Spiritual Exercises held at an unusual time of year aroused suspicion that something unexpected was afoot, but those who took part benefited from it all the same. And when the time came to leave, the departing sisters' sorrow was softened by learning that the provincial would accompany them a good part of the way, perhaps as far as Tupiza. The others, knowing nothing, remained at peace.

Retracing the Road

They set out at dawn on a clear September day with a touch of spring chill in the air. They would retrace the road the provincial had traveled on the first expedition led by Doctor Arce.

Familiar roads, a monotonous repetition of long days on horseback over mountains and valleys. Prayer, and silence.

Memory kept them company. For the future, only vague expectations. But what a wealth of memories to relive, in the peace of good work done! And the sadness of parting was softened by their now habitual surrender to God, who is a loving Father. Sr. A. Camilla kept a deeper suffering locked within her, faced with events that seemed to her ever less clear and humanly questionable.

The sisters' questions interrupted the course of her thoughts a little, but uncalled-for, the painful question kept returning: “Why go back to Italy now? Must I really leave this beloved land forever?!”

One day, to satisfy the sisters' curiosity and lighten the rather gloomy atmosphere, she agreed to tell a legend that arose in the days when the Spaniards were searching relentlessly for silver in the Potosí massif: the legend of the llama that discovered silver in that area and led others to discover it.

“It's one of the legends that circulate among the people,” said Sr. A. Camilla. “One of many, for the details change not only with the places where they arose but with the imagination of the storytellers. I'll tell it to you as it was told to me.”

“It seems that the Spaniards, though they knew that silver was hidden in the soil of Bolivia too, did not know that the Potosí area was particularly rich in it.

In that countryside there lived at the time a gentle, good and very poor Indian. He lived alone, his only companion and wealth a pure white llama that was utterly devoted to him. When the Indian had nothing at all to eat he would send the llama up the great mountain that towers over the place, while he went looking for work with the Spaniards, who exploited and ill-treated him but in the end gave him something to eat. In the evening he would go back to the mountain and find the llama waiting for him in front of his hut. The animal had grazed what grass it could find and brought its hard, dry roots to its master, who used them to light his fire for the night in front of the hut.

One day, when the Spaniards had given him less to eat and ill-treated him more, the Indian came back to his hut tired and dejected, but did not find the llama. He began searching for it in the gullies and on the crags under the clearest moonlight, until he saw something white in the distance.

It was the llama, which seemed to be waiting for him, motionless, at that very spot. The Indian went up to it and noticed that the animal had in its mouth a tuft of grass pulled from the ground but not chewed; he took it and examined it. It looked like the usual grass, but clinging to its roots was a strange grayish earth, different from what could be seen on the summit, and which the man had never seen before.

He went back down to the hut with the llama and the tuft of grass, which the next day he showed to the Spaniards. They turned pale and rushed at him. But the one who seemed to be their leader gave his companions a knowing sign and took the tuft in his hand with an air of indifference: ‘Where did you find this?’

‘My llama found it while grazing on the mountain, señor.’

‘Worthless dirt,’ said the other indifferently, ‘but the grass may be good grazing for our horses. You'll take us to see the place, understood?’

‘Yes, señor.’

The next day the Spaniards climbed the mountain led by the Indian and the llama. At a certain point they started: the silver seemed to be cropping out at the surface. After examining the place at leisure, the leader asked the Indian: ‘From here, where does Potosí lie?’

The man turned to point out the exact direction with outstretched arm, and fell to the ground, stabbed between the shoulders. None of the other men made a sound. Only the llama let out a long moan and fled far away. No one ever saw it again.

Weeks and months went by, and those men, who had kept their discovery secret, grew extraordinarily rich. The silver seemed endless. But the treacherous leader was still not satisfied; he wanted to get richer and richer, even at his companions' expense. And one night of full moon he went back alone to the mountain to dig and dig. He was wholly absorbed in his feverish work when the llama appeared on a hilltop. It came down slowly, as if wrapped in a ghostly halo. When the Spaniard noticed it and found himself stared at by two fixed, glowing eyes, he was afraid. He wanted to shout to drive the animal away, but his voice died in his throat. He dropped his digging tools and reached for his dagger. The llama kept coming.

The man began to back away, staring as if hypnotized into those two relentless eyes. And the llama kept coming. With a superhuman effort the Spaniard hurled his dagger into the middle of its chest; the weapon struck home, but the llama kept on coming and the man kept backing away, until he reached the edge of a precipice he had not been able to see and plunged over it with a terrible scream. Only then did the llama's eyes go out. It gave a moan and collapsed on the ground, while a thread of blood streaked the barren rocks.”

So ended the tale that had held the sisters spellbound. The comments that followed made the journey less monotonous for a good while.

And at last they completed the endless crossing of southern Bolivia. More freezing nights in the open, more tiring marches in the heat of sunny afternoons. For some days Sr. A. Camilla had felt unwell, which she put down to fatigue. At a certain point she could fool herself no longer. She was really ill. But she knew she could not give in: “I can't fall ill, here of all places and at this moment. I must master myself.”

A short stop at Tarija for a brief visit to the community and a few days' rest. Then Tupiza, the last house of the Daughters of St. Anne in Bolivia before the Argentine border. At Tupiza she shut herself in her room and wrote to the Bolivian Authorities to inform them of her departure for Italy, and a circular letter to all the sisters.

Deliberately brief, and marked by religious serenity. A farewell that might sound final, but did not say so and did not let her inner suffering show.

Only to the superior at Tupiza did she confide that she had reason to believe her return home was final, asking her to reveal it to the sisters only after she had left. But great was the surprise of the sisters traveling with her when, on leaving Tupiza, they realized that the provincial was still coming with them.

“Beyond Tupiza too, Provincial?”

“Yes, my daughters, I'm still coming with you.”

A spontaneous burst of joy, but then at once...

“Provincial, we're at the border now. Your company is a great joy to us, but how will you get back?”

She felt the moment had come; she stopped her mule and, pale, looked at the sisters, who had also stopped: “Sisters, forgive me for telling you only now; I too have orders to go to Rome.”

She spoke naturally, as if giving a piece of routine news. “Let's go on, then,” she continued; “we're about to enter Argentina, but Italy is still a long way off.” She paused: “And I don't feel very well.”

The sisters' sorrowful, eloquent silence answered her. Only their eyes spoke. They reached La Quiaca as the sun set over the vast distance of the Andes. There was the lonely little church, greeted with joy on a day now long ago as a sign of Christ's blessing welcome on the threshold of their new life. On the other side, the Argentine border.

Farewell, Bolivia!

The Spirit Is Willing, but the Flesh Is Weak

They went down toward Jujuy in a new frame of mind. But each kept her thoughts to herself.

More days and nights among forests and ravines. The sisters could see that Sr. A. Camilla was really ill. Fever had seized her, and try as she might it was clear she could hardly stay in the saddle. And Salta was still far away. One of the men kept constantly at her side to support her at least on the most difficult stretches. At last they were near Salta. For the night they found shelter in a modest village, but none of them slept. To their troubled thoughts was added worry about the sick woman's condition. The next morning they entered the city. They left the horses at a stable and asked a little girl who was passing where they could find a house of women religious. Fortunately she herself attended the school attached to the “Santa Rosa” Institute and showed them the way.

It was a local Congregation of Tertiaries, who welcomed the sisters with fraternal charity. The patient was put to bed at once. And the false energy that had kept her going until then gave way. It was clear they could not set off again until she recovered. Fortunately a good doctor was found who correctly diagnosed her illness and gave the necessary treatment. So in a few days the acute phase was over, but it took almost a month for the patient to regain enough strength to resume the journey.

Fortunately the journey from Salta to Tucumán was made by train. The new, shining train was a pleasant novelty for the sisters, until the rhythmic jolting of the carriages and the unchanging monotony of the arid, deserted pampa brought back, with weariness, their melancholy.

But now the vegetation reappeared; here was Córdoba. How many memories for Sr. A. Camilla! Retracing the stages of the first journey in reverse, she felt ever more keenly the painful sense of something precious lost: the joyful eagerness, the enthusiasm for a life that promised to be full of difficulties, certainly, but thrilling in its promise of good achievements. And now? She was still young. Life was beginning to pulse impatiently in her veins again after her recent illness. And was it to end like this? Why?

“Lord, give me the strength to suffer in silence. To suffer and forgive. Let someone go on weaving lies in the shadows. But let me not lose the Mother's affection, the only good I care for on earth. And yet... Lord, let it be as you will. I trust in You.”

Her will regained control over her human feelings. She had to master herself. To conquer herself: that was the true victory.

“Farewell, Bolivia! Farewell, America! God is in Italy as he is here and everywhere. And he is with me, always.”

Rosario de Santa Fe. No longer Bolivia, and not yet Italy. General weariness. But the provincial seems to have found her smile again and cheers them all up. Meanwhile the villages grow closer together and more frequent, the vegetation richer, people and herds more numerous.

Here are the outlying suburbs: Buenos Aires.

In Buenos Aires the sisters waited eight days for the departure of the steamer for Italy, the fine, modern “Nord America.” A crowd of passengers. The group of sisters joined it and was lost in it. A moment of sharper pain for all of them as they looked from the deck at the immensity of the continent they were about to leave. Perhaps forever. But already the voice of Italy was speaking deep in their hearts, already their homeland felt nearer. Montevideo. Rio de Janeiro. The Brazilian coast too receded, its outline growing ever more blurred.

At last there was only the ocean.

In Rome

What did mother and daughter say to each other in that first meeting, perhaps dramatic, certainly painful, all the more so because of the great affection that bound them?

Did God perhaps allow a veil to fall for a moment over those eyes, so skilled at reading the hearts of her daughters?

Did he perhaps allow a whirlpool of bitter waters to sweep over, for a moment, the heart of the daughter who had not trembled before the menacing eddies of the flooded river or the raging ocean?

And perhaps far away, beyond the ocean, someone was meanwhile tasting the bitter flavor of a petty, short-lived victory; petty and short-lived because the good seed would bear its good fruit all the same, and the weeds would inevitably rot.

It is not given to us to know what really passed between mother and daughter; but from the little experience of God's ways that he grants to anyone who tries to enter into them under his gaze, we may sense that, if the meeting was painful at first, it did not fail to bear fruits of goodness and joy.

In her humbly docile daughter the Mother could see more clearly than ever what a precious instrument the Lord was forging for the good of the Institute in the not distant future; and the daughter, bowing her head to the mysterious will of the Father, who incomprehensibly was tearing her away from furrows already made fruitful with tears and sweat, must have heard ring out, clear and gentle, deep in her heart, the word of the Master: “Blessed will you be when they utter every kind of evil against you falsely on my account... Blessed are you!”

And the little hospital of Noci, in Apulia, became Sr. A. Camilla's new mission field. Other sick people awaited her, other wounds, other sorrows, other miseries. There is no crossroads where suffering does not pitch its tent.

But the golden thread of affection, gratitude and friendship that would bind her forever to Bolivia did not break. And news, happy and sad, often reached her in the little faraway hospital.

The sisters wrote: the situation in the country was still tense and unsettled, the guerrilla fighting was turning into open war, work and troubles gave no respite.

A newspaper arrived from Chile: Valparaíso. A short headline over a long column of news: “The Wreck of the Cotopaxi in the Strait of Magellan.” The ship was lost, but fortunately crew and passengers were saved.

A sudden wave of memories, a fleeting shadow of nostalgia: so the Cotopaxi too is gone!

But life went on, under the gaze of God.

In Bolivia too life went on, but always turbulent and uncertain. After two years of government conducted with extreme vigor, President Arce believed he could relax the severity and return to normal. The emergency laws were repealed, political prisoners regained their freedom and exiles returned home.

But the opposition did not lay down its arms; the reforms in favor of the people disturbed too much the lazy selfishness of a powerful class of so-called liberal Freemasons. And General Camacho, constantly urged to revolt, now decided to act openly, using different tactics from those of 1888. He therefore began the movement in the outlying regions, intending to converge on the center and attack the Government in the capital itself.

The President, however, though he had shown himself willing to soften the severity of repression, had no intention of letting himself be easily deposed. Placing himself once more at the head of the government army, he first defeated the rebels attacking from the north and then turned his forces east and south. But he could not prevent a rebel detachment from carrying the fighting into the capital itself, and there was hard fighting in the streets. The government forces won again, but the victims on both sides were many and the repression harsher still.

The hospital filled with wounded once more, so many that there were not enough beds and soldiers had to be laid on the floor along the corridors. The sisters gave up their beds to the most serious cases and, as in the days of their crossing of the Cordillera, made do with lying on the floor for their few hours of rest. But feelings ran so high that patients from the rebel ranks turned even on the sisters who were nursing them, going so far as to threaten them with death along with President Arce.

And the President was tired. So many unforeseen struggles, futile in their ferocity and harmful to the nation, disappointed and deeply troubled him. This was not the government of peace and progress he had dreamed of. He had set out to prevent anarchy on one side and despotism on the other, and instead he had earned the title of “Tyrant of La Florida.”

He did not resign, as his opponents would have liked. In the brief periods of truce he expanded and improved public services, drew up the plan for the first railway, and reorganized the army; but all amid ceaseless opposition and bitterness.

At the end of his very painful years in office, disillusioned, ill and financially ruined, he retired to his country house and gave up political life for good.

From the depths of the Apulian province Sr. A. Camilla followed events and reflected.

Was President Arce a loser?

A defeated man?

No, his had not been a barren dream that vanished into nothing. There remained a purpose entrusted to a future perhaps not far off, a goal that must be reached.

His intellectual and moral superiority had made him a forerunner; but the times were not ripe for the realization of his ideals. Yet the essential soundness of his aims and efforts made him stand out all the same above the fearful selfishness of his opponents. History would do him justice.

Just as gold acquires its natural luster only in the crucible, so on the path of great souls an apparent defeat is almost inevitable, but it serves to reveal true worth - sometimes to themselves, sometimes to others, and certainly to posterity.

For the victory of truth over falsehood, of good over evil, is certain and inescapable. Only... it is not given to the clocks of men to mark its hour in advance; that is fixed solely on the sundial of God.

The “seven years” of Sr. A. Camilla Valentini certainly do not mark the end of the adventure of the Daughters of St. Anne in Bolivia.

It did not end for its protagonist, who, continuing to serve other brothers and sisters with unchanged, humble devotion in a small, obscure provincial hospital, went on fertilizing, less visibly but perhaps more effectively, the furrow she had plowed with hard-won daring in that distant land. And some years later, called to work beside Mother Rosa as General Assistant, and finally Superior General herself, she certainly never turned her mind and heart away from that land and that people, for whom she had spent a good part of her youthful strength and of her rare gifts of organization.

Nor did it end for the sisters who remained in Bolivia, as year after year others came to join them and give themselves with them to their Bolivian brothers and sisters, whose sorrows and hopes they learned to share, taking up the legacy left by Provincial Camilla; a legacy made not only of roses but also of sharp thorns.

For the history of the missions of the Daughters of St. Anne in Bolivia, while it has recorded pages of almost triumphal approval, has also written - and these are perhaps the more numerous - pages of sacrifice and renunciation.

The Municipal Councils of the Bolivian cities, knowing the dedication and efficiency of the Daughters of St. Anne, vied with one another to have them where there was suffering; but there was also the spiteful opposition of members of the liberal-Masonic parties, who out of sectarian spirit hindered the sisters' work, so much so that in quite a few cases they were forced to abandon works they had already been called to found and had built up with so much sacrifice.

So at the beginning of 1890 they had to give up the management of the hospital in Sucre - where, among other things, there were those who had still not forgiven the energetic and rather brisk way in which Sr. A. Camilla had brought order and discipline into it - and almost at the same time they had to leave the College as well, because the obstructionist maneuvers of some prevented approval of the teaching staff lists and so prevented the school from running. In this case, however, the parents reacted vigorously; considering the sisters' educational work irreplaceable and indispensable, they promptly set up a new private College and entrusted it to them. And in 1894 the protests of the whole population forced the Government to call the sisters back to the old College too and to draw up a new contract with them.

Made a “sign of contradiction,” as is inevitable for anyone who puts himself unreservedly at the service of man in the footsteps of Christ, the sisters, with the humble meekness proper to the Institute's spirituality, took up their place again in the College; what is more, since other sisters had arrived from Italy, among them one with a kindergarten teacher's diploma, the first “Kindergarten” in Bolivia was opened in Sucre that year.

In 1892 the Daughters of St. Anne accepted the invitation of the Bishop of Santa Cruz to open a College in that city. Adapting to the great hardships of that tropical climate and to the extreme poverty of the premises, they gradually managed, with the help of benefactors, to turn the wretched building into a dignified setting enhanced by a fine Chapel. Later, when Sr. A. Camilla Valentini was Superior General, they also took over the management of the hospital in the same city.

In 1894, among the nineteen sisters who left Italy for Bolivia, those assigned to Tupiza not only repeated but in a sense outdid the... misadventures of the journeys of the “seven years”: like those before them they arrived by mule, but with only one arriero as guide, and so poorly equipped that they had to go entirely without food for the last two days of the journey. On arrival they found a dark pavilion lacking every necessity, even drinking water, which they had to fetch from the river. And since the sick lay on the ground on sodden mats, after the day's work the sisters spent part of the night carding wool or other material to make mattresses. For themselves, the sisters received five mattresses from the Municipality only five months after their arrival. But in 1906 construction of the new hospital began.

Even greater hardships were suffered by the sisters charged with opening the school, so much so that the provincial of the time ordered them to leave Tupiza and withdraw to Tarija. But the people would not let the sisters leave, and a mine owner, Don Avelino Aramayo, decided to give the community a modest monthly allowance on which, together with gifts in kind from the people, the sisters were able to live. Then in 1910, through the generosity of Don Manuel Torres, a suitable building could be put up and a boarding school established, in addition to the school of music and embroidery.

So, year after year, while some work had to be given up, others grew and new ones were born: hospitals, colleges, orphanages, poorhouses...

At Corocoro, a mining area 5,000 meters up, in 1895 the sisters opened a school, El Carmel, for the elementary education of working-class girls; in the evening they taught catechism to the young women who worked in the mines by day; a fruitful activity which in 1899 had to be interrupted because of the federal revolution.

In Cochabamba in 1910 a poorhouse was opened and entrusted to the Daughters of St. Anne, where not only elderly invalids but also and above all the deaf and mute, the mentally handicapped, the paralyzed and epileptics found care, affection and protection.

In June 1923 the landowner Don Louis Soux, who had come from France in 1879 with Doctor Aniceto Arce, anticipating modern social welfare works, founded at his own expense in Potosí a sanatorium for the care and treatment of the employees and workers of his mines, but also open to the public. It was entrusted to the Daughters of St. Anne, who extended their care and moral support to the miners' families until 1950, when, the silver industry having declined, the Sanatorium could no longer support itself and the sisters had to give up a work that had proved most beneficial to a class of people so much in need of understanding, affection and gentleness.

In La Paz, the sisters' first field of work, where two of them died of infection a few days after arriving and another before the end of the same year, the two old buildings were abandoned and the whole health institution was brought together in a single complex in the Miraflores district, where the sisters too had the advantage of being able to live as one community.

In Cochabamba, in more recent and more advanced times, the Daughters of St. Anne, who had gone abroad to obtain the necessary specialization, were entrusted with some departments of the Institute of Audiology for the treatment and rehabilitation of the deaf and mute. The sisters stayed there eight years and then handed over to lay people able to run the work efficiently.

These are only some of the milestones of the first decades of the journey of the Daughters of St. Anne in Bolivia. A journey now more than a century long, marked by countless hardships and sacrifices, but always sustained by the unshakable will to help open to the Bolivian nation the paths of human advancement and civic progress, in the light of faith in God and with respect for the fundamental rights of man, of every human being.

Present on the battlefields whenever there was need, to help and care for the wounded even at the cost of their own lives, the Daughters of St. Anne took part, and today more than ever take part, in the peaceful battles waged by the Church of Christ for an authentically evangelical presence and witness, even when a firm stand in favor of the poor and the weak may arouse suspicion and provoke a reaction from those who, on the ambiguous pretext of protecting national security, try to block the way toward true renewal.

For it must be acknowledged that, unfortunately, despite the efforts of honest and courageous men, the work of the Church and the activity of the religious now numerous in Bolivia, the Nation has not yet achieved full development and progress for every section of the population, nor has it been able to give itself laws guaranteeing all citizens equal rights and the enjoyment of the inalienable goods of freedom and justice.

The decisive event of the Second Vatican Council, followed by the Special Chapter and the choices our Congregation made as a result; the strong calls of Medellín and Puebla; the clear and courageous directives of the Supreme Pontiffs and of the Church's Hierarchy: all this led the Daughters of St. Anne in Bolivia to question themselves deeply about the truest meaning of their presence in that Land and among that people. And the answer, consistent and categorical, was the one it had to be: to go resolutely to the poorest and most dispossessed.

An obvious but demanding choice: many superstructures imposed by now outdated historical and social conditions had to be dismantled and, at the cost of a reasonable scaling back of many traditional works, mission bases had to be created in places not yet reached by the work of human advancement and evangelization.

No small effort, made joyful by the awareness of a more authentic return to Mother Rosa's original choices and to the work of the first missionary sisters in Bolivia; an awareness that gave vigorous impetus toward an ever wider outreach.

To leave the cities by preference, then, and go to the scattered “campesinos” of the high plateau, to help them recover the awareness of their dignity as free men, children of God redeemed by Christ, and with it the essential values of their original identity, unjustly trampled in the days of the arbitrary “discovery” of their land, which the “discoverers” turned into the rapacious and senseless destruction of an age-old civilization whose excavated remains still fill the world with wonder.

It is a missionary program aimed at concrete evangelization, but resting on a firm foundation of human justice: on the sense of justice deeply rooted in the conscience of the Daughters of St. Anne of Bolivia.

Nor is there any distinction in this between the sisters of Italian origin, now naturally a minority because of the natural process of change and growth over time, and those born in Bolivia, who represent the unbroken continuity of a line of daughters of that Land who from the very first years after the arrival of the Daughters of St. Anne joined them, fully sharing their ideals and their generous dedication.

A shared commitment to justice that seeks to proclaim the Truth, driven by a renewed longing to live and to communicate Life. Proof of this is the fact that what was, in missionary terms, Mother Rosa's first-born Province has opened the second century of its fervent existence by itself becoming missionary toward other Lands, a proclamation of justice and Truth to other brothers and sisters. Today, in Mexico, the presence of Daughters of St. Anne who came from Bolivia bears witness that, if the first seed came from Italy, made fruitful by Mother Rosa's prayers and by the heroism of the pioneers she sent, the soil that received it was excellent, and, blessed by the Lord, it has borne and continues to bear abundant fruit for the spread of the Kingdom.
